routes.description: Climb a loose rock rib from the Rudolf Glacier (avoiding a small icecliff near the top) to reach a snow basin. Staying clear of an icecliff near the peak, head up to the Main Divide between Mt Frederick Gardiner and Mt Aurora (as for route 5.13 on topo), and head north to the summit.

routes.name: Original Route
routes.description: A small snow peak climbed via the north-east Main Divide ridge, or via the northern snow slopes from Franz Josef Névé.

routes.name: West Face
routes.description: A four-pitch route has been climbed on this small face, but details are unknown.

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Mt Aylmer
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: Mt Aylmer from above the Murchison Glacier, September 2013

routes.name: West Ridge
routes.description: From ‘Aylmer Col’ (between Mt Aylmer and Hochstetter Dome), ascend the exposed ridgeline, surmounting a small rock step partway along.
routes.ascent: Barbara Dennistoun, Jim Dennistoun, George Dennistoun, Ada Julius, Jack Clarke, December 1910

routes.name: South West Face
routes.description: From the Tasman Névé or Tasman Saddle, ascend snow and ice slopes up to 40 degrees. An excellent area for practicing snow and ice skills.

routes.name: South Ridge
routes.description: From the Tasman névé or Tasman Saddle, ascend snow and ice slopes up to 40 degrees. An excellent area for practicing snow and ice skills.

routes.name: Archbishop of Canterbury
routes.description: Climbs the moderately steep ice line up the centre of the face, with some mixed steps near the top. These upper pitches could be all rock or all ice, depending on the season. The first ascentionists completed seven pitches to gain the east ridge just down from the summit. Traverse over the summit and descend to Tasman Saddle.

routes.name: North East Ridge
routes.description: Gain the ridge from the Murchison névé via steep snow slopes near Graceful Peak, or traverse over Graceful Peak. Very loose rock has been reported on this route.

routes.name: From Christopher Col
routes.description: Traverse the divide ridge from the col to reach the peak.
routes.ascent: Archie Scott, Graham Riley, Christopher Johnson, December 1935

routes.name: West Ridge
routes.description: Pick a line from the upper Bannie Glacier, depending on crevasse conditions. The rock on the ridge is loose.

routes.name: South Ridge
routes.description: Pick a line from the upper Bannie Glacier, depending on crevasse conditions. The rock on the ridge is loose.

routes.name: East Face
routes.description: Start south of the face, traverse up the full length of a snow ramp, and then head up mixed snow and rock past a prominent large block. It would be awful in summer when more rock is exposed.

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Mt Brunner
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: Mt Sefton and Main Divide from Welcome Pass, January 2010

routes.name: West Face
routes.description: From the high basin beneath Brunner and Stephen, traverse left beneath the rock wall of the south face of Brunner and climb one pitch to reach the summit snowfields. Depending on the season, the pitch can consist of rock, snow, ice, or a combination.
routes.ascent: Bill Beavan, Don Beavan, John Gummer, Murray Spencer, Earle Riddiford, December 1946

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Mt Burns
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: Barron Saddle, Barron Saddle Hut and the upper Mueller Glacier, December 2013

routes.name: South West Ridge
routes.description: From the Welchman Glacier, gain the ridge about 300–400m north of Watch Tower via a short face climb. The upper ridge is complicated by slanting rock. The rock steps are best turned on the slabby western face. The eastern side tends to be rotten.
routes.ascent: Tom Barcham, Ash Cunningham, Alec Witten-Hannah, December 1952

routes.name: South Face
routes.description: From the Welchman Glacier, ascend the obvious ramp that angles from left to right directly under the summit. Finish up the rock rib to the summit. Another rock rib further right has also been used.

routes.name: Bernard Col Route
routes.description:
From the Welchman Glacier, gain the Main Divide at Bernard Col or one of the options further north (crux, technical grade 4). Then either follow the Main Divide to the summit, or drop down onto the western slopes and climb the top of the north–west ridge. The technical grade is from Bernard Col.
This is probably the most straightforward descent route from Burns but usually requires three abseils to get from the Main Divide to the Welchman Glacier. Down the Poet Glacier to Rubicon Torrent is less technical, but puts you in a very remote location.

routes.name: McKerrow Face
routes.description: Beginning from the McKerrow Glacier, ascend the gully at BY15 570 533, climb out to the left onto easier ground and then crampon up the north face directly to the summit. Glacial recession may mean a little more determination is needed to get through the first few hundred metres off the deck.
routes.ascent: Bill Beaven, Norm Hardie, C J Macfarlane, Earle Riddiford, January 1948

routes.name: West Ridge
routes.description: Gain height from the Landsborough River on easy ground. The serrations of the ridge crest are then turned by making a 20m abseil onto snow slopes on the north side. Sidle below the serrations, then regain the ridge and head for the summit.

routes.name: Poet Glacier Route
routes.description: Climb through the slabs at BY15 553 516 and then negotiate the Poet Glacier to the summit.

routes.name: South Ridge
routes.description: From the Tasman Glacier, ascend the south ridge up a snow and rock ridge until a broad plateau. From here ascend either to the summit directly, or gain the Main Divide ridge south-west of the summit.
routes.ascent: Peter Graham, Claude Macdonald, Jim Murphy, February 1909

routes.name: North East Ridge
routes.description: From Climbers Col, follow the Main Divide on a mixed snow and rock ridge of varying quality. Traverse any difficulties on the west.
routes.ascent: Graham McCallum, Pat Barcham, Phillip Gardiner, Bruce Waterhouse, December 1954

routes.name: From the Edwards Glacier
routes.description: From the Times Glacier, gain the Edwards névé. The north side of the Edwards névé feeds two small icefalls, which in turn feed two parallel couloirs that fall to the true left edge of the Times Glacier. Ascend the eastern couloir using rock on the climber’s left where crevasses dictate. From the névé follow a prominent couloir onto the Main Divide to reach a small rock peak well south of Climbers Col. Follow the Main Divide south to Coronet.
routes.ascent: Dave Bamford, Peter Fullerton, George Kendall, John Nankervis, January 1978

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Mt Dampier Rakiroa
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: New Zealand's third highest peak, and the second highest point on the Main Divide.

routes.name: West Ridge (Hicks–Dampier Traverse)
routes.description:
Traverse from Mt Hicks via the ridge, avoiding two prominent towers on whichever side is best in the prevailing conditions. Then go up the ridge to a schrund. From here continue up steep snow, through rocks, to the summit. It is also possible to cross the north face to the north ridge and then up to the summit.
The true summit may be harder to attain than how it appears in the literature (personal observation, Peter Dickson circa 1987).
routes.ascent: Syd Brookes, Jack Cox, Marjorie Edgar-Jones, January 1938

routes.name: Hicks–Dampier Couloir
routes.description: From the Sheila Glacier, ascend the right diagonal couloir onto the upper Hicks–Dampier ridge. Two thirds up the couloir it is possible to break left and follow an ice slope to the ridgeline that leads to Hicks.

routes.name: Fantini Dignan
routes.description: Follow ice gullies left of the Māori Route to ultimately arrive on the Hicks–Dampier Ridge. This route is mostly out of the icecliff fall-line.

routes.name: Māori Route
routes.description: Ascend the gully in the centre of the face and connect with a snow ramp leading left. Then climb steep ice on the left edge of the icecliff to gain the upper west ridge.

routes.name: Barcham Waterhouse
routes.description: Climb towards Green Saddle, but before the saddle is reached traverse left above the icecliffs to reach the top of the west ridge.

routes.name: South Ridge
routes.description: From Green Saddle, follow a ridge of rotten rock to the summit (good snow cover would help here). See also the East Face route. A variant on the Hooker side involves moving left before reaching Green Saddle and into a narrow ice couloir which leads to the upper south ridge. First ascent from the Hooker Glacier is unknown.

routes.name: South Ridge
routes.description: Gained from the upper Linda Glacier either via the snowslope to Green Saddle or up a rib on the right. Thence up a steep rotten ridge. This route is possibly the best descent route off Mt Dampier.
routes.ascent: Freda Du Faur, Peter Graham, C Milne, March 1912

routes.name: East Face
routes.description:
From the Linda Glacier it is possible to head up various routes on sound rock to arrive either on the South Ridge or near the summit.
There are no recorded ascents of gully routes on the left side of the face, or any routes at all on the right side of the face.
routes.ascent: Syd Brookes, Jack Cox, Marjorie Edgar-Jones, January 1938

routes.name: North Ridge via Mt Vancouver
routes.description: From the summit of Mt Vancouver, follow the ridge to a prominent rock step, which can be climbed via a hidden gully on the eastern side. Climbers wishing to avoid this ridge can traverse across the north face to the Hicks–Dampier Ridge. See Route 13.21.

routes.name: North West Flank
routes.description: Start up the avalanche chute to the right of Vancouver’s West Buttress, trending right to gain the left edge of a large diamond buttress of rock. Climb up to gain a snow rib above the buttress, then traverse right, to gain the large snow apron surrounding the summit block of Dampier. The easiest route from here moves right to gain the Hicks-Dampier Ridge, which is followed up steep snow to the summit. Alternatively, head left to gain the north ridge, which involves rock slabs then a sharp ridge to reach the summit. The easiest descent route from Dampier lies down into the Grand Plateau via the south ridge (Route 4.33).
routes.ascent: Bruce Graham, Gordon Hasell, Tom Nuttall, January 1957

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Mt Elie de Beaumont
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: Mt Green, Mt Walter and Elie de Beaumont, December 2010

routes.name: Anna Glacier Route
routes.description:
‘Elie’ is the throne that elegantly resides over the cluster of peaks at the head of the Tasman. Whether on skis or on foot, it is an entertaining outing, which culminates in a ballroom-sized summit plateau.
Head up the Anna Glacier (which is frequently complicated by crevasses) usually keeping close under Mt Walter. Then ascend slopes onto the col between Mt Walter and Mt Elie de Beaumont (the Elie-Walter col). Follow a snow ridge, which is often interspersed with firm, blue ice sections from the col up to the summit.
Alternatively, from the lower glacier, continue weaving directly up through the glacier if crevasses allow. From here the summit can be reached from either ridgeline.
If the lower Anna is cut off, ascend to Divers Col, traverse over Mt Walter and descend to the Elie-Walter col – a much more serious proposition (see Routes 5.37 and 5.42).

routes.name: South East Ridge
routes.description: From Lendenfeld Saddle climb the sharp and undulating ridge onto the upper Anna Plateau and on to the summit. This would be an interesting way to climb Elie when there’s plenty of snow to cover the rotten rock.
routes.ascent: Mavis Davidson, Rod Hewitt, Priestley Thomson, January 1954

routes.name: Whymper Spur
routes.description: From the Whymper Glacier, ascend the prominent spur leading onto the upper part of the Maximilian Ridge. The spur becomes steeper and more difficult towards the top, and the rock is not particularly good. The first ascent was done in deep soft snow.

routes.name: Maximilian Ridge
routes.description:
History, a spectacular position, and a feeling of commitment make this a special route. From the Burton Glacier, gain the ridge via a couloir south of Roderick Peak. Bypass the pinnacles on the lower ridge by using the névé of the Burton Glacier, then head up over a prominent step, along a level section, and up 190m of mixed ground to the Anna Plateau under the summit.
The first ascent party approached the ridge from the Tasman Glacier via Tasman Saddle, Whymper Saddle, and Callery Saddle, and descended to the Elie-Walter Col. Half the party then traversed Walter to walk out via the Tasman Glacier, while the other two members descended to the Times and Spencer Glaciers and returned to the Burton to retrieve a fifth party member, Bill Beavan (who had waited in camp with chicken pox). That group then walked out via the Tatare Route.
routes.ascent: Ed Cotter, Ed Hillary, George Lowe, Earle Riddiford, January 1951

routes.name: Maximilian Ridge Direct
routes.description: From the Burton Glacier, gain the ridge via a couloir south of Roderick Peak, and stick to the crest the entire way instead of using the Burton névé to avoid obstacles.
routes.ascent: Dave Bamford, Richard Hancock, John Nankervis, Grant Stotter, 1977

routes.name: Burton Spur
routes.description: From the lower Burton Glacier, gain the Maximilian Ridge via a couloir south of Roderick Peak and sidle into the upper névé of the Burton Glacier. Ascend left onto the crest of the spur. Mixed climbing leads onto an arête and snow slopes leading to the summit.
routes.ascent: Dave Bamford, Kevin Boekholt, Russell Braddock, John Nankervis, February 1984

routes.name: Carroll-Strong Route
routes.description: Head up the avalanche chute to the left of the Central Spur, then move left onto a snow and rock rib, which turns into an ice arête before reaching the crux icecliffs. These may vary from season to season. Finish between the west and main peaks.

routes.name: Central Spur
routes.description: An elegant and classic route. Gain the foot of the spur from the left via a couple of tricky rock pitches. Steep rock scrambling and moderately steep snow lead to the upper icecliffs, which usually provide a difficult crux. Continue on to the main summit.
routes.ascent: Bryan Pooley, Rob Rainsbury, John Stanton, John Visser, December 1972

routes.name: Right Flank
routes.description: Climb up the broad face onto the lower shoulder of Mt Elie de Beaumont, on the ridge above the Elie-Walter col. In winter this is an all-snow route. In summer, the lower section of the climb is on rock, which may be more difficult.
routes.ascent: Warrick Anderson, Wilfrid Lammerink, Paul Scaife, June 1974

pitches.description: Experienced mountaineers may attempt ascents of other peaks in the region including Elie de Beaumont (3109m). From the huts, traverse underneath the west shoulder of Hochstetter Dome and turn north into the upper Anna Glacier. There are often large crevasses on the Anna Glacier, and at times it may be impassable. It is best to scope out the glacier conditions from the summit of Hochstetter Dome the day before, to get some idea of the conditions. Beware also of possible ice avalanches from Mt Walter. Most skiers leave their skis on the south west shoulder of Elie, but under ideal conditions it is possible to ski off the summit. Advanced ski terrain. 6-10 hours return.

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Mt Elie De Beaumont West Pk
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: North Ridge and Burton Ridge of Mt Elie de Beaumont, January 2015

routes.name: Traverse from Main Peak
routes.description: A highly recommended and exhilarating addition to climbing the main summit of Mt Elie de Beaumont. From the main summit, descend and head west along a sharp, very exposed, undulating arête, traversing around a number of gendarmes, usually on the south side, before reaching the West Peak. One of the few early routes whose first ascent was in winter.

routes.name: North Ridge
routes.description:
The north ridge is gained via the Johannes Glacier, which is best reached from the lower Burton via a stream bed and couloir on the true left of the tip of the Johannes Glacier. Get to the true right side of the Johannes névé at about 2380m and ascend the rock ridge to Pt 2724m (six pitches of good red rock).
Now cross the base of a prominent spur between the north and Burton Ridges into a snow couloir, which re-joins the north ridge just below the summit. The upper couloir is frequently cut-off after midsummer.
routes.ascent: D A Carty, Jack Cox, G Somerville, December 1936

routes.name: North Ridge Direct
routes.description:
Gain the ridge via the Johannes Glacier, which is best reached from the lower Burton via a stream bed and couloir on the true left of the tip of the Johannes Glacier. Get to the true right side of the Johannes névé at about 2380m and ascend the rock ridge to Pt 2724m (six pitches of good red rock).
Now continue straight up steep snow then left onto the rock ridge which is followed for several pitches to the summit.
routes.ascent: Dave Bamford, Peter Fullerton, George Kendall, John Nankervis, February 1978

routes.name: Burton Ridge
routes.description:
A special climb. Approach this ridge either from the access route between the lower Spencer and lower Burton Glaciers, or from the lower Burton via a stream bed and couloir on the true left of the tip of the Johannes Glacier.
The first ascent party departed the Burton Ridge at about 2700m and followed snow leads out onto the great slab above the Montague Glacier, and then ascended the final 100m of the Montague Spur. The slab is completely covered in snow in early summer and completely bare by late summer – expect anything if you’re there in December-January. Most parties have descended the same way, but it could also be possible to descend back to the Times Glacier via the Elie-Walter Col, depending on the season.
January 1963, P Duncan, H Fairburn, H Gifford, J H Leonard, D Medland, Bev Price and I Simpson used the Montague Glacier to gain the upper Johannes Glacier and the upper Burton Ridge.
routes.ascent: D E Cooper, D R Lowe, J H Leonard, M Lucas, R Watts, December 1959

routes.name: Montague Spur
routes.description: A striking line. Gain the ridge separating the upper Times and Montague Glaciers (good bivouac sites here), head up the edge of the Montague Névé, and onto the right edge of the great slab dropping from the West Peak. Continue straight up to West Peak or, depending on the season, use steep snow to the left before moving right again onto the rib near the top. The best conditions occur when crevasse conditions allow for an easy approach and when the route is dry to allow pleasant rock climbing – possibly a rare combination.

routes.name: North East Ridge
routes.description: Climb to Twain Col, either from the east or the west, then follow the Main Divide over loose rock. The first ascent was from the east.

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Mt Frederick Gardiner
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: The Main Divide south of Graham Saddle, from De La Beche Ridge, September 2016

routes.name: South East Rib
routes.description: Climb a loose rock rib from the Rudolf Glacier (avoiding a small icecliff near the top) to reach a snow basin. Staying clear of an icecliff near the peak, head up to the Main Divide between Mt Frederick Gardiner and Mt Aurora. The final ridge to the summit is steep and loose.

routes.name: Divide Ridges
routes.description: From either the north (i) or south (ii), Frederick Gardiner is mostly straightforward with steeper scrambling towards the summit.
routes.ascent: Katie Gardiner, Jack Pope, probably in the early 1930s

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Mt Gold Smith
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: Named after Eric Charles Gold Smith, a surveyor, who in 1906 became Chief Surveyor and Commissioner of Crown Lands for Canterbury. Mt Gold Smith is unclimbed directly from the Haupapa Tasman Glacier.

routes.name: Via Main Divide from Mt Coronet
routes.description: Traverse the Main Divide from Mt Coronet.
routes.ascent: Harry Ayres, Mick Bowie, F F Simmons, January 1938

routes.name: Corry Glacier Route
routes.description: From the Geikie Glacier, traverse across two rock spurs running down from the Minarets to a snow basin (the Corry Glacier), and then climb onto the Main Divide and along the ridge to the summit.

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Mt Graham
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: Mt Graham to Mt Tasman

routes.name: Divide Ridges

pitches.description: A straightforward climb from either Mt Teichelmann or Silberhorn.

routes.description: A straightforward climb from either Mt Teichelmann or Silberhorn. An excellent viewpoint.

routes.name: Graham Spur

pitches.description: Gain the base of the spur from the true left of the Linda Glacier (the route may change owing to glacier movements). Then head up the spur until 100m below the top, where the route moves right up the final steep 50m of ice onto the ridge just north of the summit. This route has been used to access the Balfour Glacier from the Grand Plateau.

routes.ascent: Paul Bieleski, A W Bowden, V R McGregor, Richard Tornquist, Dec 1962.

routes.name: From the Balfour Glacier.
routes.description: A straightforward snow climb, but like Silberhorn it can be very icy in winter. Watch for shrunds and icecliffs near the bottom

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Mt Green
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: Mt Green, Mt Walter and Elie de Beaumont, December 2010

routes.name: South West Ridge
routes.description: A varied and enjoyable climb, best enjoyed on a sunny day in early summer. From Climbers Col, climb the first rock step direct, then follow a horizontal arête and up the second step to where the ridge flattens. Then up a blocky ridge to the summit.
routes.ascent: Mavis Davidson, Rod Hewitt, Priestley Thomson, December 1953 (descended)

routes.name: Little South Face
routes.description: From the basin below Climbers Col, take the gully in the centre of the face and then, depending on the condition of the upper face, join either the South West Ridge or South Buttress.

routes.name: South Buttress
routes.description: From the basin below Climbers Col head right and gain the prominent rib. Move up steep loose rock until some grey slabs (the Cod Piece) are met halfway up. Then continue up steep loose ground onto the upper part of the South West Ridge.
routes.ascent: Ian Cave, Mike Gill, John Nichols, February 1960

routes.name: Left Hand Trinity
routes.description: Take the obvious deep-cut couloir on the left hand side of the big south face. First climbed in seven pitches, with occasional 80-degree sections. The couloir tops out on the South West Ridge three or four pitches from the summit.

routes.name: Chocolate Cake
routes.description:
Climbed during a lean snow season on mainly snice with a little bit of rock/water ice.
An engaging climb from start to finish. 250m of technical climbing + 100m of steep snow.
The crux second pitch (WI4+) goes directly up a smear of steep ice - an amazing pitch of alpine climbing.
Approached via Divers Col route. Descent down this via Greens east face.

routes.name: East Face
routes.description: From the plateau below Divers Col, climb a sustained 40 degree snowslope up the east face where schrunds allow. This or the North East Ridge offer the best descent from Mt Green. First ascent unknown.

routes.name: North East Ridge
routes.description: From Divers Col, ascend mixed snow and rock on the Main Divide.
routes.ascent: Alex Graham, Peter Graham, Ebenezer Teichelmann, F W Vollmann, February 1909

routes.name: The Pink Route
routes.description: From the slopes leading down from Divers Col to the Spencer Glacier, ascend the rock face leading directly to the summit. Ten pitches.

routes.name: North West Ridge
routes.description: The north side of the Edwards Névé feeds two small icefalls, which in turn feed two parallel couloirs that fall to the true left edge of the Times Glacier. To reach the Edwards Névé from the Times Glacier, ascend the eastern couloir using rock on the climber’s left where crevasses dictate. From the névé, head left onto the ridge, and follow snow slopes and rock ribs to the summit. The ridge could also be gained from the Stevenson Glacier.
routes.ascent: D A Carty, L J Dumbleton, J D Willis, D J Stanton, January 1938

routes.name: Eaton's run
routes.description:
Access to this west face route is via an excellent gully from the upper Stevenson Glacier. From the upper Edwards Neve climb through rock band on the left of the face to the steep snowfield. Then tend right on the snowfield to the base of the rock of the South West ridge.
Climb into the obvious break and leading right at first will eventually bring you to the upper section of the South West ridge and on to the summit.
routes.ascent: Greg Duley, Emil Hansen, Don French,  31 January 2021

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Mt Haast (High Peak)
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: The three peaks of Mt Haast are actually just off the Main Divide, at the head of the Fox Glacier.

routes.name: South Face (Plateau Face)

pitches.description:
There was a large rockfall from the Haast-Dixon Ridge and the face below in January 2013. This doesn’t appear to have affected any recorded routes on Mt Haast or Mt Dixon, but the area is likely to be unstable for a while.
At least three variations exist on the Plateau Face of Mt Haast, all commencing from the névé between Syme Ridge and Mt Dixon. Climb 400m of steepish ice and then, depending on conditions and inclination, head:
(i) left through the ice bulge,
(ii) directly up through the icecliff, or
(iii) right via ice gullies through a rock band.

routes.ascent: Mike Andrews, Colin Dodge, D Warren, Jan 1972.

pitches.description: From the summit of Mt Dixon follow the rotten rock ridge over towers, usually turning difficulties on the east side.

places.name: East Face
places.description: The spurs on the east face of Mt Haast have been numbered from 1 to 5, starting at Pioneer Pass and heading right. There are no recorded ascents of Spur 1 and Spur 3.

routes.name: Authors' Route
routes.description: Ascend the prominent couloir between Spur 1 and Spur 2, beginning about 150m west of the crest of Pioneer Pass, reaching the Main Divide about 100m east of where the Haast massif abuts it. Traverse the ridge to the summit (refer to Route 11.110).
routes.ascent: Mavis Davidson, Rod Hewitt, AF Reid, Jan 1955.

routes.name: Spur 2
routes.description: Gained from a quarter of the way up Route 11.79, and leads directly to High Peak. The climbing is fairly steep without being technical. The rock is sound to begin with and very shattered towards the top.

routes.name: Goulstone-Rockell Gully
routes.description: Ascend the next obvious gully right of Spur 2, then up mixed ground to the left of the upper gully to finish near the summit.

routes.name: Hotline

pitches.description: Free climbed first 100m on first ascent.
Left through mixed terrain to gain steep ice at obvious gully. Belay on right to avoid hang fire.
Steepening ice with M4+ move to exit and belay
Up steep snow/ ice trending left to prominent spur

Up steeping snow/ ice ramp trending right until it steepens and deal to the short vertical and overhanging rock/rime/ ice bulges. Relents to find a good rock bollard belay on spur. Beware loose rock through steep section.
Follow Spur/ ridgeline until it steepens and overhangs. Step left and downclimb or rappel 3-4m
Follow exit gully to reach ridgeline. First ascent party continued to summit of High Peak via the complementary mixed ground (70m) facing north, at approx M4.

routes.description:
On the East Face of Mt Haast, start right of the triangle (Little Big Wall). Best climbed after a good freeze and/ or a cycle of melting to get rid of any hang fire or loose wet avalanche danger. This is a steep solar aspect getting sun for most of the day, hence the name 'Hotline'.
This route is as close to spur 3 (as per 2018 guidebook) as possible and is situated between route 11.81 and 11.83.

routes.name: From High Peak

pitches.description: An exposed scramble over loose rock that can be complicated by icy conditions.

routes.ascent: Frank Alack, H K Douglas, Jan 1936.

routes.name: 3/4 Couloir
routes.description: The prominent couloir on the East Face between Spur 3 and Spur 4, to the left of the Middle Peak, has been used for ascent and descent. The route comes out 80m east of the Middle Peak.
routes.ascent: Mike Rockell, Michael Venz, plus party of three, August 1979

routes.name: Vanilla Ice

pitches.description: Beautiful WI4 pitch.

routes.description: Follow up obvious ice line on the East Face, then up gully to mixed terrain to summit.

routes.name: Spur 4 (North East Ridge)
routes.description: A direct climb up a series of steps on the rib to reach Middle Peak. The lower and middle sections of the rib are somewhat loose. Crux pitches of grade 12 but nowhere very difficult unless iced up.
routes.ascent: Austin Brookes, Peter Moore, John Trotter, Jan 1973

pitches.description: Ascend from the upper Marcel Glacier via a snow couloir.

routes.name: Psychoterratica

pitches.description: A fantastic, fun line, with many styles packed into a small space. Transitions from steep ice through to a chockstone/ chimney, finishing on some steep, mix terrain....and an easy summit ridge line to the top.

routes.ascent: Josef Král, Jake Gray, Gavin Lang 24 Sept 2022

places.name: Mt Haast North Pk
places.description: This is predominantly a rock peak with plenty of scope for new variations. The North Peak of Haast has been incorrectly known for a long time as the West Peak of Mt Haast. The three peaks of Haast run perpendicular to the Main Divide, and most people assume the Main Divide runs north to south. Not always...

routes.name: Traverse of the three peaks (‘Haast GT’)
routes.description: This route involves one of the North Peak ascent routes and then traverses the Middle and High Peaks. A pleasant climb made quite committing because of its length. The rock near the Middle and High Peaks is loose. A classic traverse, first completed without crampons.

routes.name: Spur 5 (North East Rib )
routes.description: 500m of climbing on four rock buttresses with linking snow ridges to reach a gap south of North Peak. The lower buttress is comprised of solid rock, the second is steep rotten rock, and the remainder good rock.
routes.ascent: Austin Brookes, Bruce Farmer, Ralph Miller, Jan 1978.

pitches.description: Ascend the ice gully beneath North Peak with a rock crux (15/16) at two-thirds height. The top section is on generally poor rock. It has been climbed in winter as a mixed route.

routes.name: Natural Gas
routes.description: Starts left of the large corner on the left side of the North East Spur. Up the face on ice leads until steep mixed ground is encountered. The first ascentionists abandoned the climb here by traversing to the North East Spur; the route is awaiting a finish to the North Peak. The routeis best climbed when the face is heavily rimed. Choose a not too hot day, as the face gets a lot of sun and the rime ice can fall down. Dave’s comment on the route was ‘harder than the Central Gully on Douglas.’ Named after the LPG gas heater flown in to Pioneer Hut for the trip.
routes.ascent: Rich Turner, Allan Uren, Dave Vass, Aug 2002

pitches.description: A face route that starts between the Atkinson-Hall and North Spur routes. From the bottom, move gradually left until the North East Spur route is visible, then move right over chossy ground. Continue straight up, climbing 20m of superb exposed slab en route, to join the North East Spur route where it flattens, and then continue to the summit. Red rock provides cruxes of 16/17 and good protection.

routes.name: North East Spur
routes.description: Starts just right of Nash-Aimer. Traverse right across a ledge low on the spur and then ascend the rib until the large gully on the right meets the top of the rib. Climb up the ridge crest on good rock. A recommended variation at 2/3 height is to climb the face on the right, on excellent rock. Higher up, the ridge flattens out before rising again to the summit. Descended by the same route. Historically referred to as the West Ridge.
routes.ascent: Harry Ayres, Geoff Harrow, Alan Rattray, Apr 1952

pitches.description: Ascend the prominent couloir to the right of the North East Spur. At the top of the couloir, turn left to join the North East Spur route.

routes.name: North Ridge
routes.description: Ascend the rib to the right of the North East Couloir to gain the ridge proper, continue toa prominent gendarme (the top of Sun Circle), which can be turned on the north or traversed, and then up the face where the North East Spur joins the ridge, to the summit.

pitches.description:
Amongst the ramparts of Mt Haast, a stellar 60m pinnacle.
Good pro small to med wires & cams.

routes.name: Forgotten Corner
routes.description: Climb a prominent corner to the right of Eurostar for three pitches of good rock, and then seven pitches on deteriorating quality rock (crux 16), to reach the gendarme of Sun Circle. Abseil the face to the climber’s right of Sun Circle.

routes.name: Sun Circle
routes.description: Climbs the left edge of a large slab just up and right from Eurostar, to the left of a large gully. The route begins from a block of rock adjacent to where a schrund usually forms. Six pitches of steep climbing (crux 17) on some quality rock up to the top of a prominent gendarme. Abseil directly back down the face.

routes.name: Golden Eye
routes.description: A route to the right of Sun Circle, effectively following the abseil line. 5 Pitches.

routes.name: North Couloir

pitches.description: A small couloir separating the north-west extremities of the ridge

routes.description: A small couloir separating the extremities of the ridge, eventually leading to the North Ridge.
routes.ascent: E R B Graham and D J Heraud, Feb 1957

routes.name: North West Toe
routes.description: A good alternative start to the North Ridge. Access the spur from the left and scramble up to join Route 11.92.

places.name: Marcel Face
places.description: The western aspect of Mt Haast offers a good range of gullies that are usually well iced through to December. There have been several harder routes put up on the Marcel side since the 1970s, but only some have been recorded.

routes.name: Left Gully
routes.description: The obvious gully leading to the left hand notch on the skyline.

routes.name: Swimming with Sharks Direct
routes.description: The left-most and more direct of two ice runnels that lead to the right hand notch on the skyline. Similar climbing to Swimming with Sharks.

routes.name: Swimming with Sharks
routes.description: Takes the right-most of two ice runnels that lead to the right hand notch on the skyline. Generally thin ice requiring short ice screws. First ascended in eight pitches. The first ascentionists traversed the ridge to the North-Middle Peak col, but abseiling the route is recommended.

routes.name: Talula Does The Hula From Hawaii
routes.description: Five pitches of enjoyable ice climbing interspersed with some tricky mixed climbing.

routes.name: Supergroove
routes.description: A short but technically difficult route (crux M6) with a bit of everything. Ice, a strenuous chimney, a free hanging pillar, and a sting at the end.

routes.name: North-Middle Peak Col

pitches.description: Ascend from the Marcel Glacier onto the Marcel Face. up steep snow into the righthand of two narrow couloirs leading to the col. Then on up the main ridge to the summit.

routes.description: Ascend from the Marcel Glacier up steep snow into the right hand of two narrow couloirs leading to the col, and then on up the main ridge to the summit.
routes.ascent: Phil Houghton, David Herron, Fred Page, Richard Tornquist, Jan 1959.

routes.name: Middle Peak- High Peak Col
routes.description: Ascend from the upper Marcel Glacier via a snow couloir.

routes.name: Mutley's Revenge
routes.description: Start just right of the Citizen Chowdhury ramp via a short but steep pitch on an ice hose, then ease back to a couple of straight-forward pitches on steepish snow, heading straight for the summit. The fourth pitch climbs through short but steeper ice steps, then the fifth pitch climbs a steep snow gully to top out just west of the High Peak. The first ascentionists descended via the same route with five 50m abseils.

pitches.description: Start below high peak but trend right arriving about 50m east of the High Peak summit.  Involves several short but steep steps. Five pitches.

This five pitch route takes a prominent narrow gully almost directly below the high peak. The crux is at the bottom. The gully tops out between high peak and the next obvious prominence to the ). Descend to Marcel col. Cammell/Monteith climbed a steeper 3 pitch variation to left.

routes.name: Holloway-Thompson
routes.description: Begin up Route 11.109, and then up the steep cascade on the left to gain a hanging gully. From there, climb three 60m pitches directly to the south summit.

routes.name: Right Gully

pitches.description: Gully between high peak and divide peak.

routes.description:
Gully between high peak and Main Divide knob.
Don Bogie, Peter Sommerville, Jun 1979
routes.ascent: Mike Andrews, Doug Warren, Colin Dodge, Dec 1972.

routes.name: South West Ridge
routes.description: From Marcel Col, follow an easy snow ridge leading north-east off the Main Divide, and along a slightly tricky rock ridge to the summit. A regular descent route. Despite the easy access, watch for loose rock late in summer.

routes.name: Original Route
routes.description: Climb the ridge immediately north of the Haast Glacier, overcoming a final large bump to reach the Upper Kaufmann Glacier. From here the route heads up the snowface onto the South Ridge.

routes.name: White Steel
routes.description: Climbs the left ‘fang’ of ice on the right side of east face: a 4-pitch waterfall in the centre of the headwall. Mostly 70 degree ice with some vertical steps. The first ascensionists accessed the route by climbing to the lower south ridge from the Fox névé then abseiling and traversing to the base of the route.
routes.ascent: Glenn Pennycook, Tshering Pande Bhote, July 2004

routes.name: Stealing White Boys
routes.description: Climbs the right hand ‘ice fang,’ which is slightly easier than White Steel. The first ascensionists accessed the route by climbing to the lower south ridge from the Fox névé then abseiling and traversing to the base of the route.

routes.name: East Spur
routes.description:
This consists of a 400m buttress of relatively loose rock, leading to the north peak. The spur has been gained by two routes:
(i) via a rock and scree rib separating the two arms of the Kaufmann Glacier; and
(ii) up scree and rock south of the Forrest Ross Glacier to a small snow basin.
routes.ascent: Tom Fyfe, Malcolm Ross, February 1897 (via route ii)

routes.name: East Ridge
routes.description: This 350m high route meets the Main Divide some distance north of Haidinger’s north summit. Climb scree slopes and a rotten rock ridge onto Emas Dome, then drop onto the Forrest-Ross Glacier névé. Cross the névé to gain either the ridge, then climb to the prominent point on the Main Divide.
routes.ascent: Jack Clarke, J R Simpson, March 1913 (route unknown)

routes.name: North East Face
routes.description: This 350m high route meet the Main Divide some distance north of Haidinger’s north summit. Climb scree slopes and a rotten rock ridge onto Emas Dome, then drop onto the Forrest Ross Glacier névé. Cross the névé to gain either the face, then climb to the prominent point on the Main Divide.
routes.ascent: Jack Clarke, J R Simpson, March 1913 (route unknown)

places.name: West Face
places.description: The rock buttresses on this face offer excellent climbing, with many variations. The most prominent routes are listed, but the far-left buttress, the gully between the buttresses, and a narrow gully right of the Right Buttress have all been climbed.

routes.name: Pahiatua
routes.description: From the Albert névé, ascend the snow slopes left of the west face routes.
routes.ascent: Joe Fluerty, Mark Lysons, Molly Williams, February 1934 (descended)

routes.name: Left Buttress
routes.description: From the névé, 200m of pleasant scrambling on good rock, followed by 40-degree snow slopes and final exit gullies onto the South Summit. Superb.

routes.name: Right Buttress
routes.description: This route has excellent rock climbing. It’s best to follow a weakness on the right side, although the centre of the buttress has been used (grade 15). Follow the snow slope to exit onto the South Summit. In 1967, this route was a major psychological breakthrough in face climbing and was heralded as a classic.
routes.ascent: John Andrews, Graeme Dingle, Peter Gough, George Harris, Murray Jones, December 1967

routes.name: West Ridge
routes.description: From the névé, gain the rounded rib beside the west face, head up easy mixed ground, and trend out left to finish up the same summit gullies as the west face routes. The first ascent party is unknown – the party listed below took a line right of the Right Buttress.

routes.name: Albino Merino
routes.description: The couloir between the west and south ridges.

routes.name: South Ridge
routes.description:
Very popular, and the most common way up Mt Haidinger. It is also the recommended descent route. The ridge is fairly straightforward (but beware of cornices) until the last 100m of rock, which if iced can be tackled either by traversing out slightly on the east face or up the couloir to the west. The ridge can be gained at many points. The usual routes are:
(i) The ridge can be gained at many points. The most elegant way lies up the arête which reaches the ridge 400m before the summit. Joe Fluerty, Mark Lysons, Molly Williams, Feb 1934
(ii) Along the divide from Governor Col, which involves a step halfway along the ridge must be ascended, otherwise the ridge is fairly straightforward (beware of cornices) until the last 100m of rock, which if iced, can be tackled either by traversing out slightly on the East Face or up the couloir to the west.Jack Clarke, Edward FitzGerald, Mattias Zurbriggen, Feb 1895 (from Glacier Dome)
Grey Peak 2882m
The first ascent was from the Grand Plateau and Glacier Dome, then traversing across to Governor Col.
routes.ascent: Jack Clarke, Edward FitzGerald, Mattias Zurbriggen, February 1895

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Mt Hicks
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: Also known as St David's Dome. First ascended by Alex Graham, Henry Newton, R S Low, 1906. Their route via the north-west ridge has largely fallen away.

routes.name: North West Ridge
routes.description: The upper section of the North West Ridge (used on the first ascent of Hicks) fell away sometime in the late 1940s, revealing a large expanse of rotten rock that frequently rattles down the prominent corner known as ‘The Curtain’. Climbing in this area would currently be unpleasant and dangerous. For information on the standard route on Hicks, see the Curtain Route (route 3.37).
routes.ascent: Alec Graham, Robert Low, Henry Newton, February 1906

routes.name: Curtain Route
routes.description:
The Curtain Route is more commonly used as a descent from Hicks rather than a climb, and is probably one of the more complicated ‘standard’ routes on a 3000’er. From Harper Saddle, ascend diagonally up across the snow slope to the northeast, beneath a large striking corner known as ‘The Curtain’, to reach the gap in the west ridge. The Curtain formed in the late 1940s when the western end of the mountain fell off, and rockfall is still semi-frequent. Climb up the ridge for 150m, then cross left to a major couloir. Ascend the couloir, which comes out about 100m down the ridge from the final 40m rock wall below the summit ice cap.
Descent off Hicks
Initial easy travel along the summit (west) ridge leads to a short rock step that requires care. Beyond here there is a prominent ridge that intersects the main west ridge, this is the top of the North Rib (‘Biscuit Tin’ route).
Not far below the North Rib junction, at approximately 3000m, leave the main summit ridge and turn into the broad snow gully that trends north-west and narrows. Although there have been bolts placed in this gully, they are difficult to find and the top two sets are often covered in snow. Be prepared to utilise other anchor options. Lower down in the gully on the true left, two abseil stations are more prominent. One of these is at the top of The Curtain.
Do not rap down The Curtain but continue down to the right in the gully, eventually traversing out left across a rocky rib and onto snow slopes leading to Harper Saddle. It is about five 50m abseils from the top of the couloir to where the traverse out begins.

routes.name: West Ridge (Divide Route)
routes.description: From Harper Saddle, head up on snow to the left of the Divide for a short distance before crossing onto the edge of the South Face. Follow up ledges and bluffs overlooking the South Face until the Divide flattens out, then follow the ridge up the final 40m wall to the summit.

places.name: South Face
places.description:
The south face of Mt Hicks is the stuff of legend. Due to the face’s proximity to Empress Hut it is sometimes considered a large crag (‘large’ being the key word there). The face has some of the best hard climbing in the region; for most routes the first two to three pitches provide the crux.
There is no easy descent route from the top of Mt Hicks. If you’ve summited via one of the rock routes in summer, the best descent is probably Route 3.37. If you’ve climbed an ice route it’s probably easier to abseil on v-threads, either down the route you’ve climbed or down the Right Icefields (Route 3.60).

routes.name: Divide Route
routes.description:
From Harper Saddle, head up on snow to the left of the Divide for a short distance before crossing onto the edge of the South Face. Follow up ledges and bluffs overlooking the South Face until the Divide flattens out, then follow the ridge up the final 40m wall to the summit. The "modern way" would be to climb the complete Dingle/Button route (3.39).
Harry Ayres, Oscar Coberger, Feb 1951.

routes.name: Dingle-Button
routes.description:
This route is popular due to its accessibility and
lack of commitment, compared to other routes
on the face. It is seldom climbed to the summit.
Start at the second obvious gully right from
Harper Saddle. A couple of pitches of moderately
steep ice followed by 200m of lesser-angled snow
and ice leads to the Divide Route. A number of
variations have been added further left, all of a
similar grade.

routes.name: Dance Commander

pitches.description: Starts up Dingle Button traverses into Deardissima to the shelf then finishes up Highway to Hell/Heavens Door. An easy way to the summit on moderate ground.

routes.description:
Start up Dingle-Button, traverse into Deardissima to
gain the large shelf, then traverse right and finish
up Highway to Hell. A comparatively easy way to the
summit on moderate ground.

pitches.description:
Start at the bottom of the D-B couloir and climb the rib on the
right of the gully (crux 13). Join the Divide Route after six rope lengths.

routes.name: Deardissima
routes.description:
Gully immediately right of Dingle-Button. Crosses
Tales of Choss to join the top of Dingle-Button

routes.name: King Hit
routes.description: Follows a line of weakness through the steep area just left of Highway to Hell. Cross the obvious right-trending ramp system between the second and third shelves, then climb the final headwall to reach an extensive area of easy ground half way up the left side of the face. The first ascentionists descended from here by traversing left downclimbing Dingle-Button. Five or six pitches.

pitches.description: Start just left of HD in a right trending gully on 65-85 degree ice (probably thin) then traverse right across a snowslope and step into a narrow gully. Follow the obvious gully and short steep walls. After the first shelf continue up a narrow gully to the second shelf and easy ground. Move left across the shelf then up right through the rock band to gain the summit icefield. Thirteen pitches.

routes.name: Heaven’s Door
routes.description:
This route aims for the prominent ice flow
immediately right of the large shelf on the left
side of the face. Start up steep, loose ground to
the right of Highway to Hell. Five pitches of hard
climbing lead to easier ground to the right of the
large shelf. Take the line of least resistance from
there to the summit icefields, usually as shown in
topo opposite, but variations between there and
the upper section of Route 3.47 have also been
climbed.
routes.ascent: Russell Braddock, Kim Logan, Jan 1983.	Nick Cradock, Paul Aubrey, Jul, 1987

routes.name: The Curver Direct
routes.description: This route seems to have been unaffected by the rockfall. The usual start is about 20-30m left of the very steep cliff on the left side of the rockfall gully, but there are a few different versions. Climb about five pitches of steep terrain to join Route 3.47 at an obvious small shelf.

routes.name: The Curver Neo-classic
routes.description:
The lower half of the original Curver ‘Classic’
has been destroyed by the rockfalls. The new
version of The Curver, up the rear left side of the
new gully, is likely to turn into one of the most
popular hard ice routes on the South Face, as it
forms regularly.
Climb the obvious steep ice flow in the back
of the gully, which is usually thin, to reach the
right end of an obvious small shelf, then traverse
slightly left and take your pick of the best looking
line above, up ice gullies and possibly some
mixed ground for about six pitches to reach the
summit icefields.

routes.name: One for Pavle
routes.description:
A strong Slovenian team climbed the difficult
lower pitches of the Gunbarrels during the brief
period between rockfall events, then traversed
delicately towards The Curver before finishing
further right with a new extended finish.
Depending on conditions, the upper part of this
route looks like a great alternate finish to Route
3.47. The grade reflects the difficulty of the upper
variant line only. The lower pitches of this route
were about Technical Grade 7.
routes.ascent: Pavle Kozjek, Grega Kresal, Simon Slejko, Mar 2004

routes.name: Gunbarrels

pitches.description: Original: Up two difficult pitches, into the bottom of the Curver Gully, then up three pitches until a diagonal gully cuts back right to the foot of the prominent double ice couloirs (the Gunbarrels). The first two or so original pitches fell off in 1999.

routes.description:
Pick a line up the upper-right region of the recent
rockfall wedge, probably climbing a new route
as you go, to reach a gully that leads up and right
to the base of the prominent double ice couloirs
(the Gunbarrels). Climb the Gunbarrels (grade 6),
then climb sustained moderate-angled ice to
the summit.
On the impressive first ascent of the original
Gunbarrels, Bill Denz aided the first two vertical to
overhanging pitches (including a 50m ice pillar)
on Doubek ice screws. Then in a game of oneupmanship,
numerous parties attempted to free
the lower pitches. Allan Uren and Julian White made the first free ascent, only to have the lower
2.5 pitches obliterated by the 1999 rockfall. These
lower pitches were climbed in November 1999 by a
strong kiwi team, but it was visiting climber Gren
Hinton who was the first to climb the full route
post-rockfall. Only one more party got to climb
the route before the 2007 rockfall, which appears
to have made the lower area quite thin and steep.
routes.ascent: Bill Denz, Phil Herron, Murray Judge, Jun 1975.	with aid

routes.name: Yankee-Kiwi Couloir

pitches.description:
Ascends the Direct Start of the Left Hand Buttress Route, then up a steep ice couloir to the left of the Left
Buttress to the base of the  Original Gunbarrels

routes.description:
When this classic route was first climbed it
followed the steepest line into the Gunbarrels that
existed at the time.
Climb either 3.51i or 3.51ii, then up a steep
ice couloir to the left of the Left Buttress (the
Yankee-Kiwi Couloir) to the base of the Gunbarrels.
Continue as for Route 3.48. Awesome fun on a
sustained line.

routes.name: Left Buttress Direct Start
routes.description:
Climb directly to the ledge traversed by the
Original Route by either (i) the sustained face to
the left of the lowest promontory of rock, possibly
dealing with a couple of small overhangs en route,
or (ii) a corner system directly below the upper
buttress. Some parties have started up 3.51ii and
traversed into 3.51i. From the ledge, continue up
prominent wide cracks in the bottom cliffs to the
right of the crest of the buttress (grade 18). Joins
the Original Route where the gradient eases.

routes.name: Left Buttress
routes.description: Ascend two pitches on the bottom wall nearer the Central Gullies, then traverse left directly below the main buttress to reach an ice ramp left of the buttress. Then either ascend directly up the buttress crest (crux 15), or up the ramp for a short distance before regaining the buttress, or up a short buttress left of the ramp before cutting back right again. Follow the buttress up progressively easier rock until the icefields. Then, depending on the state of the icecliffs, traverse left and up, or else through the cliffs. Superb.

routes.name: Desolation Row
routes.description:
Start up Route 3.52, then traverse slightly right
for 50m and up diagonally left for another 100m
before ascending directly to emerge near the top
of the Left Buttress.

routes.name: Generation Y
routes.description:
A variation direct start to Central Gullies. Start from a thin gully just
right of Desolation Row (MC6). Difficult mixed terrain on the third pitch
where the variation exited the thin gully and tended right towards Central
Gullies. Seven pitches.

routes.name: Central Gullies

pitches.description: There are a number of variation starts and finishes. Choose a start and head up ice, sustained climbing through ice couloirs and icefields until easier 45o slopes lead to the icecliffs. Depending on the state of the cliffs, find a route through them to the summit.

routes.description:
The first of the big ice climbs on this face. There
are a number of variation starts and finishes—all
of the main ice flows between the Left and Right
buttresses generally count as the ‘Central Gullies’.
The climbing is fairly sustained, through ice
couloirs and icefields, until easier 45 degree
slopes lead to the icecliffs. Depending on the
state of the cliffs, find a route through them to
the summit. More recently the cliffs have ablated
back to a slightly protruding shield, but this may
change again in the future.
routes.ascent: Bill Denz, Peter Gough, Etienne Kummer, Nov 1972.

routes.name: Logan’s Run
routes.description:
One of the stand-out lines on the face,
involving steep and sustained climbing up to
WI4 and M5. From the edge of the Central
Gullies, climb the upper of the two major
vertical couloirs which run up the left side of
the Right Buttress. If sections are devoid of ice,
then it is possible to dry-tool/aid climb through
them. Near the top of the couloir it is possible
to traverse onto the crest of the buttress to avoid one final pitch of ice.  Finish
up the Right Buttress route, or rappel off.
There is some fixed gear, but it would be
unwise to trust or rely on it. In 1985, Nick
Cradock and Kevin Boekholt eliminated the
aid used in the first ascent and completed the
top of the route, which is where the ‘Logan’s
Retreat’ jibe came from (check out the old
journals for more).
This previously great route hasn't got enough ice to be climbable for well over a decade now.

routes.name: Tingler
routes.description:
Ascend the lower of the two major vertical
couloirs on the left side of the Right Buttress.
Five or six pitches of very steep, mixed ice and
rock lead onto the Right Buttress. The second
pitch is the crux with a small overhung section
of ice. This is a shorter, good hard technical
route, without the commitment of the routes on
the main face. It is straightforward to abseil.

routes.name: Right Buttress

pitches.description: Avoid the first 60m by using the icefield on the right. Traverse onto the crest of the buttress then directly up on or right of the crest (crux 14). Then head up the icefields and through the icecliffs.

routes.description:
Avoid the first 60m by using the icefield on the
right. Traverse onto the crest of the buttress then
directly up on or right of the crest (crux 14). Then
head up the icefields and through the icecliffs.

routes.name: Ice Trek
routes.description: A good one if ice conditions are on (not threatened by ice cliffs) and you feel like something slightly harder than Route 3.60. Links the ice sections of the bluffs on the right side of the Right Buttress. The first ascentionists abseiled the route after gaining the top of the buttress.

pitches.description: Climb through the bottom cliffs which usually have two pitches of hard climbing, then up a sustained shield of ice. There are a number of variations. [6-7 pitches to the ridge , approx 8 x 60m abseils.]

places.name: North Face
places.access:
Usually accessed from the Hooker via Harper Saddle but sometimes via Clarke Saddle from Grand Plateau.
Access to the La Perouse Glacier from the Hooker Glacier
Route 13F, grade III, 3
The lower La Perouse Glacier can be accessed from Empress Hut via Harper Saddle.
To reach the La Perouse névé, descend 200m from Harper Saddle, keeping right, then ascend 150m snow or loose rock to the horizontal section of the ridge running down from Mt Hicks (the north-west ridge), reaching a small névé.
From this point, to reach the La Perouse Glacier between the upper and lower icefalls, follow down snow slopes on the true right of the lower north-west ridge. Otherwise, to reach the upper La Perouse Névé, cross towards the North Rib of Mt Hicks, descend a short distance beneath a rock buttress, and cross to a flat ridge. Using the right of two obvious notches, descend 150m down a steep rotten rock gully (which usually requires an abseil) and snow slope to reach the main glacier below the north face of Hicks. This is one of the most committing areas in the park. Tread carefully.
Access to the La Perouse Glacier from the Grand Plateau
Route 13G, grade IV, 3+
The crossing of Clarke Saddle is high, steep, and usually only possible in early summer but, in condition, it provides fast access to the upper La Perouse névé.
There are usually good snow caving sites near the base of the west ridge of Malaspina.
Plateau Hut to the upper La Perouse névé in good conditions: 6–8 hrs
places.description: North Face of Mt Hicks in summer conditions

routes.name: Left Buttress
routes.description: Head up the obvious large five-pitch corner on the right side of buttress, avoiding the roof by taking the right variant corner. The next 200m of easy climbing leads to a steep wall (crux) followed by easier climbing as the buttress lies back.
routes.ascent: David Elphick, Barry Smith, February 1957 (avoided first five pitches)

routes.name: Weeping Gash
routes.description: The gully between the Left and Central Buttresses. A startlingly steep couloir with frequent crux walls. Climbed in winter when the ice is solid. Required two bivvies.

routes.name: Central Buttress
routes.description: This isn’t a route you’ll forget quickly. Start up a crack on a small block below the main buttress, then go right off a ledge and into the obvious groove that takes you right up the climb. Hardest at the bottom except for a slight sting at the top. With glacial recession there may be another pitch at the bottom which is harder.
routes.ascent: Bill Denz, Phil Herron, Murray Judge, June 1974

routes.name: Central Buttress variant: Monks-Sunderland
routes.description: Follow an obvious system of cracks parallel to and left of the crest of the buttress, joining the original route where the angle starts to ease. Sustained climbing with two harder pitches. Good rock although shattered in places.

routes.name: Central Buttress variant: McAuley-Wong
routes.description: Follow the original route for 3–4 pitches, then move right just before a widening chimney with an overhanging start. Continue 15m along a ledge to a steep crack system (crux). The route runs along the nose of the buttress parallel to and right of the original route, rejoining it after 8 pitches.

routes.name: Right Buttress
routes.description: Start up steep dark chimneys to the right of the prominent gully keeping left of the bottom. The first six pitches are sustained on excellent rock. The next eight pitches are easier and on good rock. Higher still the climbing becomes more broken.
routes.ascent: Merv English, John Fantini, Noel Sissons, January 1975

routes.name: Book of Days
routes.description: Next rock rib right of Right Buttress. Access is via snow slopes and a gully, which ends in a cul-de-sac, beside the Right Buttress (the face between these routes has also been climbed, by Marty Beare and Lindsay Main). Climb a ramp to the right of a corner to gain the crest of a rib, and follow this to a striking red tower. Continue on the crest to the summit. The first pitch (crux) is followed by sustained climbing on solid red rock, which rarely relents. First climbed in 13 pitches.

routes.name: North Rib aka Biscuit Tin Route
routes.description: Take the access route from Harper Saddle to the base of the rib. Climb good rock on the face to the right of the rib, following the line of least resistance onto the rib itself. The rib steepens towards the top (crux). Then follow a flattening ridge for 250m to join the summit ridge at the top of the couloir on the Curtain Route.
routes.ascent: P Barry, D Drake, Peter Gough, Aat Vervoorn, November 1969

routes.name: Red Wall
routes.description: An eight-pitch route up red rock to the left of the couloir on the Curtain Route, finishing high on the North Rib.

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Mt Humdinger
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: From the col with Grey Peak it is an easy ascent. The rock on the western slopes offers pleasant climbing. The first ascent from this direction was by Frank Alack, H K Douglas, W E Wilson, Dec 1934.

routes.name: South East Ridge
routes.description: Climb to the col between Grey Peak and Humdinger via the slopes beneath Mt Haidinger or from the approach to Pioneer Pass. From the col, a short but quite exposed arête leads to the summit of Mt Humdinger.

routes.name: North East Face
routes.description: Exact route unknown. Reported to be pleasant climbing.
routes.ascent: Frank Alack, Harold Douglas, Bill Wilson, Dec 1934

routes.name: North Rib
routes.description:
150m of sound climbing on red rock, crux 14. The snow couloir to the left has also been climbed and provides good gully climbing practice (also II, 3).
Variation: the next major arete to the right (18): Dennis Haskell, Llewellyn Murdoch, 2009

pitches.description:
The route takes a direct line towards & through the red pillar that leads through the roofs on the left hand side.
Start. Look for a crack that leads out of of a small alcove just to the right of the red rock. Climb past the the vertical crack out of the alcove & move onto orangr textured rock. Traverse right directly under a pink, blank piece of rock and move up to belay in a crack.
Traverse left and up the slab. Move to the lefthand crack (watch the hollow flakes). Pass through the steepest ground on the right crack before moving left into a crack/ corner belay.
Step right onto the pillarand climb through techical ground heading first left then right & up to belay in cracks.
Climb up the dark coloured groove to the base of a clean left facing corner & big belay ledge.
Climb the corner & belay above the top of the tower.
Trend left & towards the left side of the hole/ cave above the belay just beyond this.
Climb up to the ledge.To finish, scramble right to join Kahu.

The route take the right side of the face and passes through the roof on the Rh-Side of the rectangular feature on it.
Climb the crack & belay under the Lh-facing corner.
Climb the triple cracks & the Lh- facing corner. From the top of the tower step left & climb through the bulge.
Climb up, then right to gain the Lh-trending ramp. Follow this then climb the chimney before breaking left past the orange block.

Follow the break left, then head right & up onto clean orange rock.
Belay on a flat spot.
Climb up on easy ground heading right of the big hole/ cave above.
Follow the Rh- Trending breakto the top of the light coloured headwall & find a bolted rap anchor.

routes.name: Humdinger Abseil Line
routes.description:
Bolted anchors allow a descent of mostly 30m abseils, although there is one abseil about 32m long; rope stretch with a 60m rope should do the trick! Eight abseils all up, or four if you’ve got two 60m ropes.
Equipped by Nick Cradock, 2011

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Mt Isabel
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: Mt Isabel from the Wicks Glacier, January 2010

routes.name: North East Ridge
routes.description:
From Mt Eric (via Twain Col), follow the Main Divide, initially along a straightforward broad ridge and then along a narrow ridge with a few 10–20m steep steps. The ridge is comprised of very rotten rock, but it goes.
Climbed from the west in February 1950 by W Hunt, R Johnson, M Nelson and R Newton .

routes.name: North West Ridge
routes.description:
From Harpers Rock, climb towards the Hooker Range between Douglas Pass and Awatea, and then traverse around the northern slopes of Awatea to reach the Awatea–Isabel col.
From the col, climb the ridge for about 150m on excellent rock. A short, exposed, rising traverse (one 45m pitch) leads to an easy ledge and the base of a short steep corner. The corner is the crux of the route. From the top of the corner, about 130m of steep scrambling leads to the summit.
Descent was via the north-east ridge (the original ascent route) to the Isabel–Eric Col, then down a short icefall back to the base of the route. The Divide ridge was appallingly loose rock over several steep towers and the first ascensionists did three short abseils to get through.

routes.name: South East Face
routes.description: Via a prominent snow arête from the upper Hooker. Since the first ascent, a rock band has become exposed near the top of the route, which may present additional difficulties.
routes.ascent: A D Jackson, V I E Whitehead, 1941

routes.name: Main Divide Route
routes.description: Gain the Main Divide at Harper Saddle or either side of Mt Sturdee, depending on schrunds and snow conditions. Then either follow the rotten divide ridge or negotiate a less technical route using slopes on the west side of the ridge.
routes.ascent: Hugh Chambers, Conrad Kain, Hugh Wright, February 1915

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Mt Jervois
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: Some short crag-style routes have been developed on the rock buttresses near Centennial Hut by Peter Taw and John Entwisle. The first route (crux 18) is situated south-west of the hut, on the third buttress from the left as you face it. The second route (crux 20) follows a groove on the distinctive red buttress north-east of the hut, and north of Jervois.

routes.name: East (Main Divide) Ridge
routes.description: Easy scrambling.

routes.name: North Face
routes.description: A gully system on this face has been descended using a combination of downclimbing and abseiling (about 150m).
routes.ascent: Lars Andersson, Francesca Eldridge, Glenn Pennycook (descended), November 2008

routes.name: North West Ridge
routes.description: Follow the ridge above Centennial Hut over two distinct gendarmes and onto the summit. Good rock. The snow arête of the upper ridge can be very narrow and exposed.

routes.name: Team Piha
routes.description: Follows a gully on the left side of the face, with four pitches of moderately steep ice to the knife-edge ridgeline and another pitch to easier ground on the ridge. Continue along straight-forward ground to the summit (two pitches). The first ascentionists believed this would be a good beginners’ route for those wanting to cut their teeth on more technical ground.
routes.ascent: Lars Andersson, Francesca Eldridge, Glenn Pennycook, November 2008

routes.name: The Guide Who Shagged Me
routes.description: A four-pitch rock climb up a prominent corner crack on the right side of the face.

routes.name: Peter Plus Haut Que Son Cul
routes.description: A four-pitch rock buttress. Exact location and crux grade unknown.
routes.ascent: Genevieve Lemaire, Tim Robertson, Paul Scaife, Michael Veuillet, January 2003

routes.name: Main Divide Route
routes.description: Follow the Main Divde Route to the summit of Mt Jellicoe, after which the traverse along the ridge to Mt Low is simple.
routes.ascent: Hugh Chambers, Conrad Kain, Hugh Wright, February 1915

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Mt Meeson
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: Mt Meeson and Mt Vic from the Spencer Glacier, November 2010

routes.name: Via Main Divide
routes.description: From the summit of Mt Coronet, traverse the Main Divide to the summit of Mt Meeson.
routes.ascent: Hugh Chambers, Conrad Kain, Prof. Robinson, J Robertson, Hugh Wright, February 1915

routes.name: Eastern Slopes
routes.description: Use either of the Haupapa Tasman Glacier routes onto Mt Coronet and cross the basin beneath that peak to reach the Main Divide.

routes.name: North Rib
routes.description: From the glacier to the left of the rib, traverse into a narrow couloir breaching the length of the lower rib. Ascend the couloir to a snow slope and then up the rock arête for eleven pitches on good rock. The easiest descent is probably via Mt Coronet.
routes.ascent: Dave Bamford, Peter Fullerton, George Kendall, John Nankervis, January 1978

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Mt Montgomerie
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: Mt Burns to Black Tower across the head of the Landsborough, January 2006

routes.name: North West Ridge
routes.description: An easy scramble from Fyfe Pass.

routes.name: South Ridge
routes.description: Follow the Main Divide from Edith Peak. There is an 80m high steep section to gain the summit of Raureka, which appears to be the crux of the Divide when traversing from Copland Pass to Mt Beatrice.
routes.ascent: (Probably) Hugh Chambers, Peter Graham, Dorothy Holdsworth, January 1914

routes.name: East Spur
routes.description: Via a prominent spur leading up from the Hooker Valley. Access onto the base of this spur is likely to become increasingly difficult due to recession of the Hooker Glacier.

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Mt Rudolf
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: West face of Mt Rudolf, December 2017

routes.name: South East Face
routes.description: From the upper Rudolf Glacier, up steep snow slopes to the col between Rudolf and Moonlight, then along the ridge to the summit.
routes.ascent: Bill Crawshaw, Bruce Milburn, Ralph Warburton, January 1948

routes.name: East Ridge
routes.description: Relatively easy scrambling on rock and snow. Probably the easiest descent route.

routes.name: Dawe-McInnes Buttress
routes.description: From the Franz Josef névé, follow directly up the buttress (north-west ridge) to the summit.

routes.name: A Nice Affair
routes.description: Ascend ice using a small corner just right of the direct line to the summit (not the big corner on the right of the face). When the small corner, offering 70-degree ice runs out, break left through a short step. Continue up the snowfield to the summit. The first ascentionist descended to the north via two steep abseils to the névé.

routes.name: Big Day Out
routes.description: A line right of A Nice Affair.

routes.name: Right Gully
routes.description: An obvious gully to the right of Rudolf (further right of the prominent Y-shaped gully) provides an enjoyable ice climb in spring/winter. It joins the Main Divide approximately 200m south of the summit. A cruisy half-day option.

routes.name: Little Day Out
routes.description: Follows the zig-zag gully right of Right Side Gully. Five pitches with the crux being the fourth pitch, where the ice may run out.
routes.ascent: Paul Prince, Alex Ross, Graham Zimmerman, August 2005

routes.name: South West Ridge
routes.description: Mostly straightforward rock and snow scrambling, with a couple of short, moderately steep sections. A good place to practice some slightly exposed ridge travel.

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Mt Sefton
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: The Footstool, Mt Sefton and Welcome Pass

routes.name: Frind’s Route
routes.description:
A pioneering first ascent, now rarely undertaken because the Copland valley provides much easier access to the west side of Sefton.
The route begins from the Frind-Mueller confluence. From the true right edge of the lower Frind Glacier, head up a gully onto a rock rib north of the Ngaroimata Falls, gaining height and tending right to reach the frequently broken Donne Glacier. Ascend northwards across the glacier under Sharks Teeth to reach Brunner Col (grade IV, 3 to the col). The Donne Glacier has retreated considerably in recent years, and by midsummer most of this route is on glacier-worn rock.
Cross Brunner Col and drop onto the west side (the given technical grade of 2+ is from Brunner Col). Exposed and avalanche prone slopes under Brunner give access to the Douglas névé and the west ridge. Complicated crevasses can make crossing the névé time consuming in late summer. The final 400m to the summit is on moderately steep snow, which can be icy.
routes.ascent: Otto Frind, Conrad Kain, Dick Young, March 1914

routes.name: South Ridge Original Route
routes.description: From the Douglas névé beneath Mt Brunner, begin climbing up the couloir that leads to the gap between Brunner and Sefton. About halfway up the couloir, turn left and traverse a snow shelf between large rock cliffs. A pitch of rock may be required to gain the bottom of the shelf in late summer. At the top of the shelf, one or two pitches of rock lead to an upper snowfield, which is followed to a prominent snow peak (Pt 3048m). Descend from the peak to a col below a rock buttress, which is avoided by traversing snow slopes on the west then climbing back up to reach the col between the two summits of Sefton.
routes.ascent: Bill Beavan, Norman Hardie, Jim McFarlane, Earle Riddiford, January 1948

routes.name: South Ridge Direct
routes.description:
This jaw-dropping skyline ridge is clearly visible from Aoraki Mt Cook village and deserves more attention as it provides an exhilaratingly exposed and challenging climb, staying on the crest all the way.
From the gap between Brunner and Sefton ascend a prominent rock step (crux) and head on up a blocky rock ridge and then a snow arête to reach Pt 3048m. Descend to a small col, climb a steep rock buttress, follow another snow arête, and up a final small rock step to the south summit and main summit.
It has been climbed only once, from Harpers Rock via Mt Stephen and Mt Brunner. The ridge could be reached from the Mueller Glacier via Brunner Col.
routes.ascent: Stu Allan, Olly McCahon, Rob Rowlands, Brin Williman, January 1971

routes.name: North East Ridge
routes.description:
A bold route used on the first ascent of Sefton. From Sefton Biv (see Hooker Glacier for access) head up the rib behind the bivvy to where a broad bench runs across the top of the Huddleston Glacier. Negotiate your way into the upper Huddleston and continue up to access the Main Divide near Tuckett Col.
From Tuckett Col, ascend three prominent steps in the ridge to the summit. The upper step can be avoided by traversing to the right across a snow shelf to gain the upper west ridge (but then you’d be avoiding the best climbing). The rock is appallingly loose in the lower sections but improves dramatically towards the top. In 1924, Frank Milne and Harold Porter ascended and descended the ridge in four hours and reported that the upper step provided terrific rock climbing. The ridge is now rarely climbed due to a lack of enthusiasm for rotten rock.

routes.name: North Ridge
routes.description:
A magnificent climb involving 2400m of height gain from Douglas Rock Hut.
From the hut, travel 20–30min up the Copland track, then climb up scree and avalanche debris next to the Jasper Glacier Stream.
Ascend the slabs on the true right of the stream (don't drift true left on the slabs), which merge into easier angled scree at about 1600m (bivvy sites possible before the ridge proper), and then gain the crest of the north ridge. Above here are three prominent rock buttresses, which are generally broad, with several route possibilities. The rock isn’t bad. The climbing mostly involves exposed scrambling with some short steps. The true ridge offers the easiest climbing through the buttresses with difficulties often overcome on the east side. Most parties appreciate using a rope in at least one location. (An alpine rack of 5 nuts and 3-4 cams is often sufficient with good route finding.)
Above the buttress, the ridge flattens out (another good bivy site) before merging into a glacial bulge. There is sometimes an icecliff here. Above the icecliffs, ascend a vague snow rib to reach a shelf just below the summit. Either climb direct to the summit or traverse onto the west ridge.
Parties must be confident climbing unroped on exposed ground for the majority of this route, as pitching the entire ridge would take days. The first ascent party completed the route within a day return to Douglas rock. It has more recently been completed in two days from the road end.
Descent is usually via Welcome Pass.
routes.ascent: Bruce Harrison, Nick Von Tunzelmann, Aat Vervoorn, December 1964

routes.name: West Ridge
routes.description:
The actual west ridge of Mt Sefton is a relatively straightforward climb on snow. However, the overall route is a serious undertaking, with a long approach across untracked terrain, which requires good navigation skills. The climb begins on Welcome Pass.
From Welcome Pass, follow the crest of the Sierra Range eastwards along a classic, exposed snow aréte.
Late in the season there are sections of loose rock near Welcome Pass, but these are not difficult. Alternatively, from Welcome Pass, an early season option is to use the Douglas Névé to access the west ridge where it steepens. Complicated crevasses make this option more time-consuming in late summer. The final 400m to the summit is on moderately steep snow, which can be icy.
Beware of afternoon mist during the descent. Very fit parties can climb the ridge as a day trip from as low as 1300m, but bivvying on Welcome Pass makes the summit day much easier.
