routes.ascent: Jack Clarke, Laurence Earle, Alec Graham, Bernard Head, December 1909

places.name: East Face
places.description: This iconic and immensely visible face can be climbed a number of ways, starting either direct from the Mueller Glacier or via Sefton Bivvy and across the slopes under the Footstool ridge, and finishing by a variety of routes. Study the face well before your attempt.

routes.name: For Whom the Bell Tolls
routes.description: A visionary climb. Gain the Frind Glacier by either (i) climbing a steep, loose moraine wall as on the first ascent, or (ii) climbing up the lower Frind Glacier itself (both options are severely threatened by icecliff avalanche hazard). From the Frind Glacier head up the right side of a buttress, which is in the centre of the serac wall (crux 14). There is an exhilarating bivouac site at the top of the buttress, potentially safe from icecliff avalanche hazard. Negotiate the icecliff, cross the Shelf Glacier and finish up The Sun Also Rises.

routes.name: Triple Direct
routes.description: Audacious. From the lower Mueller Glacier, follow the Direct Route to the upper Frind Glacier (aka the Lower Shelf) and then cross this to reach the prominent central buttress on the middle tier. Climb the rock buttress (the stand-out feature of this route) and scale the edge of the Shelf Glacier. Cross the glacier where crevasses permit, and then ascend the 3 of 3 route to the col between the summits. 2150m of ascent, and the plum line of the face.

routes.name: Direct Route

pitches.description: Scale scree and bluffs above the Mueller Glacier, to reach the lower Shelf Glacier, beneath and just north of the prominent cliffs of the upper Shelf Glacier. Ascend the lower Shelf Glacier onto a snow face below and to the right of the icecliffs. Use the snow face to reach an arête on the right hand edge of the upper Shelf. At this point the two access routes from Sefton Bivvy join.

routes.description:
The first ascent of this route was an important part of the changing psychological approach to mountaineering occurring in New Zealand from the late 60s to early 70s. Murray Jones had begun soloing a more direct line, but joined Ross Gooder and John Stanton when they moved ahead of him. The three climbers completed the route as one party.
Scale scree and bluffs above the Mueller Glacier to reach the upper Frind Glacier, beneath the prominent cliffs of the Shelf Glacier. Ascend a snow face below and to the right of the icecliffs. Use the snow face to reach an arête on the true left edge of the Shelf Glacier, then take one of the routes from the Shelf Glacier to the summit (the first ascentionists used the Direct).
routes.ascent: Ross Gooder, Murray Jones, John Stanton, January 1971

routes.name: From Sefton Bivvy
routes.description:
See Hooker Glacier for access to Sefton Bivvy.
Head up the rib behind the bivvy to where a broad bench runs across the top of the Huddleston Glacier. Negotiate your way into the upper Huddleston, from where you have two options:
(i) Continue up onto the Main Divide ridgeline left of Tuckett Col, and along to where the north-east ridge steepens. Traverse across a short section of broken, rocky ground on the face to rejoin the snow that leads into the upper Shelf.
(ii) Cross the prominent spur that bisects the Huddleston and Tuckett Glaciers at about 2500m, and continue traversing, angling towards the uppermost icefall that feeds the Tuckett Glacier. Once at the point between the rock band and the icefall, head up the true-right of the icefall (which is relatively protected from this point) and over the rib into the upper Shelf.
Then take one of the routes from the Shelf Glacier to the summit.

routes.name: The Sun Also Rises
routes.description: From the Shelf Glacier, climb a series of ice gullies separated by steep snowfields directly to the summit of Pt 3048m.

routes.name: Harrow Ramp
routes.description: From the Shelf Glacier, head out on the prominent left-trending ramp to gain the upper south ridge, then traverse across the western slopes of Sefton to reach the summit.
routes.ascent: Bert Barley, Fred Edwards, Geoff Harrow, January 1953

routes.name: 3 of 3
routes.description: Climb the bluffs to the right of the Harrow Ramp using a dribble of ice, then up snow slopes directly to the South Summit.

routes.name: Goldsmith Route
routes.description: Up a short snow and ice couloir then up snow slopes leading onto the South Summit.
routes.ascent: Kobi Bosshard, Mike Goldsmith, Fritz Schaumberg, January 1963

routes.name: Direct
routes.description: Straight up the couloir dropping beneath the two summits.

places.name: North Face
places.access: The access used on the F.A of this face was via Sefton Bivy and Tuckett Col.
places.description: The North Face of Sefton overlooks the Copland Valley and is bounded by the East Ridge on the left and the classic North Ridge on the right.

routes.name: Kiss of the Spiderwoman
routes.description:
Access to this face is from Sefton Biv via Tuckett Col: Head up the rib behind the bivvy to where a broad bench runs across the top of the Huddleston Glacier. Negotiate your way into the upper Huddleston and continue up to cross the divide at Tuckett Col.
Ascend a snow ramp right towards the centre of the face, then head up on fairly good rock, tending left towards the east ridge. The route breaks out onto a shelf some 180m below the summit. Either veer right to ascend snow slopes above the north ridge (as on the first ascent) or keep things interesting by veering left to climb the top step of the North East Ridge.

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Mt Spencer
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: The Main Divide ridges of Spencer, especially the south ridge, are notoriously rotten. A rockfall on the north-western aspect of the peak occurred in April 2008. Most rocks fell down a gully to the east of the North West Pinnacle, but some made their way down to the west of the pinnacle or were part of a second collapse. The western aspects are mostly comprised of excellent rock, and the south-west face offers plenty of scope for winter/spring ice routes.

routes.name: South East Face
routes.description: A route lies up the icefalls well north of the Grant Duff Glacier and then up a rib of steep shattered rock and snow directly to the south summit. The rock on the Main Divide is notoriously loose in this area.
routes.ascent: Tim Barfoot, John Luxton, Richard Tornquist, January 1962

routes.name: North East Ridge
routes.description: Climb the snow slope between Frederick Gardiner and Spencer, then ascend a mixture of good and bad rock just west of the northern Main Divide ridge. The route tops out on the central summit; the north-west peak is the true summit. This route serves as a good descent route, but beware of an open schrund on the snow slope.

routes.name: North West Ridge
routes.description: This route starts from about halfway up the snowslope between Frederick Gardiner and Spencer. Two to three pitches of moderate climbing on good rock leads to pleasant scrambling up the ridge to the summit.

routes.name: Nash-Longhurst
routes.description: A great route on mostly excellent rock. Climbs the right-most spur between the North Ridge and the big ugly gully left of the North West Pinnacle. The first pitch and a half is fairly low-angle (grade 6–12) and is followed by four to five pitches of grade 14–16 climbing, to where it meets the North Ridge. Some small roofs provide the cruxes. There is room for a few variations – Bob McKerrow and S Drake climbed a variant in the general area in April 1991.

routes.name: North West Pinnacle
routes.description: Between the deep chossy gullies on the north-west side of the mountain lies a steep rib of surprisingly good rock, ending in a small pinnacle. Does not continue to the summit. Descend by abseiling the route.

routes.name: First Light
routes.description:
A winter/spring route that climbs the obvious gully between the North West Pinnacle and the West Buttress. Fantastic moderate ice and mixed climbing with the crux near the top. Don’t go anywhere near this in summer.
P1: Climb the snow ramp, pitching can begin out of the schrund. Up steep bulge then right leaning ice ramp over second bulge.
P2: Series of bulges leading to open snow gully
P3: Snow gully leading to right leaning steeper ice
P4: Two steeper bulges
P5: (Crux) Straight up narrowing ice lead. Some rock pro on either side, and mixed feel to the moves and placements  (0.4 cam, slings and medium nut)
The route and summit catches the sun by midday and hang fire can be a problem on descent if rappelling the route.

routes.name: West Buttress
routes.description: A relatively long route, on excellent quality and steep rock, which leads directly to the summit.

routes.name: Acid Punch
routes.description: An ice route that follows the gully immediately to the right of the West Buttress. It arrives on the summit ridge 10m west of the summit. Roughly four pitches (the first two can be thin). Best conditions are found in late winter/spring. The lower gully was accessed from right of Jungle Drums (route 10.39) on the first ascent; there is no recorded direct ascent.

routes.name: Jungle Drums (South West Buttress)
routes.description: This route is situated just right of the West Buttress and follows nine pitches of excellent rock. Claimed by many, but first climbed by Bryon and Taw.

routes.name: Pitch Black
routes.description: Takes the second narrow ice gully about 30m right of Jungle Drums. The climb arrives on a col 20m east of the summit. Again, good in winter or spring.

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Mt Stephen
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: Mt Sefton and Main Divide from Welcome Pass, January 2010

routes.name: From Douglas névé
routes.description: An early season climb these days (before the snow disappears from the slabs). Gain the shelf beneath Brunner and Stephen, then walk up snow to the summit. Also see Route 15I.
routes.ascent: Frank Alack, Katie Gardiner, Peter Graham, February 1931

routes.name: South Ridge from Brunner Col
routes.description: A straightforward ridge traverse with some steep rock scrambling. First climbed from Harpers Rock, but the ridge could also be reached from the Mueller Glacier.
routes.ascent: Stu Allan, Olly McCahon, Rob Rowlands, Brin Williman, January 1971

routes.name: Silberhorn Arête (South Ridge)
routes.description: From the summit of Silberhorn, ascend the moderately steep snow and ice arête; a classically beautiful climb. This ridge usually consists of very hard ice, especially in winter. Descend the same way, or give yourself a grand adventure by descending Syme Ridge (Route 4.50).
routes.ascent: Jack Clarke, Edward FitzGerald, Mattias Zurbriggen, Feb 1895.

routes.name: Direct to the south of the Summit

pitches.description: Up directly to the col between Silberhorn and Mt Tasman.

routes.name: Direct to the North Shoulder

pitches.description: Up slopes under the summit of Mt Tasman parallel to Syme Ridge, finishing either directly to the summit or onto the North Shoulder.

routes.ascent: Hans Leitner, Eberhard von Terzi, Jan 1960.

routes.name: North Shoulder
routes.description: A classic climb. From the summit of Lendenfeld, Tasman appears very close and, if conditions are good enough that you do not have to pitch the route, then it should not take long. However, several parties have found themselves on overnight epics due to pitching the entire Plateau Face, usually due to hard ice. There is nothing very steep on this climb, but you need to be comfortable with a lot of air under your feet.The climb is best approached by traversing over Lendenfeld to reach Engineer Col. Above Engineer Col, there is often an icecliff straddling the ridge crest. The route usually follows moderately steep ice gullies on the Plateau Face to where Syme Ridge joins the North Shoulder. Although the section above the col has changed markedly over the last few decades, it still provides a relatively straightforward route onto the shoulder. The broad North Shoulder eventually narrows into an exhilarating ridge, which leads to the summit. Also used as a descent route.

places.name: East Face
places.description: Two recognised routes directly on the East Face exist, but the line of ascent may alter owing to changing ice conditions. Both routes are threatened by ice avalanches.

routes.name: To Silberhorn-Tasman Col
routes.description: Up directly to the col between Silberhorn and Mt Tasman.

routes.name: Central Route
routes.description:
Up the slopes left of Syme Ridge, then veering left to finish directly on the summit.
Descended (in a storm) by David Hall, Duncan Hall, and John Pascoe, Dec 1938
routes.ascent: Descended (in a storm) by David Hall, Duncan Hall, and John Pascoe, Dec 1938

routes.name: Leitner/ Von Terzi

pitches.description: Up the slopes left of Syme Ridge, finishing on the north shoulder.

routes.ascent: Hans Leitner, Eberhard von Terzi, Jan 1960.

routes.name: Syme Ridge
routes.description:
Another classic, especially when combined with Silberhorn Arête (Route 4.46) to make a traverse of Mt Tasman. Access onto the base of the ridge is via:
(i) The slopes under the East Face (the ‘Mad Mile’), if option (ii) is cut off, this provides the most reliable option, but is prone to frequent ice fall.
(ii) A broad gully on the toe of the ridge itself—the best route if not cut off by crevasses or blank rock.
(iii) From the north-east side of the ridge, usually slightly safer than option (i), but things can change…
Then follow a narrow winding arête, which gradually broadens, to gain the north shoulder of Mt Tasman. From here follow the Main Divide, which narrows before rising to the summit.
Dan Bryant, Rod Syme, 1930
Bill McLeod, winter 1983

places.name: Heemskerck Face
places.description: Accessed from the Heemskerck Glacier part of the Fox Névé

routes.name: Original Route
routes.description: Start up a broad gully on the right of the face until above the prominent central icecliff. Then move up left towards the North Shoulder. The icecliff is currently threatening the route.

routes.name: Arapiles, Oh Arapiles

pitches.description: Follow the ridge between the Heemskirk Face and North Buttress. Poor rock. First ascent team descended a couloir into the Abel Janszoon after reaching the top of the North Buttress.

routes.description: Follow an arête between Heemskerck Face and North Buttress to join the North Buttress route. Poor rock. The first ascent team descended a couloir into the Abel Janszoon from the top of the North Buttress

routes.name: North Buttress
routes.description:
Ascend snow slopes towards Witches Col at the foot of the buttress, and head up the northern side of the rib. After 200m, cut back onto the rib and follow it to the prominent notch (may require an abseil). Above here, cut left and find the best and safest route through the icecliffs.
-The Heemskerck and Abel Janzoon Faces are topped by the enormous icecap of the North Shoulder. This seems to have cycles of serac building and although generally stable, it has been known to calve in cataclysmic fashion- – Dave Vass.
Dave Vass, Nick Cradock, July 1998

places.name: Abel Janszoon Face
places.description: Above the Abel Janszoon Glacier. Witches Col, between the North Buttress route on Mt Tasman and The Buttress can provide a access point to the Abel Janszoon Glacier

routes.name: Centurion
routes.description:
The major zigzag buttress right of the North Buttress. There are approximately 15 pitches of excellent mixed climbing involving three major rock steps. The first ascent team avoided the second rock step by ‘dropping into the gully on the right.’ Variation: climb the second buttress directly (Tech Grade 6, crux 18).
This route is best climbed in the spring or winter when a bit of ice holds any loose rock together. The first ascent team bivvied twice en route (a good site is at two thirds height on a narrow ice arête).
routes.ascent: Dave Crow, Andy MacFarlane, Jon Taylor, Jun 1994

pitches.description: Start up the same gully as the original route (11.134) to gain the broad rock buttress on the left. Follow the buttress tending left to exit via a hidden couloir that leads through the final rock curtain below the icecliffs. Ascend through the icecliffs onto the North Shoulder.

routes.name: Elder
routes.description: Ascend the gully start of the Original Route (11.134) and, instead of moving right on the large snowfields, continue straight up the gully systems onto the North Shoulder.

pitches.description: Ascend a gully line to the left of the prominent icecliffs in the middle of the face, moving right onto the central snowfields. Finish up steep sastrugied ice to the left of the summit.

routes.name: Nipple Rib
routes.description: Starting on the left side of the Stevenson-Dick Couloir, head up steep snow to the foot of a major rib leading to the west ridge. Ascend rock of reasonable quality for 15 pitches to emerge onto a prominent rock tower known as the Nipple, 130m below the summit of Tasman.

routes.name: Harris-Jones Rib
routes.description: The route ascends the lower Stevenson-Dick Couloir, and then moves left onto a subsidiary rib beside the couloir. The rock on the rib is of variable quality but nowhere is severe climbing.

routes.name: Stevenson-Dick Couloir

pitches.description: A continuous 800m slope descending from the West Ridge, averaging 40-50o. Beware soft snow avalanches and rockfall. Has been skied!

routes.description: A continuous 800m slope descending from the West ridge, averaging 40–50 degrees. Beware soft snow avalanches and rockfall. Has been skied.

routes.name: The Dream of the Dutch Sailors
routes.description: Gain the buttress between the icecliff and the base of the Stevenson-Dick Couloir, and head straight up snow and mixed steps on the crest of the buttress, aiming for the mixed gully that breaches the headwall, and then continue up the crest. A terrific big moderate route with enough variety in the climbing to keep it interesting, but easy enough to travel fast. Continue up the West Ridge and down the North Shoulder.
routes.ascent: Stuart Hollaway and Dale Thistlethwaite 23–24 December 2012

routes.name: Path of Manolin
routes.description: Up the 550m rock buttress immediately left of the Torres-Tasman Col to reach the start of the ice on the west ridge. There are two pitches of grade 17, which are steep and well protected. The rest of the climbing is around grade 12 with, just a bit of scruffy mucking about. Being situated on a buttress gives it a feeling of being safe from most of the objective hazards above.

routes.name: West Ridge
routes.description:
One of the great New Zealand classics, involving remoteness, exposure, and absolutely engaging ridge climbing. The normal
route traverses Torres Peak, making this a long, committing route.
Above Torres-Tasman Col, use the rock ribs on the Balfour Glacier side, and then follow the narrow arête upward. The arête gradually broadens out towards the summit of Tasman. Knowing this takes the sting out of the commitment of the route. If you need to escape from low down on the ridge, the best option is probably back up to the summit of Torres, and then down the North East Couloir. Just make sure you can descend the Abel Janszoon Glacier, as it sometimes gets cut off with large crevasses.
routes.ascent: Les Cleveland, Neil Hamilton, John Lange, Jan 1951 (descended during the first Tasman-Torres Traverse).

routes.name: Full West Ridge via the Fox Range
routes.description: This is a classic journey starting 3330m below the summit of Tasman. Requires creativity in your planning, a good weather window, and about three days. It’s possible to skirt around Big Mac on the Balfour side on a narrow snow ledge. This avoids dropping down long snow slopes on the Fox side to Katies Col.

routes.name: Torres -Tasman Col
routes.description: A short route of steep snow and ice, which unfortunately tends to act as a funnel for any rubbish falling from the surrounding slopes. Stay away.

places.name: Hidden Face
places.description:
This face hosts some of the most serious climbs in the book. Descent is usually over Tasman then Lendenfeld or Silberhorn. Access may be difficult due to a humongous crevasse scything through the icefall below the face.
All routes start on the Balfour Neve

pitches.description: Ascend a corner system 50m left of the Direct route. Exit onto the Torres-Tasman ridge just above the buttress above the col. Dave used to have a stuffed toy hippopotamus, and on the ascent Hippo was strapped to the outside of his pack. He may have been some comfort when Dave and Brian became trapped in a storm on the descent. Not much of a holiday for a hippo.

routes.name: Direct
routes.description: Begin up the gully left of the Sissons Buttress, and then ascend a narrow gully and rock pitch to gain the right edge of a prominent snowfield. Head up a pitch of steep bulging ice (crux), and then follow the broad gully out right. A fierce climb.

pitches.description: The route heads up a deep gully left of the Sissons Buttress. The gully widens out, and the route tends right and leads to an amphitheatre. Move right again and up to the ridge.

routes.name: Sissons Buttress
routes.description: Ascend the prominent rib just right of centre of the face. The rock is comparatively solid and the climbing sustained. The rib peters out and is followed by 200m of snow and ice.

routes.name: One Longer Day
routes.description: To the right of the Sissons Buttress is an area of steep ice. This route takes the line on the left edge of the ice, against the right edge of the buttress. Finish up a long steep ice wall behind the arête then top out via Route 12.13. Conditions on the first ascent were a mixture of ice climbing and thin mixed climbing. Seven 60m pitches to the crest of the buttress.

routes.name: Balfour Rib
routes.description: A super classic route and bold for its time. The bottom section of buttress is usually avoided by snow slopes beside the Balfour Face, although the first ascent climbed the buttress. It also appears possible to access the rib from below the Hidden Face. Once on the rib, climb up, around, and through ice bulges to join the West Ridge of Mt Tasman.
routes.ascent: John Harrison, Brian Hearfield, Wally Romanes, Jim Wilson, Dec 1959.

places.name: Balfour Face
places.description: All routes are accessed from the Upper Balfour Neve

routes.name: Surreal Insomnia
routes.description: The nature of this route may change depending on the state of the ice cliffs. On the first ascent, the cliffs were considered ‘inactive-looking’ but this may not always be the case. You decide. The crux on the first ascent involved navigating an awkward ramp that breached a 20m overhanging ice cliff. The first few pitches are pretty staunch too. A wild and exciting climb.

routes.name: Mists of Avalon
routes.description: Ascend steep ice left of the Left Buttress. The first ascent was completed in 13 pitches, the first four being the crux. This could be a nice alternative to the Original if you don’t like the prospect of the amphitheatre, but look up and left to decide if it’s really worth it.

routes.name: Left Buttress
routes.description: Ascend the rock buttress on the left side of the face but right of the prominent icecliffs. Steep climbing on rock gives way to mixed ground and then steep ice onto the summit icefields.

routes.name: Rattus Balfourus
routes.description: Just right of the Left Buttress is a narrow couloir leading up to the headwall ice shared with Route 12.20. Prior to the first ascent, an attempt on this route nearly ended with the rats in a trap after a lead fall and broken ankle. The climbers had to self-rescue, which must have been harrowing.

routes.name: Original Route
routes.description:
This route is considered a classic of its genre, the mountaineer’s piece-de-resistance—steep, sustained, and aesthetic. The first ascent, and the first winter ascent, are up there with Bill Denz’s most well-known achievements in the region. It has since been soloed numerous times.
Ascend the gully (or the rib on its right) in the centre of the face, before finding yourself in a steep amphitheatre surrounded by rising ice walls, which are climbed by tending left. Exiting the amphitheatre can be the crux, as these slopes are steep, sustained, and often covered in hard rime ice feathers. Finish up several pitches of 45-degree ice slopes to the summit. Some parties have climbed the ice walls more directly and finished on the Tasman-Silberhorn ridge.

pitches.description: Gully right of the Original Route. Joins the original route in the ampitheatre. Steep, with hard ice in winter.

routes.name: Right Buttress
routes.description: Depending on the season, this route involves linking either rock pitches or ice runnels. The steepest and most solid rock is on the lower pitches (crux 16 when it’s actually exposed). Higher up the rock quality isn’t so good, but the angle eases off. Tops out below icecliffs on a 50 degree shelf, which is traversed to the right to gain the Silberhorn-Tasman Ridge. Great fun in winter, apparently.

routes.name: Right side gullies

pitches.description: Many variations (not necessarily recorded)  have been climbed around the gullies and buttresses to the right of Route 12.22, all finishing on the Silberhorn-Tasman Ridge. However, the large rock buttress capped by a prominent arête appears to be unclimbed.

routes.ascent: (i) A buttress route: Jeff Sandifort, Thai Vervonsi, Jan 1997

places.name: The Buttress
places.description: A two kilometre long ridge extends north from the foot of Tasman’s North Shoulder separating the Heemskerck and Abel Janszoon Glaciers. There are many more lines to do on The Buttress.

routes.name: COMAC
routes.description: A seven-pitch route up an arête, climbed from the lower Heemskerck Glacier.
routes.ascent: Nick Cradock, D Owen, Susan McNair, Feb 1987.

routes.name: Deuce

pitches.description: Progressive increase in steepness and technical difficulty. Crux near the top in the form of a short overhang.

routes.ascent: Josef Král, Jake Gray, Gavin Lang 22 Sept 2022

routes.name: Son of a Witch
routes.description: Near Witches Col on the south-west side of the buttress is a short, steep ice route which allows good rock protection. The first ascentionists encountered WI3-4 ice. Begins just left of a tongue of rock that trends down and right.

places.name: 11.124  Witches Col
places.description: A snow col situated at the base of the North Buttress. Witches Col enables access (grade II, 3) to the Abel Janszoon Face.

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Mt Teichelmann Rakirua
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: Balfour and La Perouse névés, December 2011

routes.name: South Ridge

pitches.description: Via Clarke Saddle, the route up the Main Divide to the peak is straightforward until the final summit cone where steep rock can be difficult and iced. If not covered by snow the rock is very loose.

routes.ascent: Katie Gardiner, Harold Porter, Vic Williams, Feb 1929.

routes.name: East Ridge
routes.description: From Mt Graham the Main Divide ridge is a simple traverse until the exposed summit cone, which usually involves mixed snow and rock.

routes.name: Via the Main Divide

pitches.description: Either via Silberhorn or Mt Graham, there is little difficulty apart from the final rock cone (it's choss). Also see route 4.43

routes.ascent: First ascent from the Balfour Glacier: Alan Berry, A Clough, R C Western, Dec 1955.

routes.name: Couloir Route

pitches.description: This gully on the north-western side of Mt Teichelmann has also been used as a descent route.

routes.ascent: Nick Von Tunzelmann, A Bowden, Bob Cunninghame, Alex Parton, Jan 1967.

routes.name: Outlier Buttress
routes.description: A prominent rib leading onto the knob between Mts Teichelmann and Magellan is climbed by way of a crack system (crux 14) up the centre.

routes.name: South West Face
routes.description: Begin up steep gullies at the bottom centre of the face. Two pitches of steep ice in these gullies are the crux. They can be avoided by traversing in from the right. Several pitches up icefields lead to steep gullies that run up to the south ridge. First climbed in 13 pitches.

routes.name: Original Route
routes.description:
Access the Donne Glacier from the Frind-Mueller confluence. From the true right edge of the lower Frind Glacier, head up a gully onto a rock rib north of the Ngaroimata Falls, gaining height and tending right to reach the frequently broken Donne.
Ascend left towards the col between Thomson and Eagle Peak, but well before the col head up a rock rib onto the south (Main Divide) ridge.
A large rockfall from the east face onto the Frind Glacier during 1996 may have affected this route.

routes.name: South East Ridge
routes.description: Start up the lower south face, then angle right up a snow lead to the col north of Pt 2453m. Follow the Divide ridge to the summit.

routes.name: Direct #2
routes.description:
Access the Donne Glacier from the Frind-Mueller confluence. From the true right edge of the lower Frind Glacier, head up a gully onto a rock rib north of the Ngaroimata Falls, gaining height and tending right to reach the frequently broken Donne.
Head up the face on Thomson via a rib left of the prominent overhang on the face.
A large rockfall from the east face onto the Frind Glacier during 1996 may have affected this route.

routes.name: Direct #1
routes.description:
Access the Donne Glacier from the Frind-Mueller confluence. From the true right edge of the lower Frind Glacier, head up a gully onto a rock rib north of the Ngaroimata Falls, gaining height and tending right to reach the frequently broken Donne.
Ascend the face and turn the prominent overhang on its northern extremity.
A large rockfall from the east face onto the Frind Glacier during 1996 may have affected this route.
routes.ascent: Otto Von Allmen, Paul Von Kanel, January 1973

routes.name: West Ridge
routes.description: This ridge provides an excellent access route between Harpers Rock and the area around Brunner Col. From Harpers Rock, ascend easy slopes of the broad lower ridge. Avoid a sharper section of the ridge between 2000m and 2140m by sidling on the north. Above 2200m, either stay on the crest of the ridge itself (straightforward snow and rock with some moderate slabs in late summer) or continue sidling on the north to access snowfields north of the summit, from where 150m of steep scrambling leads to the summit.
routes.ascent: Christopher Johnson, Graham Riley, Archie Scott, December 1935

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Mt Vancouver
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: Peaks above the La Perouse névé, December 2011

routes.name: North West Face
routes.description: Climb up into the cirque separating Malaspina and Vancouver, then ascend a gully onto Vancouver.
routes.ascent: Bill King, Ian McAlpine, Steve Rawnsley, February 1985

routes.name: West Buttress
routes.description: Begin up slabs to the left of the buttress crest and follow on up the edge of the buttress on good rock. The climbing becomes harder towards the top. Then follow a snow arête to the summit.

pitches.description: From the Linda Glacier climb up diagonally to the right to gain a steep snow arête leading to the summit. . Occasionally used as a descent route.

routes.name: North East Face

pitches.description: The ridge from Dampier is relatively straightforward (refer to the North Ridge, via Mt Vancouver, Route), on Mt Dampier. Whereas from Malaspina requires traversing rock towers and rock scrambling on unsound rock, which could prove time consuming for a slow party.

routes.description: From the Linda Glacier climb the broad snow slope, which narrows into a prominent gully after a short steeper section. About three quarters of the way up the gully, trend left into a tributary gully and cross another short steep section to gain the Main Divide. Travel is straightforward from here to the summit.

routes.name: North Ridge
routes.description: The ridge from Clarke Saddle over Mt Malaspina involves numerous rock towers and rock scrambling on rotten rock, which can be time consuming.

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Mt Vic
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: Mt Vic is unclimbed directly from the Haupapa Tasman Glacier.

routes.name: Via Main Divide from Coronet
routes.description: Traverse the Main Divide from Mt Coronet.
routes.ascent: Harry Ayres, Mick Bowie, F F Simmons, January 1938

routes.name: North Rib
routes.description: From the Spencer Glacier, the lower rib involves climbing in gullies on the right of the icefall (watch out for ice blocks). The gullies may be snow-filled. The route emerges onto a rock arête that continues in a series of buttresses and arêtes before the final snow and rock ridge to the summit. Rock crux in the lower section. The route could have a number of variations. The easiest descent is probably via Mt Meeson and Mt Coronet.
routes.ascent: Mike Andrews, Bill King, Pete Swanson, January 1981

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Mt Walter
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description:
The east face hosts the Tasman’s most accessible ice routes. They are only moderately long yet many inexperienced/slow parties have been benighted near the summit.
Good quality rock climbs on a sub-peak of Walter (Pt 2782m) can be accessed from Divers Col, and longer rock climbs on the main west face of Walter are accessed from the Elie-Walter Col.

routes.name: South West Ridge
routes.description:
Climb to the plateau below Divers Col (crux), then ascend the snow ridge, veering around schrunds as required. This is the standard descent route.
Has been climbed from the Spenser Glacier (grade III, 1+) by Patrick Duncan, Hanno Fairburn, Ham Gifford, John Leonard, David Medland, Beverley Price, and Ian Simpson in December 1962.
routes.ascent: Alex Graham, Peter Graham, Ebenezer Teichelmann, F W Vollmann, February 1909

routes.name: Geriatric
routes.description: A 400m route starting just right and below where the major icecliffs begin to develop. The route follows a right ascending traverse for four pitches and then heads straight up steep ice onto the ridge 200m from the summit of Mt Walter.

routes.name: Ice Crème
routes.description: Ascend an obvious gully for 300m, which broadens out to join the snowfields left of the summit.

routes.name: Curtains
routes.description: Climb a steep ice curtain, which leads into a broad gully. The gully leads left and finishes directly at the summit.

routes.name: Original
routes.description: Ascend a steep couloir on the right side of the face for 150m, then traverse left into the same gully ascended by Curtains.
routes.ascent: Nick Cradock, Barry Jury, Nic Kagan, June 1977

routes.name: North East Ridge
routes.description:
This ridge is used either to access Elie de Beaumont when the Anna Glacier is cut off, or as a descent option after climbing the East Face. Previously, this ridge had good snow cover and straightforward travel almost year-round. However, over the last few years, because of its northern aspect the snow starts to ablate back to bare rock by early summer. There can be up to 150m of rock to descend or climb. If en-route to Elie, only commit to descending if you’re comfortable climbing grade 12–14 to get back up.
Heading north east from the summit of Mt Walter, the ridge is initially a fairly level, exposed snow arête. The ridge then becomes truncated as it drops down to the Elie-Walter col – i.e. it broadens out to form a vague triangular face above the broad col. The route stays near the true left side of this face, near the edge of the Spencer Face of Walter. A combination of abseiling and downclimbing will get you down without too much hassle. In dry conditions, don’t use the other side, down the edge of Mt Walter’s East Face – the rock is rotten there.
If climbing the ridge from the Elie-Walter col, start on the right side and follow your nose.
routes.ascent: John Read, Stuart Read, Kurt Suter, February 1934

places.name: West Face
places.description: Spencer faces of Mts Elie de Beaumont, Walter and Green, December 2010

routes.name: The Assessor
routes.description: Starting at the lowermost rocks on the face, ascend very good rock for 12 pitches crossing two overlaps, en route to the summit.

routes.name: The Assessed
routes.description: Begins 100m higher and to the right of The Assessor, then follows the left slanting corner to finish north of the summit.

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Pt 2782
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: The west face of Pt 2782m offers comparatively accessible alpine rock climbing for Westland Tai Poutini National Park as it can be accessed from the east via Divers Col.

routes.name: West Rib
routes.description: Begin on the true right of the upper Stevenson Glacier at about 2500m, to the climber’s right of a prominent tongue of snow. Ascend a rib of very good rock for about eight pitches. Recommended for the atmosphere.
routes.ascent: Kester Brown, Paul Hersey, Shelley Hersey, Jamie Vinton-Boot, January 2011

routes.name: Stuntman and Chronic
routes.description: From the upper Stevenson Glacier near Divers Col, ascend a rock spur for five pitches onto the south-west (divide) ridge of Pt 2782m. Recommended for the excellent rock. Sustained.

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Scissors
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: Barron Saddle, Barron Saddle Hut and the upper Mueller Glacier, December 2013

routes.name: East Ridge
routes.description: A blocky ridge. Mostly easy scrambling with a few small steps. Easier when there is more snow around.

routes.name: North East Face

pitches.description: Ascend sound rock which gradually eases back.

routes.description: From Mueller Glacier ascend the steep rock, which gradually eases back.

routes.name: Crew Cut
routes.description: In the centre of the wall between Scissors and Mt Montgomerie there is a broad gully where ice forms in the cooler months. A steep headwall caps the gully and is bypassed on the right, and then straight up slopes to ridge.

routes.name: Scissors–Montgomerie Ridge
routes.description: Exposed rock scrambling. An obvious access route is to ascend under Mt Montgomerie from the lower Welchman Glacier.

routes.name: West Face
routes.description: A long climb on moderately-angled slabs.

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Sharks Teeth
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: Mt Sefton and Main Divide from Welcome Pass, January 2010

routes.name: North Ridge
routes.description: Reach Brunner Col (crux, technical grade 3). Now follow the divide.
routes.ascent: Otto Frind, Conrad Kain, Dick Young, March 1914

routes.name: From Douglas névé
routes.description: Straightforward snow slopes, with some rock scrambling in late summer.
routes.ascent: Bruce Menzies, Earle Riddiford, F O Tozer, January 1942 (southern summit)

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Silberhorn
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: Mt Graham to Mt Tasman

routes.name: Silberhorn Ridge (South East Ridge)*
routes.description:
A significant feature of the Grand Plateau area. Most parties approach either from the lower Linda or beneath Mt Tasman, but a direct line near the crest can sometimes be feasible. All approaches converge beneath a large step of moderately steep rotten rock, which is up to two pitches long by late January. After the rock step, follow a classic snow ridge, sometimes crevassed, to the summit.
Deteriorating conditions on the mid-height rock step over the last few years means that this route is more difficult and dangerous than it used to be. It’s not recommended when the step involves more than half a pitch of exposed rock.
routes.ascent: Jack Clarke, Edward FitzGerald, Mattias Zurbriggen, Feb 1895.

routes.name: From the Balfour Glacier.

pitches.description: An easy, but remote snow climb from the Balfour Glacier.

routes.description: A relatively easy, but remote snow climb. Can be complicated by large schrunds. In winter the slopes are usually covered in hard rime ice.
routes.ascent: Bill Beaven, Norman Hardie, Jim MacFarlane, Earle Riddiford, Dec 1948.

routes.name: East Ridge
routes.description: A scramble from Harper Saddle.
routes.ascent: Hugh Chambers, Conrad Kain, Hugh Wright, February 1915

routes.name: North West Rib
routes.description: Three pitches of very good rock.

routes.name: South West Ridge
routes.description: Gain the Main Divide at Bernard Col or one of the options further north (crux – technical grade 4). Then follow north along rotten rock on the Main Divide (much nicer with plenty of snow). It’s also possible to drop down to the west and climb the north west ridge. The technical grade is from Bernard Col.

routes.name: North East Ridge
routes.description:
Via the Bannie Glacier and Christopher Col, then south over and around several rotten rock towers on the Main Divide.
The first ascentionists then traversed Mt Burns and descended to the Spence Glacier via the Poet Glacier.

places.name: South East Face
places.description:
On Vampire’s South East Face and ‘Left Fang’ (the peak to the left of Far From The Madding Crowd) there have been at least two large rock fall events that have altered the shape of the mountain. These rockfall avalanches occurred in 2003 on the main face, and 2008 on the ‘Left Fang’. The 2003 event was only discovered after study of the 2008 event.
A report by GNS concludes: ‘The south [east] face of Vampire is still considered to be quite unstable … While specifically identified for this site, the hazard is not necessarily greater than beneath many other, steep, fractured slopes within Aoraki / Mount Cook National Park.’
Very little climbing has been recorded on the face since the rockfalls, so little information is available on its stability or difficulty. A climbing party who climbed Nosferatu after 2003 commented that it seemed harder than the published grade. This is due to the gully in the upper part of the route having fallen away, leaving a near vertical gully/headwall. Another party attempted a new route up the middle of the main face after the 2003 event and reported good climbing on steep ice.
The best way to descend from Vampire is probably via Bernard Col – scope out the best looking line from Barron Saddle Hut first.

routes.name: Notforustwo

pitches.description: Vampire’s left fang. The line starts beside a big block, then weaves through to a prominent pillar in a gully, then straight up to the top of the South Peak.

routes.description: Vampire’s left fang. This route starts beside a big block, then weaves through to a prominent pillar in a gully, and then straight up to the top of the South Peak. The route doesn’t appear to have been significantly affected by the rockfall events.

routes.name: Far from the Madding Crowd
routes.description: Ascend the obvious deep, broad gully to the left of the summit for 12 pitches. A classic climb.
routes.ascent: Geoff Gabites, Colin Monteath, Hugh Nicholson, June 1988

routes.name: Single and Searching
routes.description: Start up 'Far from the maddening crowd' a few pitches, to where the angle kicks back, then at the first opportunity, break up the right hand wall, aiming for the obvious ice hose spilling down the steep cliffs near the summit.  Climb initially thin curtains of ice to easier angle ground.  Continue up past another crux (thin pillar), which on the FA was bypassed by tenuous mixed climbing on the right - with a dry tooling traverse back left to rejoin the gully just above the pillar - then continue up good WI2 - 3 to the base of the hanging crux pillar on the headwall.  Mixed climbing to M6 for a few metres on the right, then step left onto the pillar and continue up with angle gradually easing to WI4.  The first 10m of this pitch were rope soloed on the first ascent (otherwise ropeless).  Continue up steep water ice then steep snow slopes to top out shortly SW of the summit.  On FA, Descent was by downclimbing snow slopes/gullies on W face vampire, then walking to Bernard Col and downclimbing the couloir and snow slopes back to the base of Vampire. See NZAJ 2020 for details.

routes.name: Nosferatu
routes.description: Follow the gully that starts on the left side of the lowest rock buttress beneath the summit. This gully eases back after five pitches. Further up an obvious snow ramp leads left to gain the main summit gully. It appears that since the 2003 rockfall the snow ramp has been replaced by a near-vertical headwall of about two pitches. (A couple of options are indicated in the topo photo.) After this the angle eases and the gully continues to exit 30m left of the summit. The first ascent took fifteen pitches in all.

routes.name: Bram Stoker
routes.description: An obvious deep-cut gully that starts just right of the lowest point of rock beneath Vampire. Well up the face, the gully ends, but the route continues tending left. Exit on the ridge just beneath the summit tower. Eleven pitches.

routes.name: Twilight
routes.description: 7 pitchs to WI3, topping out on the ridge and rapping the route.  Sometimes thin ice during the first ascent.

routes.name: Swiss Virgins
routes.description: Ascend a couloir right of Bram Stoker for six rope lengths to reach the Main Divide north of the summit. If descending from here, it may be quicker to descend via Christopher Col than to continue over the summit to Bernard Col.

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Watch Tower
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: Barron Saddle, Barron Saddle Hut and the upper Mueller Glacier, December 2013

routes.name: South East Ridge
routes.description: From Fyfe Pass, this short but sharp ridge involves exposed scrambling.

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Aiguilles Rouges
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.access: The lower half of the north ridge is equipped (2017) with double bolt anchors to allow for 30m abseils.
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: An excellent peak for those wanting to sample similar climbing to that found on Malte Brun, but on a smaller scale and with an easier descent.

routes.name: South Face
routes.description: From the approach to the East Ridge, traverse across the Onslow Glacier to gain the broad rib on the right side of the face. Head up the rib, which eventually merges into the 45–50 degree slopes of the upper face, arriving on the summit ridge between the East and High Peaks. Quite threatened by icecliffs (2018).

routes.name: Central Spur
routes.description: A vague series of spurs and shingle ledges leading to a prominent snowfield (could be shingle in late summer), then up the small spur left of the Central Gully. Joins the North Ridge below the summit.

routes.name: East Ridge
routes.description: An enjoyable climb with plenty of variety. From Onslow Hut, cross the stream draining the Onslow Glacier and then climb north to Pt 2195m. Apart from a short section of rotten rock at about 1700m, this lower part of the climb is straightforward. Above Pt 2195m, the flat sections of the east ridge can be avoided by keeping to the Onslow Glacier, but two prominent rock steps have to be climbed where the ridge begins to steepen, and another 200m further on a snow bulge is climbed. The route then gradually lies back up to the East Peak. Descend the North East Flank down to Malte Brun Pass.
routes.ascent: M J P Glasgow, Harry Stevenson, December 1951 (to East Pk)

routes.name: North East Ridge
routes.description: This ridge starts in the Cascade Glacier, but is usually gained at half height by traversing from Malte Brun Pass. Ascend on mediocre rock over the East Peak and on to the High Peak.

routes.name: North East Flank
routes.description: This is the easiest route on Aiguilles Rouges, and the standard descent route. From Malte Brun Pass, make your way up the large snowfield to the left (east) of the north ridge. Take your pick from three couloirs from the top of the snowfield, the left one leading up to near the East Peak, the central one providing access to broad snowslopes leading to the main summit, and the right one leading to high on the north ridge.
routes.ascent: Freda Du Faur, Peter Graham, March 1913

routes.name: North Ridge
routes.description:
Put this on your list. From Malte Brun Pass, pick a line up the beautiful red rock of the broad lower ridge. The lower part of the ridge is made up of several sub-ridges that eventually lead into the main ridgeline around half height. Don’t climb too far right unless you want steeper rock. After 300m the ridge narrows and relents, but the rock quality decreases somewhat.
The lower half of the ridge is equipped (2017) with double bolt anchors to allow for 30m abseils. This line can be climbed directly (crux grade 12–13). If descending the ridge, the anchors are easy to find if you stay near the crest, unless the ridge is covered in snow. One of the upper abseils involves a slightly awkward leftwards traverse to avoid a gully. An intermediate bolt has been placed to assist with the traverse.

routes.name: Left Spur
routes.description:
The first prominent spur on the North West Face, to the right of the Malte Brun Pass approach gully. Start either:
(i) from the upper Beetham Stream, climbing the lower buttress (crux) as on the first ascent; or
(ii) by traversing in from Malte Brun Pass on shingle ledges.
The upper ridge has slightly easier climbing, and finishes on the North Ridge.

routes.name: Central Gully
routes.description: Beginning in the Beetham valley, climb the gully left of the west ridge. Climbed when filled with snow/ice.
routes.ascent: Murray Ball and four mountaineering course participants, January 1983

routes.name: West Ridge
routes.description: Gain the prominent snowfield/scree ledge, either by traversing from Malte Brun Pass or by ascending the lower part of one of the above three routes. Gain the west ridge from the right edge of the snow/scree, then ascend good rock with some surprisingly difficult sections.
routes.ascent: Ian Cave, Mike Gill, John Nichols, February 1960

routes.name: Tiddley Pom
routes.description: Ascend the left most of three prominent couloirs on the south-west face.

routes.name: South Ridge
routes.description: Gained by the right most of three prominent couloirs on the south-west face, which is large, winding, and ends in a short, rotten rock face. The south ridge is rather rotten at first but improves towards the top.
routes.ascent: J Boyd, M McPhail, John Nankervis, January 1973

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Frind Pk
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: Malte Brun and Frind Peak above the Murchison Glacier, May 2017

routes.name: From Cascade Glacier
routes.description: This used to be a straightforward climb up the snow slope beginning at about 1950m on the true left edge of the Cascade Glacier. Glacial recession has steepened the base of this slope, but it’s probably still not too difficult.

routes.name: South East Ridge
routes.description: If you can access the base of this ridge, it’s mostly a straightforward climb, although there is a small notch that can be time consuming to get through.
routes.ascent: R M Crockett, W G McClymont, J H Rose, F F Simmons, December 1934

routes.name: East Face
routes.description: From the Baker Glacier just above the main icefall, climb direct to summit.

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Haeckel Pk
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: Mt Hamilton, Haeckel Peak and Rose Peak from the Murchison valley, December 2016

routes.name: North Ridge
routes.description: From the Annan-Haeckel Col, follow the rubbly but straightforward ridge.
routes.ascent: R M Crockett, W G McClymont, F F Simmons, December 1934 (descended)

routes.name: First World War
routes.description: Climbs the far right edge of the west face. From the Darwin Glacier, ascend the lower section of a tributary glacier that leads towards Mt Hamilton, then cross a rock spur that leads to Pt 2835m to gain a large snowfield below and right of the Haeckel summit block. From the snowfield, climb to a square snow patch on the west face (could be a rocky shelf in late summer), then onto the upper South West Ridge. Ernst Haeckel was the first person known to use the term ‘First World War’, the same year Frind and Kain used this route.

routes.name: South West Ridge
routes.description:
Gain the Hamilton-Haeckel Col via:
(i) the snowpatch below and right of Haeckel (as per First World War);
(ii) up the lower North Ridge of Hamilton to Pt 2633m, then traverse to the col; or
(iii) from the Bonney Glacier, across the North Ridge of Hamilton near Pt 2633m.
From the col, ascend the loose rock ridge.
routes.ascent: Jack Clarke, Bernard Head, Jim Murphy, January 1912

routes.name: East Ridge
routes.description: Gain the base of the ridge at 2580m via one of the following options: (i) the Dixon Glacier, (ii) Rose Peak, or (iii) the upper Mannering. Then climb the ridge on straightforward snow and rock slopes to the summit.
routes.ascent: R M Crockett, W G McClymont, F F Simmons, December 1934

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Malcher Pk
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: Lower Malte Brun Range and Murchison River flats, May 2017

routes.name: North East Ridge
routes.description: A straightforward ascent from Dorothy Stream.

routes.name: South West Ridge
routes.description: A straightforward ascent from Dorothy Stream.

routes.name: East Rib
routes.description: From the Murchison flats, begin at the stream 800m down valley from Burnett Stream. Head up the stream to about 1200m, climb north-east onto a ridge, then drop down steep scree to reach Burnett Stream at about 1300m. From the Burnett Stream basin, ascend the central of three prominent ribs to reach the main range about 250m south of the summit.

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Malte Brun
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.access:
Most routes on Malte Brun begin on the Bonney Glacier. The upper Bonney can be accessed either up the Darwin Glacier and lower Bonney (there is sometimes a marginal route through the icefalls until New Year), or more reliably up the Turnbull Glacier (use ledges on the true left to get around the rock step).
The Malte Brun Glacier should not be used as an access route to the Bonney – it has almost completely disappeared, and there is now an unpleasant 3-pitch climb on terrible rock to reach the col at the head of the glacier.
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: Malte Brun is a grand mountain that has been seducing mountaineers for more than 120 years. The north and west aspects offer excellent, long climbs on mostly good rock, and the South West Face hosts a range of ice/snow climbs.

routes.name: North East Ridge
routes.description: Descend the South West Ridge of Mt Hamilton to a narrow rubbly notch (the Hamilton-Malte Brun col). Alternatively, ascend directly to the col via a narrow couloir from the Bonney Glacier. From the col, climb up a steep slab for 100m, then on up the ridge, which rises in a series of short steps of good rock.

routes.name: Multi Sport
routes.description: Up prominent a rock rib to the right of the gully on the north face from the Bonney Glacier, 15-20 pitches. The first two thirds of the route is on fantastic rock. The last third is quite chossy. The first ascent was done with bivvy gear and the team descended the Bonney Rib.

routes.name: Malte Brun’s Treasure Box
routes.description: This climb is a variation on Multi Sport and shares the same first 7 pitches. The climb is 16 full pitches at which point the route meets the North East Ridge at 3000m.  From here to the summit a lot of chossy Jenga tower ridge line traversing is required. The first ascent was done with bivvy gear and descent was down the Bonney Rib.

routes.name: North Face
routes.description: From the lower Bonney Glacier, ascend the ribs and slabs of good rock between the North East and North Ridges. There’s plenty of room for variations.
routes.ascent: A C Rattray, J C Stamers-Smith, December 1958

routes.name: North Ridge
routes.description: Similar in difficulty to the Bonney Rib—combining these routes would make an excellent traverse of Malte Brun. Most parties begin from the Bonney Glacier just above the upper icefall, but there is wide scope for variations. The first 25m involves delicate climbing on rounded holds, where the glacier has retreated in recent years. Above this the rock is good and the holds more positive (sustained climbing), with a short cheval section higher up. Highly recommended.

routes.name: North West Face
routes.description: The scene of Tom Fyfe’s remarkable 1894 solo climb. Fyfe’s route ascends to the left of a shallow couloir in the centre of the face. Other routes ascend to the right of the couloir while some variations keep closer to the North Ridge. Sustained climbing on generally good rock.

routes.name: The Big Couloir
routes.description: From the névé of the Bonney Glacier, ascend the prominent snow and ice couloir to within 200m of the summit. Not recommended, especially in late summer, as some of the worst rock on Malte becomes exposed in the upper couloir. This is not the couloir famously glissaded by Fyfe, which is smaller and further left.
routes.ascent: F McMahon, A Simpson, R Yates, December 1964

routes.name: Bonney Headwall
routes.description:
The Bonney Headwall is a good late season option for the West Ridge when access to the base of the Bonney Rib is cut off.
From the head of the Bonney Glacier, scramble up and left on slabs/snow for 100m. Pick a line up compact rock that steepens progressively to a crux before reaching a ledge (two or three pitches). Continue up another three or four pitches to the cheval, or follow the ledge to the right to meet the top of the Bonney Rib.
routes.ascent: Brendan Gaynor, Ewan Reid, John Zapp, John Menin, December 1971

routes.name: Bonney Rib
routes.description:
Highly recommended. Now that the Yak Route has become frequently difficult to access, the Bonney Rib is the best way to sample the delights of Malte Brun’s famous cheval – a spectacularly exposed and narrow section of solid red rock. Many parties start this climb from a good bivvy/camp spot on the col between the Bonney and Malte Brun Glaciers, below the prominent gendarmes at the base of the Bonney Rib.
From the Bonney névé, use snowfields to access the rib above the gendarmes, then climb good rock (crux) to join the West Ridge. Turn left and follow the ridge, which narrows until the cheval is reached. After negotiating the cheval, the ridge broadens and becomes slightly easier, but the rock quality deteriorates. The summit is another 200m higher and can take a surprisingly long time from the cheval.
This is now the standard descent route and most parties require a few abseils to return down the rib. On your way up make a note of where to turn off the ridge. Please take old tat from previous climbs with you on your way down – it’s unsightly and unsafe.
First ascent unknown.

routes.name: Biophilia

pitches.description: Head up from obvious start to join weakness. Chimney moves are the crux
Follow weakness/ crack then head left to Arete.
Continue up arete to large ledge, then follow right trending cracks up to belay ledge.
Step up to tiny roof, step right, then follow red rock keeping approx 10m right of grey corner.
Continue up 12m then cross left over grey corner onto new red rib. Steep and fun. Best pitch **
25m to ledge, ignore existing rap station 10m out left. Plug in .5 cam into grey roof, then step onto red prow.
Easy scrambling to apex of West Ridge. Some existing anchors/ bollards in place at approx 25m intervals.

routes.description:
An objectively 'safe' rock route with compact featured slabs. A great way to access the West Ridge and descend. Reached from the top of the Malte Brun Glacier either at the left hand edge (grade 16), or more easily up the right hand ramp (see white lines on photo). Rap stations (pitons and nuts) have been established at roughly 60m length on ascent. The route was first attempted up to pitch 4.5 in mountain boots in 2015, and retreat was due to lack of gear. The first complete ascent was done with rock shoes in optimal climbing conditions, switching to approach shoes at the apex of the West Ridge. BYO rap cord and expect to replace it completely.
Route photo taken from summit of Rumdoodle in February 2015 with slightly more snow on the route than on the first complete ascent.
Useful GPS waypoints, current in 2020 are:
The point to aim for when climbing the moraine wall (this will get you to the old Malte Brun hut site:
Lat: -43.54864
Long: 170.28069
NZTM 1380331  5174664
Elevation: 1640m
Top of the access gully:
Lat: -43.55025
Long:170.28311
Elev: 1828m
Bivvy site (there are many others):
Lat: -43.55298
Long: 170.28782
Elev: 2036m

routes.name: Yak Route
routes.description:
This has long been a popular route, as it provided the least technical way to the upper West Ridge. However, over the last few years there has been rampant recession of the Malte Brun Glacier, which has exposed more difficult rock. By late summer there can also be sections of steep, hard, old basal ice that require good mountaineering skills to negotiate.
From the true left edge of the upper Malte Brun Glacier, negotiate one to two pitches of glacier-worn rock (crux), tend right up a ramp, then head up the line of least resistance to gain the West Ridge (a number of options exist). Follow the ridge to the top of the Bonney Rib, after which the ridge narrows until the cheval is reached. After negotiating the cheval, the ridge broadens and becomes slightly easier, but the rock quality deteriorates. The summit is another 200m higher and can take a surprisingly long time from the cheval.

routes.name: West Ridge
routes.description: A very long climb, recently made slightly more difficult due to rockfall. The lower ridge is straightforward, but some parties have opted to avoid it by sidling on scree on the north side of the ridge, climbing back up to regain the ridge at a col at 2250m. From there, follow the ridge on good rock. At one point, a large chunk of the ridge has fallen off, leaving a notch with a very steep, smooth pillar of rock on the uphill (eastern) side. From the notch, traverse horizontally on the left (north) side – about grade 12, but very exposed – to bypass the difficult rock, then climb up to regain the ridge. The ridge has some sustained sections of climbing before it eases off. Cross the cheval and continue another 200m higher to the summit.
routes.ascent: Laurence Earle, Freda Du Faur, Peter Graham, January 1910

routes.name: Maxi the Taxi
routes.description: A pillar on the north side of the lower west ridge provides excellent climbing.
routes.ascent: Max Dorflinger, Otto Von Allmen, December 1972

places.name: South West Face
places.description: South West Face of Malte Brun – right side – from Malte Brun Pass, December 2009

routes.name: Moore Gully
routes.description: Ascend the prominent gully on the left side of the face to reach the West Ridge below the cheval.

routes.name: Central Rib
routes.description: From halfway up the Beetham Glacier, ascend broken spurs and ridges on the left side of the prominent central rib to join the upper West Ridge.
routes.ascent: Ian Cave, Mike Gill, John Nichols, February 1960

routes.name: The Christmas Turkey
routes.description: Start up a prominent couloir in the centre of the face (between two distinct arêtes), and ascend until the couloir peters out. Traverse left around a buttress then ascend gullies to the upper West Ridge.
routes.ascent: Roddie MacKenzie, Craig Nottle, Graham Sanders, December 1981

routes.name: Snuff
routes.description: Climbs the distinct arete to the right of the Christmas Turkey, beginning just to the left of the ‘big red spot’ at the bottom of the face. A couple of scrambly pitches on poor rock lead to steepening ground with good rock (two crux pitches). The upper part of the route is again easier angled with poor rock. The first ascentionists climbed the route in 16 pitches.

routes.name: Rock n Roll Part 1
routes.description: Ascend the third prominent snow cone left of the South Ridge, then on up mixed snow and rock, with two short steep steps. After 200m, easier ground leads up rightwards towards the summit. If clear of snow and ice, the rock is not very sound.
routes.ascent: Dave Fearnley, Fiona MacKenzie, Craig Nottle, December 1983

routes.name: Rock n Roll Part 2
routes.description: Left of Rightside Direct. When good ice covers the ‘forgettable rock’ then this route could be worth a look, otherwise probably not.
routes.ascent: Craig Nottle, Dave Fearnley, Fiona MacKenzie, January 1984

routes.name: Rightside Direct
routes.description:
Ascend the second prominent snow cone left of the South Ridge and, ignoring a ramp leading right to the Zig Zag route, ascend five steep ice pitches to reach easier-angled snow slopes leading to the summit.
A route between Rock n Roll Part 2 and Rightside Direct was soloed by Greg Aimer in late 1984, which may have involved a large portion of Rightside Direct.

routes.name: Zig Zag
routes.description: A classic, which is often in condition when the other ice routes on the face are not. Ascend the second prominent snow cone from the South Ridge and follow a ramp out right and into an amphitheatre. Move up left onto the crest of a buttress, then follow snowfields to the summit. The route was skied in the spring of 2017.

routes.name: South Ridge
routes.description: From Malte Brun Pass, skirt around the first few pinnacles on the west side of the lower ridge, then head up the crest of the ridge, which rises in two long steps. The rock is very rotten and in parts the ridge is quite exposed. Not recommended as a summer climb, but rather when it is covered with snow and ice (this doesn’t stop some people though). Probably the best way to descend if you’ve just climbed the South West Face.
routes.ascent: Peter Graham, Claude Macdonald, Jim Murphy, February 1909

places.name: East Face
places.access: To access Malte Brun’s east face, climb Frind Peak, and then cross the Baker névé.
places.description: East face of Malte Brun, August 2016

routes.name: Central Buttress
routes.description: Near the centre of the east face is a broad gully with a prominent rock rib on the left, a snow and rock rib on the right, and a steep rocky headwall. From the Baker névé, head up the gully on moderately steep snow/ice (up to 55 degrees), then below the headwall move right onto the mixed snow and rock arête and up to the summit ridge. A route best done fairly quickly due to risk from ice avalanches and rockfall.

routes.name: Original Route
routes.description: From the Baker névé, ascend the moderately steep snow slope to the left of the East Rib into an ice couloir that leads onto the upper East Rib.
routes.ascent: Bernie Gunn, Fred Hollows, Barrie Jackson, Gillian Soper, December 1952

routes.name: East Rib
routes.description: A classic route. From the Baker névé, gain the rib via snow slopes on the left and ascend the mixed snow and rock steps. The rib eases into a snow arête and joins the top of the north-east ridge.
routes.ascent: Bill Beaven, Ian Gibbs, Earle Riddiford, Hugh Tyndale-Biscoe, January 1953

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Mt Abel
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: Previously known as Peak 9144, Close to Kelman and Tasman Saddle huts, Mt Abel has a number of short popular routes. The summit is an excellent viewpoint. Descent is usually by the Red Buttress or the Pencil Couloir. See the Kelman Hut logbook for up-to-date information on fixed gear for abseiling.

routes.name: East Ridge
routes.description: The most satisfying was to approach this ridge is all the way from Starvation Saddle (along mixed snow and rock), but it can also be gained from the upper Murchison below the north-east face of Mt Abel. The final 250m rock ridge leading up to the summit is generally loose.
routes.ascent: F J Austin, J B Butchers, J C Mathews, December 1957

routes.name: Kelmanator Left
routes.description: Start up the main gully on the left side of the north-west face, then break left to follow the easiest-looking route. Best when there’s plenty of snow around. A funnel for rock fall. First ascent unknown.

routes.name: Kelmanator Right
routes.description: Start up the main gully on the left side of the north-west face, then stay right to climb the gully on the left of the large buttress. A winter and spring route involving M3 climbing. First ascent unknown.

routes.name: Brown Buttress
routes.description: The buttress left of Red Buttress. First ascent unknown.

routes.name: Red Buttress
routes.description: The best route on Abel when thereʻs not much snow around, with around 180m of good rock at grade 10–12 followed by scrambling to the summit. There are four bolted abseil stations, all a full 30m apart. Two of these are not on the ascent route, so donʻt be fooled on your way up. The top-most station is about as low as is possible to scramble without a rope. When abseiling from the distinct notch in the buttress, head down the Pencil Couloir side.

routes.name: Pencil Couloir
routes.description: Popular when there is plenty of snow around. About 200m of 35–40 degree snow with some short steeper steps. First ascent unknown.

routes.name: West Ridge
routes.description: From the Abel-Kain col, the ridge involves moderately steep scrambling on loose rock.

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Mt Annan
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: The northern aspects of Mt Annan and Mt Darwin above Tasman Saddle Hut, December 2017

routes.name: North East Ridge
routes.description: Scramble up loose rock.

routes.name: Couloir Route
routes.description: Ascend the gully beside the North East Ridge, mostly on moderately angled snow. This is the most commonly used descent route from Annan.
routes.ascent: D Smyth, J B Waterhouse, February 1966

routes.name: Annan Buttress
routes.description: Ascend three prominent rocksteps on good rock, interspersed with short snow sections. A number of variations are possible.
routes.ascent: Brian Dawkins, Bob McKegg, Bruce Popplewell, Bill Stephenson, December 1968

routes.name: South Ridge
routes.description: Starts at the Annan-Haeckel Col, which is accessed either directly from the Darwin Glacier (complicated by an icefall) or (as on the first ascent) over Haeckel Peak. Above the Annan-Haeckel Col, the ridge provides little difficulty.
routes.ascent: R M Crockett, W G McClymont, F F Simmons, December 1934

routes.name: East Rib
routes.description:
The Mannering Glacier comprises two arms – the lower Mannering Glacier (draining Starvation Saddle) and the upper Mannering Glacier (draining Haeckel, Mt Annan, Mt Kain, and Mt Abel). To access the upper Mannering Glacier, climb the rock step on the true left of the icefall.
Cross the névé below Mt Abel to gain the crest of the rib, which leads directly to the summit of Mt Annan. The rib involves a mix of wide snow slopes and rock bands.
routes.ascent: Bob Gunn, John Nankervis, John Wild, December 1968

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Mt Chudleigh
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description:
Mt Chudleigh is a prominent massif that offers several moderate mountaineering routes. The Reay valley approach makes the peak relatively accessible. Yet there has been a lack of attention in recent years – could the reason simply be the peak’s name? E R Chudleigh was a hard-working sheep farmer in the Rangitata, who climbed frequently in the Murchison and Godley. Don’t be put off just because the name doesn’t have a ring to it: this is an area that hosts some enjoyable outings on reasonable rock.
The exact locations of the routes on the south-east face are uncertain – the descriptions are taken from journal articles and previous editions of this guide.

routes.name: South East Face Direct
routes.description: Begin in the centre of the face with one pitch of tricky mixed climbing (limited protection), followed by two pitches traversing to the right, and then three pitches straight up. The next two pitches are the crux, and were about M5 with poor protection for the first ascentionists. Three more pitches up 45–50 degree snow leads to the summit ridge. The first ascentionists accessed the face from the Tasman via the Reay Glacier.

routes.name: Walking the Dog
routes.description: This route on the south-esat face may share its start with the Direct. From the Lecky Glacier névé, ascend mixed ground on the left of the face, and then ascend and traverse right to an arête, topped by an exit gully 100m north of the summit.

routes.name: Spaghetti Route
routes.description: From the Lecky névé, ascend steep mixed ground ‘directly under the summit’ to gain a snowfield, then traverse left and up to gain a prominent snow arête (possibly the same arête as Walking the Dog). Finish up gullies to the north of the summit.

routes.name: East Ridge Variation
routes.description: From the true left edge of the Lecky Glacier, climb onto the ridge where it begins the final sweep to the summit. Ascend for 300m, then traverse diagonally left for at least five rope lengths to finish at the same point as the Spaghetti Route.

routes.name: North East Ridge
routes.description: From the Barkley Glacier, ascend a couloir to the low point in the ridge (Barkley Col) then climb the ridge, which is at first pinnacled and then rises steadily. The rock is loose.

routes.name: North Face
routes.description: From the upper true right branch of the Barkley Glacier, head right up a small ice ramp to gain a large snow/scree shelf low on the main north face. Climb rock to the right of the big gully to join the top of the North West Ridge.

routes.name: North West Ridge
routes.description: Best approached from the Reay valley via the Walpole Glaciers, but can also be reached from the Langdale or Barkley Glaciers. Once on the ridge, ascend a pleasant snow arête that leads high onto the mountain, then climb a short stretch of rotten rock to the summit. A good descent route.
routes.ascent: Hugh Chambers, Freda Du Faur, Jim Murphy, January 1911

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Mt Chudleigh Middle Pk
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: Mt Chudleigh’s Middle Peak was first climbed by Alex Graham, Peter Graham and Ebenezer Teichelmann in February 1910, via the Reay Glacier Route to the Low Peak.

routes.name: Walpole Buttress
routes.description: The buttress leads up to the summit ridge just left of the Middle Peak. The route follows poor rock on the left side of the buttress.

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Mt Chudleigh South Pk
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: Aiguilles Rouges and Mts Nathan, Chudleigh and Johnson from near the Grand Plateau, January 2013

routes.name: Walpole Face
routes.description: From the head of the true left branch of the Walpole Glacier, ascend a broad rock buttress to the summit, with some snow/ice the gullies in early summer.
routes.ascent: I B Pledger, Kurt Suter, Peter Weenink, December 1934

routes.name: West Ridge
routes.description: Originally climbed from the corner of the Walpole valley. The ridge provides a varied fare of rock climbing over pinnacles, across chevals, and up short walls. The rock is variable and in places offers some difficult moves. The final rise to the South Peak is up short slabs interspersed with ledges. The climbing here is easier than lower on the ridge.

routes.name: Left Buttress
routes.description: On the Reay face of the West Ridge, climb the pillar on the right of the dark argillite band. Enjoyable rock climbing for ten pitches, finishing on Pt 2477m.
routes.ascent: Dave Begg, Hugh Logan, E Neve, N Reeves, November 1977

routes.name: Central Buttress
routes.description: This buttress on the Reay face of the West Ridge finishes on Pt 2617m. Climb the line of weakness up the obvious slabs on the right of the buttress. Five pitches of good rock of mostly grade 12 (avoidable cruxes of 14 and 18) are followed by 12 pitches of loose rock (crux 17). The first ascensionists descended a gully between the Left and Central Buttresses.

routes.name: Main Buttress Left Side
routes.description: On the Reay face of the West Ridge, begin near the base of the Central Buttress, then follow up the left side of the Main Buttress to finish on the summit ridge of Mt Chudleigh, 300m southwest of the South Peak.

routes.name: Main Buttress
routes.description: On the Reay face, climb the centre of the buttress to finish on the summit ridge of Mt Chudleigh, 300m southwest of the South Peak. The crux of the route is up high.

routes.name: Reay Glacier Route
routes.description:
From the upper Reay Glacier, either:
(i) head up the edge of snow slopes west of Pt 2605m to gain the upper snowfields; or
(ii) climb to Reay Col then scramble over Pt 2605m on loose rock.
The upper snowfields lead to the South Peak. If crevasses are problematic, sticking close to the west edge of the face is likely to give the best travel. A good descent route, which appears to offer a way through even in late summer.
routes.ascent: Alec Graham, Peter Graham, Ebenezer Teichelmann, February 1910

routes.name: Lecky Glacier Route
routes.description: From the Murchison, ascend toward Reay Col, but 200m below the col head straight up steep snow, keeping left of some icecliffs, to reach the upper snowfields.

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Mt Cooper
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: Mt Annan and the Mannering Glacier, December 2016

routes.name: From Starvation Saddle
routes.description: A straightforward climb from Starvation Saddle – and also from the Mannering névé or the upper Murchison.

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Mt Darwin
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: The northern aspects of Mt Annan and Mt Darwin above Tasman Saddle Hut, December 2017

routes.name: Annan-Darwin Ridge
routes.description: A long rock ridge involving five (but you might find more) major rock steps of dubious quality rock.
routes.ascent: D Smyth, J B Waterhouse, February 1966

routes.name: Horn/McLean Rib
routes.description: Ascend the prominent rib onto the Annan-Darwin Ridge. The lower half of the rib is good rock, but the upper section contains some evil looking, loose black gullies.

routes.name: Couloir Route
routes.description: Climb the couloir between the Horn/McLean Rib and the Central Buttress.

routes.name: Central Buttress
routes.description: Commence up solid rock from the right toe of the buttress and ascend to the first snowfield. Then traverse right and up to a second snowfield before taking the left of two prominent rock buttresses. Above here the climbing becomes easy scrambling on broken rock.
routes.ascent: Geoff Wayatt, A Cross, M Douglas, T Terry, R Smith, January 1967

routes.name: Lost Bolt Buttress
routes.description: Ascend the original route but take the right of the two prominent rock buttresses. So named because a Japanese party placed a bolt ladder that no one has found again.

routes.name: North West Arête
routes.description:
Ascend the prominent rock spur leading up onto the West Ridge.
