Several routes have been descended to the left (north) of the North West Arête, but be careful as some couloirs end in bluffs.

routes.name: West Ridge
routes.description: A long climb gained from the névé feeding the Tasman Glacier above Darwin Corner. Narrow and loose in places. This is the recommended descent route from Darwin.
routes.ascent: Jack Clarke, Tom Fyfe, Franz Von Kronecker, March 1894

routes.name: Natural Selection
routes.description: Climbs Darwin’s south-west face. Up easy snow slopes trending slightly left of the black thumbnail and the corniced ridge above. Steep climbing and technical crux (AI4) lessening to 70 degree ice leads left up a snow-ice couloir to a ridgeline. Traverse left and straight up a headwall for 80m of 60 degree ice.

routes.name: Arbon-Waterhouse
routes.description: On the south face above the Darwin Glacier, head up the left edge of a large snow/ice field, winding around icecliffs and crevasses where necessary. Finish via a couloir onto the west ridge at about 2800m, then continue to the summit.

routes.name: Original Route
routes.description: Ascend towards the saddle at the head of the Darwin Glacier, weaving around crevasses as required, then cut left up snowslopes on the south face to reach the west ridge 150m from the summit.
routes.ascent: B Carter, J Cruse, R H Peate, J M Rowe, December 1955

pitches.description: Ski initially downhill from Kelman or Tasman Saddle Huts, and then up a broad slope to a shoulder at 933840, where there are great views across to Mt Malte Brun. A good ski run of around 500 vertical metres may be obtained back to the floor of the Tasman Glacier.

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Mt Hamilton
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: Mt Hamilton and the Baker, Wheeler and Dixon Glaciers, March 2013

routes.name: North Ridge
routes.description: This is the most straightforward route on Mt Hamilton. From the Bonney Glacier, climb snowslopes to a prominent col on the north ridge near Pt 2633m. Then either ascend the rock ridge, the snow gully on the left, or further left to the north-east ridge, which is a narrow affair that gradually broadens. These routes converge about 200m north of the summit.
routes.ascent: Jack Clarke, Laurence Earle, Alec Graham, December 1909

routes.name: West Flank
routes.description: From above the lower icefall in the Bonney Glacier, ascend the obvious gut in the West Flank (the face left of the major central gully). At the headwall of the gut, break left to the upper snow slope, then join the top of the North Ridge. The climbing was on a mix of snow and rock during the first ascent.

routes.name: West Wall
routes.description:
Begins about 80m right (south) of the base of the major gully. Climb up for three pitches (crux) and then head left on a rising traverse to reach a rib of good rock in the middle of the face. Climb this, then:
(i) head right on a rising traverse to top out sooner, as on the first ascent; or
(ii) finish directly up the unclimbed rib, which appears to offer some of the best climbing on the face.
Rock quality on this route is good apart from two chossy pitches on the leftwards traverse.

routes.name: South West Ridge
routes.description: Usually descended in conjunction with a climb of the North East Ridge of Malte Brun. The ridge is relatively straightforward, but becomes rotten near the Hamilton-Malte Brun col. There is also a direct route onto the col, which ascends a narrow couloir from the Bonney Glacier.

routes.name: South East Arête
routes.description: A rarely climbed but beautiful line. From the Murchison Valley floor, ascend the ridge between the Baker and Wheeler Glaciers onto a subsidiary peak, then up the snow arête to an ice bulge. The shape of the bulge, and its difficulty, changes over time. As at 2018, icecliff cut off the route, but the face to the left may offer a feasible route. After negotiating the bulge, continue up the face to the summit. Probably best in early summer.
routes.ascent: Bernie Gunn, Fred Hollows, Barrie Jackson, Gillian Soper, December 1952

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Mt Johnson
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.access:
Access to the Reay valley is currently straightforward (February 2015). Walk up the Tasman Glacier then ascend a prominent, rightwards-leaning moraine ledge on the true right of the valley entrance (the true left looks impenetrable). Once in the valley, sidle upwards on the true right to the confluence of the Reay and Walpole Streams where small campsites among snowgrass can be found. From Ball Shelter to the confluence of the Reay and Walpole Streams takes about 6 hours.
Above the Murchison valley, access to the terraces beneath Novara Peak and Mt Johnson can be found up the slopes beside the Burnett Glacier. Between the Burnett and Lecky glaciers lie tussock basins with good campsites, but there are steep walls leading from these terraces down to the river.
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: Lower Malte Brun Range and Murchison River flats, May 2017

routes.name: North East Ridge
routes.description: An adventurous climb. From Reay Col, traverse a 2km ridge of jumbled rock with steps becoming increasingly harder. From a sharp notch just north of the summit, ascend a final face of three pitches (crux) to the summit.
routes.ascent: Ray Arbon, Lindsay Main, Bruce Waterhouse, December 1978

routes.name: North West Ridge
routes.description: This ridge begins at Dorothy Col, east of Pt 2493m. Get to the col either (i) up a moderately steep couloir from the Reay valley, or (ii) via the Dorothy Glacier (see Haupapa Tasman Glacier for access details). From the col, follow the pleasant rock ridge to the summit. First ascent unknown.

routes.name: West Face
routes.description: Climb to the head of Dorothy Stream, but before the top of the Dorothy Glacier is reached, turn right and head straight up good, fairly easy rock to the summit.

routes.name: South West Ridge
routes.description: Climb to ridge between Mt Malcher and Mt Johnson, then along the undulating ridge to the summit. First ascent unknown.

routes.name: South East Face
routes.description: From the Burnett Glacier, ascend the prominent rock rib leading to the summit.
routes.ascent: Rob Blackburne, Mike Brosnahan, Ross Cullen, Nick Shearer, March 1983

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Mt Kain
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: The companion peak to Mt Abel, 400m along the range towards Mt Annan. Conrad Kain was a prolific guide during the first decades of the twentieth century, completing more than 40 first ascents in New Zealand. Mt Kain hosts some good quality, accessible routes on Kelman Buttress. These short but steep routes provide some fun climbing and are a good place for practising skills close to Kelman Hut.

routes.name: East Ridge
routes.description: Without snow, this is probably the worst climb you could possibly do in the region. A steep and exposed scramble on awful rock. It might be okay in winter or spring with show on it. What were Clarke and Earle thinking?

routes.name: Raising Kain
routes.description: Climbs directly up the full height arete opposite Kelman Hut. First climbed in six pitches. Descend by abseiling the route, or by abseil using the fixed anchors on Zero Politics.

routes.name: Zero Politics
routes.description: The next arete right of Raising Kain terminates on a shelf at half height. Climb this arete, cross the shelf and then up the prominent corner immediately right of Raising Kain. Bolted to enable 30m abseils (Nick Cradock, 2013).
routes.ascent: Murray Ball, Nick Morgan, Reza, December 2004

routes.name: The Gift
routes.description: Climbs mixed ground in the corner system to the right of the Zero Politics buttress. Descend Zero Politics.
routes.ascent: Murray Ball, Tom Perwick, Chris Sillars, Rowan Bashford, Wouter van Beerschoten, July 2014

routes.name: West Ridge
routes.description: A straightforward ascent from the Annan-Kain col. First ascent unknown.

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Mt Nathan
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: Aiguilles Rouges and Mt Nathan from Rudolf, November 2010

routes.name: North East Ridge
routes.description: Gained at the lowest col between Mt Nathan and Aiguilles Rouges. Exposed climbing on rotten rock.

routes.name: Beetham Buttress
routes.description: Ascend the buttress staying right of the central gully, on mediocre quality rock.

routes.name: South West Ridge
routes.description: Gained from the head of the Barkley Glacier via a couloir to the col between Mt Nathan and Mt Chudleigh. Some parties have gained the Barkley via the North West Ridge of Mt Chudleigh. From here follow the ridge up loose rock to the summit. Probably the easiest descent route from Mt Nathan.

routes.name: From Bonney Glacier
routes.description: The easiest way to climb this peak is from the Bonney Glacier but ascents have been made from all directions. First ascent unknown.

routes.name: West Face
routes.description: Two routes have been climbed on this face (a rock route on the main face, and an ice route on the right side of the face above the upper Malte Brun Glacier) but details are hard to find. Any routes in the future could probably be treated as new routes.
routes.ascent: Stella Sweney, Stuart Eadie, January 1978 (rock route)

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Mt Turnbull
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: Darwin Glacier peaks and Malte Brun from the Minarets, November 2009

routes.name: From Turnbull Glacier
routes.description: Easily climbed from beside the Turnbull Glacier, but ascents have been made from all directions.

routes.name: Loganvillea
routes.description: Climbs the crest of the buttress that tops out about 300m east of the summit of Mt Turnbull. 300m of climbing on good rock.
routes.ascent: Dave Bamford, Huge Logan, Paul Maxim, January 2015

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Novara Pk North Twin
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: Lower Malte Brun Range and Murchison River flats, May 2017

routes.name: South East Ridge
routes.description: From the Murchison flats, begin at the stream 800m down valley from Burnett Stream Head up the stream to about 1200m, then climb north-east to gain the ridge, which meets the main range about 400m east of the summit.

routes.name: Twins Route
routes.description:
Originally an easy ascent from beside the Tasman Glacier or from the junction of the Tasman and Murchison valleys, but the current condition of the moraine walls would make this quite an achievement! If climbing from the Tasman, Novara is best climbed via Dorothy Stream.
From the Haupapa Tasman Glacier, travel about 500m up the true left (south) bank of Dorothy Stream until opposite a prominent rock gut on the true right, then climb up scree and light scrub to gain the ridge at the 1450m shoulder. Once on the ridge, climb up to the shelf at 1700m and then scramble to the top.

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Novara Pk South Twin
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: Lower Malte Brun Range and Murchison River flats, May 2017

routes.name: Murchison Spur
routes.description: From the Murchison flats, ascend the spur that reaches the main range at about 2080m, which involves straightforward scrambling, then continue up along the range crest to the summit.

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Petit Heap
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.access: Access is from the Reay valley.
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: Some excellent routes on great rock have been climbed on the ribs on the north side of Pt 2235m.

routes.name: So Called Arthur King

pitches.description: Climb the right side of a pink column just left of an eroded grey streak to finish at a large belay ledge.
Trend left up slabby terrain to a shallow vertical corner. A couple of strenuous moves lead to a sloping ledge at the base of the main corner.
Up the main corner to a sitting belay ledge. Pitch could be split in two if climbing on 50m ropes.
Up a short face to an arête then follow a large crack diagonally up and right.
Climb the shallow and exposed rightward-trending corner.
Up a shallow, cracked groove then follow the prow to topout on a flat ledge with fantastic views of the valley and peaks above the Grand Plateau.

routes.description:
Takes the skyline pillar (as viewed from the confluence of the Reay and Walpole Streams in the Reay Valley) via a series of corners and arêtes to the lower North West Ridge of Mt Johnson. Six or seven pitches of generally good quality rock with some exposed climbing, good protection and a really nice topout ledge before an easy-angled scramble to point 2235m.
To access the route from the upper Reay valley, continue sidling on the true right of the Reay Stream until a crossing point is reached a short way above an impressive chasm.
Descend by heading south along the Northwest Ridge to a col and then dropping down scree and easy-angled snow to the upper Reay Valley.

routes.name: Max Johnson
routes.description: Begin at the top of the scree slope beneath the most prominent buttress in the centre of the face. Traverse in from the left, aiming for the prominent 60m corner, shared with So Called Arthur King. Veer left after the corner then follow your nose to the top. Seven pitches of good rock followed by a short scramble to the summit. The first three pitches are the crux. Descend south to a prominent col, then descend the gully to the west (one abseil) to scree slopes.

routes.name: Tim Fin
routes.description: The westernmost of a series of prominent north-facing arêtes west of Pt 2235m. Two pitches up the arête on rough red sandstone, then 200m of easier climbing to the top. Easy descent down scree to the south.

routes.name: West Ridge
routes.description: Begin at the lowest point of the ridge. Follow the ridgeline via short faces of clean red rock, interspersed with some loose gullies. Routefinding choices will determine difficulty and quality of rock. Descend south to a prominent col, then descend the gully to the west (one abseil) to scree slopes. The first ascent took 12 hours.

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Rose Pk
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: Mt Hamilton, Haeckel Peak and Rose Peak from the Murchison valley, December 2016

routes.name: South East Ridge
routes.description: From the lower Dixon Glacier, ascend a snow slope leading onto the ridge, which comprises straightforward snow and rock slopes.
routes.ascent: R M Crockett, W G McClymont, F F Simmons, December 1934

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Mt Alec
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: Western aspects of Maximilian Range from Goatpath Ridge (Baird Range), January 2015

routes.name: East Face
routes.description: From Whymper Hut, follow the gully draining between Mt Wilczek and Mt Alec, then snowfields beyond Pt 1573 metres up towards the Maximilian Range.

routes.name: From Leonard Glacier
routes.description: Gain the ridge between Pt 2296m and Mt Alec, from where a short easy climb leads to the summit. The traverse of Pt 2296m is also reportedly quite pleasant.

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Mt Park
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: Callery Saddle and Glacier from the slopes of McFetrick Peak

routes.name: East Face

pitches.description:
From Whymper Hut follow the valley draining between Mt Wilczek and Mt Alec, bypassing a
steeper section by utilising easier slopes near Pt 1573 metres. Near the range, head north on snow
to access snow slopes leading to the summit from the south-east.

routes.ascent: Dave Dawe, Roger Evans (from the Leonard Glacier), January 1954

routes.name: From Callery Glacier
routes.description: A short scramble from the upper Callery Glacier. The northern and south-eastern slopes appear to offer the easiest routes. If starting via the Leonard Glacier, the upper Callery Glacier can be reached by climbing a broad snow gully north-west of Wilczek Peak. The final route of the first ascent is unknown.

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Mt Peter
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: Western aspects of Maximilian Range from Goatpath Ridge (Baird Range), January 2015

routes.name: East Face
routes.description: From Whymper Hut, follow the gully draining between Mt Wilczek and Mt Alec, then snowfields beyond Pt 1573 metres up towards the Maximilian Range. The Maximilian Range and snow slopes on it can now be followed south over Pt 2328 metres to Mt Peter.

routes.name: Traverse from Mt Alec
routes.description: Gain the ridge south of Pt 2296m, from where a short easy climb leads to Mt Alec. The first ascent party to traverse from Mt Alec to Mt Peter via Pt 2328m reported no difficulties.

routes.name: West Face
routes.description: From the Burton Glacier, climb steep slabs to reach the snowfield between Pt 2328m and Mt Peter, from where the climbing is straightforward to the summit.

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Neophyte Pk
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: Western aspects of Maximilian Range from Goatpath Ridge (Baird Range), January 2015

routes.name: Original Route
routes.description: Where New Zealand’s first great guide got his first taste of a summit. From the true left bank of the Callery River approximately 1km above the Burton confluence, pick a route onto the ridge rising from Pt 1123m to Pt 2063m, and follow this to the upper edge of the Leonard Glacier. Low angle snow slopes and a final rock scramble lead to the summit.

routes.name: From Burton Glacier
routes.description: A rock scramble from the lower Burton Glacier to the western edge of the Leonard Glacier, then as for the Original Route.
routes.ascent: D A Carty, L J Dumbleton, D J Stanton, J D Willis, 1937

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Roderick Pk
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: Named after Rod Syme by the first ascent party.

routes.name: South Ridge
routes.description: From the Burton Glacier, gain the ridge via a couloir south of Roderick (formerly the Carty Glacier), which could involve a difficult rock step near the base, depending on the season. Then ascend mixed snow and rock slopes near the ridge crest to the summit.
routes.ascent: D A Carty, L J Dumbleton, D J Stanton, J D Willis, 29 December 1937

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Wilczek Pk
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: Wilczek Peak was named by the German zoologist and mountaineer Robert Von Lendenfeld in 1884.

routes.name: From Callery Glacier
routes.description:
A short scramble from the head of the Callery Glacier. If northern slopes are bare of snow, further around to the east may offer an easier route.
The first ascent party accessed this climb from the Burton Glacier via the Leonard Glacier and a snow couloir between Wilczek and Pt 2160m.
Wilczek can also be climbed from Whymper Hut: either follow the Callery Saddle route to the snow basin east of the pass and climb to a col south of Pt 2093m to access the Callery Glacier; or climb directly to the Park-Wilczek Col.
routes.ascent: D A Carty, L J Dumbleton, D J Stanton, J D Willis, 26 December 1937

pitches.description:
From Whymper Hut, follow the gully draining between Mt Wilczek and Mt Alec, then snowfields
beyond Pt 1573 metres up towards the Maximilian Range. The pleasant rock scramble
along the South Ridge is a little longer and more challenging than that along the North West
Ridge, and leads over a subsidiary peak en route.

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Anzac Pks
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: Easy climb from the Grand Plateau.

routes.name: West Ridge
routes.description: The ridge from Cinerama Col.

routes.name: Reasonably Out the Gate
routes.description: Located above the Caroline glacier on the SW face of West Anzac Peak, follow the obvious ice line in the corner system on the right side of the face. 5 - 6 pitches of sustained ice with cruxes of WI3+/M3+. Quality rock provides protection through sections of thin ice. Cornice can form at the top of the gully but top out unobstructed.

routes.name: South Ridge
routes.description: The ridge from Boys Col, harder than the West Ridge.

routes.name: South East Face
routes.description: Mixed snow and rock from the north side of the Boys Glacier.
routes.ascent: Hugh Chambers, Peter Graham, Dorothy Theomin, Feb 1922

routes.name: Standard Route
routes.description: Climb the wide gully between the two peaks (first ascent route) or up the north east ridge from the edge of the Plateau.

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Dent Noire
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: Welcome Flat and Navigator Range peaks above the Ruera catchment

routes.name: From Lyttle Peak
routes.description: First climbed as part of a Lyttle to The Fang traverse, involving exposed rock scrambling, with limited protection in some places, and straightforward snow ridges.
routes.ascent: Stewart Bain, Maurice Conway, Walter Fowlie, Wayne McIlwraith, February 1969

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: The Fang
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: Welcome Flat and Navigator Range peaks above the Ruera catchment

routes.name: From Lyttle Glacier
routes.description: From the Lyttle Peak High Peak approach route, cross the Lyttle Glacier névé and then climb to the col between The Nick and The Fang. A snow slope and 50m of easy angled but rotten schist lead to the summit. A great viewpoint.

routes.name: Crumbling Ridge
routes.description: Beginning from a delightful tussock basin at 1000m above the Darkwater–Lyttle confluence, this route generally comprises straightforward snowgrass, rock, and snow slopes, apart from an 80m section of steep slabs around 1600m. Stay on the north-west side of the ridge above 1500m. The final summit block is best tackled by traversing around the west side to the northern slopes.
routes.ascent: Stewart Bain, Maurice Conway, Walter Fowlie, Wayne McIlwraith (descended), February 1969

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Lyttle Pk
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.access:
Architect Creek: Head up Architect Creek from just above the swing bridge, going high through the bush on the true right.  It‘s blazed with pink and orange ribbon and emerges onto the river flats just past the gorge.
Descent from the summit to Architect Creek is via the Northern slopes, staying close to the North Ridge.  At 1900m, descend the easy snow gully down to the base of the West Face.
Shiels Creek: The 1969 Bain, Conway, Fowlie and McIlwraith party accessed the snowfields below Lyttle Peak by bashing up the true left tributary of Shiels Creek and traversing around the eastern slopes of Shiels Peak. This involved six hours of scrub-bashing, but overall probably took less time than reaching the same point via the Ruera.
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: Lyttle Peak from Architect Creek, April 2014

routes.name: North Ridge
routes.description:
From one to two hours below the La Perouse Glacier terminal lake, ascend to the 1450m basin north east of Lyttle Peak and then climb up snow, tussock, and shingle slopes on the right to gain the north ridge, which is followed to the summit. The steep rock of the upper ridge is reportedly easier than it looks. Most difficulties can be avoided by using gullies on the east side of the ridge.
No recorded ascent from Architect Creek. From Whales Saddle there is a steep, unclimbed rock step on the ridge between 1600m and 1700m.
The upper part of the ridge can be accessed at 1880m via a snow gully from the head of Architect Creek (this has been descended).
routes.ascent: Dave Bamford, Phil Grover, Barry Kivell, John Nankervis, February 1979

routes.name: The Architect
routes.description: From the head of Architect Creek, ascend the slabby buttress directly beneath the high peak for 250m to meet the 200m upper face. The rock is slightly crumbly on the buttress, but good and compact on the upper face. Climb near the right edge of the upper face (crux), traverse left beneath the steep summit block, and then climb one pitch up the North Ridge to the summit.

routes.name: Low Peak from Bannister Rock
routes.description: The route of the first ascent of the 2225m low peak is unknown.
routes.ascent: Dora de Beer, Alec Graham, Louie Roberts, Tom Sheerhan, March 1931

routes.name: Traverse from High Peak
routes.description: The traverse to the low peak (2225m) appears to consist of slow travel over rock towers and steep snow.
routes.ascent: Frank Alack, Tom Christie, Marjorie Edgar Jones, Katie Gardiner, February 1934

routes.name: From Bannister Rock
routes.description: The original route is unknown, but the easiest line appears to gain the steep south-eastern snow face at the bottom left, through a break in the line of bluffs below the face. To reach this point from the Lyttle-Darkwater confluence, ascend a tussock ridge past numerous large boulders, and traverse north across the top of a prominent waterfall to gain a sloping shelf leading towards the peak.

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Mt Copland
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: The Strauchon and upper Copland valleys from Tekano Peak, December 2012

routes.name: Aurora Ridge
routes.description: This ridge affords spectacular views of the Strauchon valley. From Darkwater Saddle, follow the ridge north-east, passing rock steps using slabs and snow slopes on the west side of the ridge. The final 100m to reach the Navigator Range crest involves steep snow and usually a schrund or two, but there are a few options here. Traverse snowfields on the north side of the range to reach the summit, which is actually Pt 2331m.
routes.ascent: Dave Bamford, Phil Grover, Barry Kivell, John Nankervis, February 1979

routes.name: Gulch Face
routes.description: From a camp on the lower Gulch Glacier, the first ascent party climbed a steep shingle and snowgrass spur to reach the large snowfield below Pt 2325m, and then traversed to the summit.
routes.ascent: Alec Graham, Louie Roberts, Tom Sheerhan, February 1932

routes.name: North Ridge
routes.description: From the stream draining the Gulch Glacier, climb up through steep vegetated slopes to the 1500m shoulder on the north ridge, and then scramble up the ridge until a steep headwall is encountered at 1900m. Traverse left and up to gain the large snowfield (crux), and then pick a line to the summit.

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: The Nick
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: Welcome Flat and Navigator Range peaks above the Ruera catchment

routes.name: From Lyttle Peak
routes.description: First climbed as part of a Lyttle to The Fang traverse, involving exposed rock scrambling, with limited protection in some places, and straightforward snow ridges. It appears the first ascent party identified the peak currently mapped as Dent Noire as The Nick, and noted that the west ridge of that peak was the only section of the traverse that required the use of their piton.
routes.ascent: Stewart Bain, Maurice Conway, Walter Fowlie, Wayne McIlwraith, February 1969

routes.name: From the Cook valley
routes.description: From the 1450m basin north-east of Lyttle Peak, climb mixed snow and rock slopes to the left of the major gully leading to the Dent Noire-Lyttle Col. From the col, traverse beneath the summit block of Dent Noire on the north side, and then climb a narrow snow and scree gully which leads to the crest about 100m east of Dent Noire. Follow the crest of the Navigator Range along easy snow to The Nick.

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Shiels Pk
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: Welcome Flat and Navigator Range peaks above the Ruera catchment

routes.name: North East Ridge
routes.description: From Bannister Rock, ascend tussock and snow slopes to the Shiels-Lyttle Ridge, then traverse along a straightforward snow ridge past the 1798m col to the summit (first ascent), or take a more direct line using snow basins and scree slopes further south.

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Mt Alack
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: Despite being a relatively small peak, Mt Alack is fairly steep, with no simple way off. The easiest descent is to scramble/pitch down either the North West Ridge or South West Ridge. If this idea makes you squeamish, go as far down either ridge as you feel comfortable, then abseil down the west face to the Cleves Glacier. In winter, with two ropes, abseiling the south face on v-threads is usually the best option.

routes.name: North West Ridge
routes.description:
Reportedly very loose, but in a great setting and begins very close to Pioneer Hut.
Some gullies on the south side of the lower section of Alack’s North West Ridge provide fun ice and mixed climbing—there are many variations.
routes.ascent: Frank Alack, Harold Douglas, Bill Wilson, December 1934

routes.name: The TV Slab

pitches.description: Pitch 1: climb 40m on good rock (grade 16) to a double bolt belay.
Scramble up loose but not obnoxious rock, past one bolt. You can use this as a runner but it was primarily placed for abseiling.
The TV Crack. A 40m, grade 17 hand crack that requires some bigger natural protection (#2 to #3 Camalots). Stonking. Double-bolt abseil rings at the top. Two ropes are required for abseiling off.

routes.description:
On the left side (looking up) of the South West Ridge of Alack, above the Cleves Glacier, is a beautiful proud slab with a prominent hand crack near the top. It gained notoriety and a name when Graeme Dingle and Murray Jones climbed it for a TV crew during the 70s. Recently, Nick Cradock added a couple of bolt belays making this a must do route.
Pitch 1: climb 40m on good rock (grade 16) to a double bolt belay. Pitch 2: scramble up loose, but not obnoxious rock, past one bolt. You can use this as a runner but it was primarily placed for abseiling. Pitch 3: the TV Crack. A 40m, grade 17 hand crack that requires some bigger natural protection (#2 to #3 Camalots). Stonking. Double-bolt abseil rings at the top. Two ropes are required for abseiling off.
Graeme Dingle, Murray Jones, 1970

routes.name: South West Ridge
routes.description:
Better rock than the North West Ridge, but still loose in places. A few parties will want a rope for some short steps. If you’re tempted to descend
by abseiling the south face, remember that it’s further than it looks.
routes.ascent: Lella Davidson, Alastair Duthie, Greta Stevenson, Kurt Suter, November 1933

routes.name: Alack Attack
routes.description: A fairly direct seven-pitch line leading to the right of the summit. The first three pitches are on the icefields and the next four are on the upper wall. A good technical climb that usually involves some mixed ground.

routes.name: Southern Gully
routes.description: Six pitches of 50–60 degree ice.

routes.name: Sharp
routes.description: A steep start followed by a 50–60 degree gully for a couple of pitches. After the gully steepens and curves right, take the left branch to continue straight up, finishing near the top of Southern Gully.

routes.name: Blunt
routes.description: Shares its start with Sharp, but heads right, following a weakness over the buttress to join the upper pitches of Frank.

routes.name: Frank
routes.description: Start at the base of the gully below the Alack–Douglas col, but head left, parallel to Sharp. The upper mixed pitches provide the crux.

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Pt 2298
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: On Pioneer Ridge, 1.5km west of Pioneer Hut.

routes.name: Fintastic

pitches.description: Good natural anchors, mainly slings, wires & cams at 30m intervals.

routes.ascent: Murray Ball and Aspiring Guide's  Steep Ice Course,   Feb 2005  ( info rec'd 2/21)

routes.name: Traverse
routes.description: An easy scramble on shale-like rock leads to the summit from the south and east. From the north-west, a lightly exposed scramble leads along the Price Range. The ridge up to the Price Range from Pt 1527 metres, however, is of loose, friable schist that is steep, eroding, exposed and impractical.

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Mt Annette
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: The Sealy Range from Mt Wakefield, January 2013.

routes.name: Hoophorn Spur
routes.description: Leads to the edge of the upper Annette Plateau. Not as steep as Sebastopol Ridge at the top, but requires careful route-finding low down to avoid thick scrub. Descend via the Mueller Hut track, be prepared for a very long day. Shave up to 6 hours off the trip by going up on the true right of Hoophorn Stream from the end of the 4WD track, up until about 980m altitude. Then start walking up the scree slope between the two contributaries on the true left, between which the word "Hoophorn Stream" is printed in blue on the topomap, aiming to meet the ridge between letters "p" and "h" of the word "Hoophorn Spur" printed in black on the topomap, west of Pt 1490. Beware, this slope is prone to avalanches in winter. Once on the ridge, follow the ridge to approximately 2060m altitude, and then follow the shelf that leads straight to Mount Annette on the right.

routes.name: Sebastopol Ridge
routes.description:
This climb makes an enjoyable long day trip in summer when combined with a descent via Mueller Hut and Sealy Tarns.
Take the track to the Red Tarns, climb on an ascending sidle to the ridge south of the Sebastopol summit, and then follow the ridge crest south. There are three options at the top:

Climb diagonally left across the snow slope above Sawyer Stream to gain the edge of the Annette Plateau about 300m south of Mt Annette. Make sure you assess avalanche conditions first (II, 2).
Climb the final 150m high rock step at the top of the ridge directly (crux grade 8, II, 2+). * Climb the steep slope of snow (rock in late summer) on the right to reach the Annette Plateau north of Mt Annette (II, 2+).
The latter two options ‘are easier than they look from a distance, but offer a good opportunity to practice belaying in a spot where a rope is a genuine comfort' (Bruce Jenkinson).
routes.ascent: Freda du Faur, Peter Graham, November 1910

routes.name: From Mueller Hut
routes.description: From Mueller Hut traverse keeping about 200m below Ollivier and Kitchener and then climb gradually up onto the Annette Plateau. There are two bumps on the eastern edge of the plateau, 500m apart. Mt Annette is the southern one.

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Mt Darby
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: Mt Jean, Mt Jeanette (partly obscured) and Mt Darby from upper Sladden Glacier, July 2011

routes.name: East Flank
routes.description: Follow the snow slope to the ridge east of the summit.

routes.name: North Ridge
routes.description: This ridge can be reached at almost any point, but the best is probably the small col around 2390m. Rock scrambling on a blocky ridge leads to the summit.
routes.ascent: Freda Du Faur, Peter Graham, November 1910

routes.name: North West Flank
routes.description: From Barron Saddle via the Williams Glacier. Climb the rib up the middle of the face.

routes.name: West Ridge
routes.description: Gain the ridge from the true left edge of the Williams Glacier. Exposed rock scrambling, similar in difficulty to the North Ridge.

routes.name: Bengal
routes.description:
Access to the south face of Mt Darby is easy, descend from Barron Saddle,
then follow a gully up to the snow slopes beneath the face. Bengal is a 300m
rock route at grade 12 which begins in the centre of the face on the right
hand side of the black gully, crosses left through the gully to gain the left
tending corner. Follow the broad ramp which leads to the summit.

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Mt Jean
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: Mt Jean, Mt Jeanette (partly obscured) and Mt Darby from upper Sladden Glacier, July 2011

routes.name: North West Face
routes.description: A short climb on snow or rock depending on the season.
routes.ascent: W Fisher, Maughan, M Sloman, Conrad Kain, December 1914

routes.name: Vanity Fare
routes.description:
The route begins at the centre of the south face, and goes up through bulges
to the main gully. The gully exits 70 metres left of the summit, but when
well up a smaller gully breaks right and finishes on the summit. Close to
1000m of vertical height gain, of which 600 m are steep.

routes.name: North East Face
routes.description: Interesting mixed snow and/or rock scrambling. A number of routes are possible – please add details for specific lines.

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Mt Jeanette
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: Mt Jean, Mt Jeanette (partly obscured) and Mt Darby from upper Sladden Glacier, July 2011

routes.name: Please Keep Your Seats
routes.description:
The Dobson face has been ascended in a bold summer climb. Approach the climb
from the right hand side by angling up the face to gain the rock. About ten
pitches of steady climbing on fractured rock with the crux on the last pitch
at grade 15.

routes.name: Various Routes
routes.description: From snow slopes above the true left of the Sladden Glacier, choose from a variety of short climbs up to technical grade 2+.

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Mt Kitchener
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: The Sealy Range from Mt Wakefield, January 2013.

routes.name: Watertank Ridge
routes.description: Starts directly from the watertanks above the Hermitage, accessed via the Glencoe track. There’s some light scrub to push through low down, and later a few sections of exposed scrambling. The step 100m below the top is climbed using a right-to-left ledge system. Descend via Mueller Hut and Sealy Tarns. A great day out.

routes.name: From Mueller Hut
routes.description: Up easy rock from the slopes behind Mueller Hut. There are numerous variations. Take care if cloud comes in while you’re out – the hut is harder to find when descending than you think. The ridge from Ollivier to Kitchener has some very exposed sections, but is not technically difficult.

routes.name: Various Routes
routes.description: Choose from a variety of short climbs on snow and/or rock up to technical grade 2+ above the Sladden Glacier, depending on the aspect and season.

routes.name: Birdland
routes.description:
Ascend the south spur by an excellent rock rib, gain height on snow then
climb two challenging rock pitches. Easy snow fields lead to the summit tower
and five zig zag pitches up snow and ice to the summit.

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Mt Massey
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: Sealy Range

routes.name: From Mettelille & Sladden Glaciers

pitches.description: Routes may be found almost anywhere up either the North Face from the Metelille Glacier or the short South Face from the Sladden Glacier. Rock buttresses further down the South Face should give good rock climbing.

routes.description: Routes may be found almost anywhere up either the north-east face from the Metelille Glacier or the short south-west face from the Sladden Glacier. Rock buttresses further down the south-west face should give good rock climbing.

routes.name: Pink Bits
routes.description: A three-pitch route up the steepest rock in the middle of the face ‘above Sladden Saddle’ has been climbed on ‘good, pink greywacke,’ but the exact location of the route is unknown. Reported to be on Mt Marie but more likely on Mt Massey.
routes.ascent: Louis Braddock, Russell Braddock, Greg Low, Julie Robinson, 2006

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Mt Sealy
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: Sealy Range from Sefton Biv, May 2010

routes.name: East Ridge
routes.description: From the Metelille Glacier climb steep snow to the col between the low and high peaks, or traverse to the col from the low peak. This is Barrow Col, marked incorrectly on topo maps. Follow rotten rock to the summit.
routes.ascent: Jack Clarke, C L Barrow, Edward FitzGerald, Mattias Zurbriggen (possibly), January 1895

routes.name: North Face Couloir
routes.description: A steep couloir leading almost directly to the summit. A ‘couloir and chimney’ somewhere on the face were climbed by O Bainbridge, Jack Clarke and W Tennant in March 1903.

routes.name: North West Ridge
routes.description: Exposed rock scrambling with a steep step or two. Sometimes reached from Sladden Saddle, but usually gained via the couloirs on the north or west faces.

routes.name: West Face
routes.description:
This is the standard ascent and descent route on Mt Sealy but is suffering heavily from loss of permanent snow and ice. After midsummer the route comprises loose rock and steep, hard snow slopes, increasing the grade. Winter, spring and early summer are the best times.
Ascend to Sladden Saddle, circle round the back of the peak, head up the 150m moderately angled face, and then either:

follow the top of the rotten north-west ridge over a short step; or
traverse right across a shelf to gain easier-angled snow and rock slopes (the preferred route if conditions allow).
routes.ascent: Peter Graham, Mr & Mrs L H Lindon, B Spencer, W Fisher (descended), January 1911

routes.name: North Face
routes.description: The rock face ‘to the right of the couloir’. The exact location of this route is uncertain.
routes.ascent: Freda Du Faur, Peter Graham, December 1909

places.name: South Face
places.description: The South Face of Mt Sealy, at the head of the Dobson Valley, is steep and broken.

routes.name: Ice Gangsters

pitches.description: Generally classic grade 4 climbing.

routes.description:
The major gully on the left side of the face tops out on the Sladden Glacier
just below the final summit pyramid. The majority of the route is 50–60º
with three short 80º sections plus the final mixed step to the glacier. A
direct finish up the summit headwall via a corner system would be possible,
instead of going left, if the corner is iced up. More detail at
http://jamievintonboot.wordpress.com/2012/07/30/ice-gangsters-south-face-of-mt-sealy/

routes.name: Prime Time
routes.description:
This route follows the rock buttress up the centre of the south face, passes
right of the snow field on the face and finishes 50m east of the summit.
Initial steep pitches on sound rock, are followed by an easier section at mid
level moving left before the buttress steepens again and provides constant
resistance.

routes.name: Hello Darkness
routes.description:
The route ascends the obvious snow/ice gully on the right side of the south
face, heading directly to the low point between the summit and the east peak.
About 650m high, the route complements the earlier completed route Prime
Time, further left on the face.

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Mt Sealy Low Pk
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: Sealy Range from Sefton Biv, May 2010

routes.name: From Metelille Glacier
routes.description: From the head of the glacier this is a straightforward snow climb which provides a terrific view from the summit.

routes.name: South East Ridge
routes.description: The long ridge connecting Mt Edgar Thomson with Mt Sealy provides exposed steep scrambling, but is very loose in places. Some parties have loved it; others not so much! This route has also been known as the Hoophorn Ridge – just don't confuse it with Hoophorn Spur. Descend to the Metelille Glacier.

routes.name: North Ridge
routes.description: From the 2428m col at the head of the Metelille Glacier (incorrectly labelled Barrow Col on Topo50 maps), follow a series of steep rotten steps to the summit.
routes.ascent: C L Barrow, Jack Clarke, Edward FitzGerald, Mattias Zurbriggen (possibly), January 1895

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: Mt Sebastopol
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.access: The easiest approach is via Red Tarns
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: It's thought that Glenthorne shepards may have climbed Mt Sebastopol early in the 1800s, no doubt looking for wayward merinos. - Aoraki Tai Poutini, Rob Frost.

routes.name: Traverse
routes.description: An east–west traverse of Sebastopol provides accessible scrambling but with some loose sections.

routes.name: North Buttress

pitches.description: Climb good easy rock to a shrubby ledge.
Follow the ridge to a prominent ledge with a large boulder to use as a belay station.
Climb two small towers and arrive at an obvious headwall with little options for anchors.
Climb a steep section with loose rocks and little pro and either pull directly over the crux (14) or siddle around to the climbers right. Climb some more, stopping right before a narrow flat section.
Climb easy terrain with a couple of fun options until you reach a prominent rock above a small ledge to set up the next belay.
Follow a narrow flat section to a prominent wall for easy climbing (10) and ascend until you see easy shrubby terrain.
Scramble up shrubs and rocks to the summit.

routes.description: The prominent rib seen from Red Tarns

routes.name: From Horace Walker névé
routes.description: A straightforward snow climb. The highest point in the area west of Scott Peak.
routes.ascent: Peter Graham, R B Seagar, March 1918

routes.name: From Wicks Col
routes.description: ‘An easy scramble up to the final 15 or 20 feet which was a steep rectangular rock which we had to climb barefoot,’ according to the first ascentionists.
routes.ascent: Christopher Johnson, Graham Riley, Archie Scott, January 1936

routes.name: From Horace Walker névé
routes.description: A straightforward snow climb, with some rock scrambling in late summer.
routes.ascent: Frank Alack, Tom Christie, H G Courtenay, 1935

routes.name: From the Callery River
routes.description: ‘An uninspiring but steep snow plod,’ according to the first ascentionists.
routes.ascent: Barbara Chinn, Trevor Chinn, Noel Read, December 1962

routes.name: Wigley Glacier Route
routes.description:
From the upper Gunn River, head up tussock slopes towards a buttressed spur on the true left of the stream draining the Wigley Glacier. A steep but negotiable gully (requiring scrambling on bedrock), about 100 metres before the Wigley River issues from a slit gorge, leads through bluffs to rocky knolls above and gravel flats further up the valley. Lower ice shown on the map below 1600 metres has now largely gone.
From BW16 858 909, gain access to the upper Wigley Glacier via a diagonal ledge that doesn’t look promising from below on the true right of the icefall. This gravel ledge leads easily up beside the icefall to where the ice and upper glacier can be accessed. Crevasses may make this more difficult with ice recession and later in summer. From the upper glacier, snow slopes lead to the ridge and the peak is a bit beyond that.

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.name: McFetrick Pk
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki-tai-.description: Probably named after Alex and Hughie McFetterich, who farmed Tartare Flat. Sometimes traversed en route to or from the head of the Callery River.

routes.name: West Ridge
routes.description: Appears to be a straightforward snow ridge traverse from Mt Downe.
routes.ascent: Jack Cox, Marjorie Edgar Jones, C Parfitt, February 1936

routes.name: From Tatare Saddle
routes.description: Straightforward snow and gravel slopes via Panorama Rocks (Pt 2001m). An excellent viewpoint. The first ascentionists were dropped off by ski plane near Tatare Saddle. Barbara Chinn, Trevor Chinn and Noel Read climbed via the saddle from the Callery valley in December 1962.
routes.ascent: D E Cooper, H Leonard, DR Lowe, M Lucas, R Watts, December 1959

routes.name: North West Ridge
routes.description:
From about the 1300m contour in the upper Gunn River, head north-west up moraine, then scree and snow slopes, to the crest of the range. Easy travel along the range leads to the summit.
To continue to the Callery, follow the range south over normally easy schrunds to Tartare Saddle. A steep spur at I35 912509 / BX16 812 893 can be used to descend to the valley, where the Callery River is normally easily crossed below the lake. Traversing around the lake is really only practical on the true left.
Frank Pearson, Alan Gill, and Gordon Howitt used this route to exit the Callery via the Gunn River and Price Range at Easter 1964.
routes.ascent: Frank Pearson, Alan Gill, Gordon Howitt, March 1964

routes.name: Via Middleton Snowfield
routes.description: An easy ascent from the Middleton Snowfield, accessed from the head of the Tatare valley. The snowfield can also the gained more strenuously from Franz Joesph township via the bush route over Cole Spur (route 9K, grade II, 2+).
routes.ascent: Jack Cox, Marjorie Edgar Jones, C Parfitt, February 1936

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki/fox-.name: Big Mac
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki/fox-.description: A tricky little number. Before you get any ideas, this name first appeared on maps in 1929. It was not named after a burger.

routes.name: South East Ridge

pitches.description: From the col between Big Mac and Le Receveur.

routes.ascent: Frank Alack, H K Douglas, W E Wilson, Dec 1934.

routes.name: Mistaken Identity

pitches.description: Climb the buttress overlooking the Fox Névé. An abseil may be required to get off.

routes.ascent: Dave McLeod, Tim Morrison, Rob Hughes, Mar 1983.

routes.name: Castries Glacier route
routes.description: Gain the Castries Glacier to the west of the peak, and then up via easy snow slopes and a steep punch in the guts rock pitch near the summit.
routes.ascent: Frank Alack, G C Arras, D Mackie, Feb 1932.

pitches.description: A beautiful snow arête from Katies Col, however schrunds may prove difficult late in the season.

routes.name: North West Face
routes.description: From the Monk Glacier, climb a couloir/gully to the summit. First climbed from the Murchison valley via Abbey Pass. In 1953 C S Brockett and party climbed the ridge from Pinnacle Stream.
routes.ascent: J Milne, Harold Porter, Jim Rose, January 1925

routes.name: South East Ridge
routes.description: Follow ramps west of the ridge base to gain a wide chimney. Continue on good rock and loose ledges up the ridge, deviating west as required. Climb 4 pitches of 13-15 through a large pyramid shaped slab at c2000m trending east till a traverse on the east side ends at a col behind the pyramid with a good bivvy ledge. Follow the west side of the ridge till it turns west and the glacier is reached. Climb exposed grade 13-15 on good rock then gain summit via loose slopes and the ridge from the south. Straightforward descent off the NW face. A long fun route on mostly good rock. Around 10 pitches.

routes.name: From Mona Glacier
routes.description: From the Hooker Glacier ascend the Mona Glacier onto either the north face or north-east (divide) ridge, which both involve a short scramble up the summit block.

routes.name: North West Spur
routes.description: Climbs good rock to two-thirds height, after which the rock quality deteriorates such that it’s ‘verging on a bit dangerous’. Tops out at the point where the West Ridge eases. Follow the West Ridge to the summit.

routes.name: The Shaft (West Face)
routes.description: A 12 pitch climb involving some fun, but often poorly protected, mixed climbing. Climb the gully immediately right of the north-west spur, which involves some WI3 ice, then veer right as you gain height with some easy mixed climbing for a few pitches. The main snow gully was avoided on the first ascent due to soft conditions. Traverse across a thin mixed pitch to reach the base of ‘The Shaft’, which is an obvious 50m ice runnel above the main snow gully, capped by a vertical bulging chimney. This is the crux of the route. Above the ‘Shaft’, climb up then left to reach a final mixed gully, topping out where the West Ridge eases. Follow the West Ridge to the summit.

routes.name: West Ridge
routes.description: An eye-catching line. Access the base of the ridge from the Mona Glacier, then stay on the crest all the way to the summit. The rock is good lower down, but deteriorates towards the top.
routes.ascent: Freda Du Faur, Peter Graham, December 1912

routes.name: Left Gully
routes.description: The prominent gully on the left side of the south face. Climb a short section of 60 degree ice, then ascend the right-trending gully on moderately steep snow.

routes.name: Central Rib
routes.description: A mixed climb that begins up the middle of the prominent rib. Climb this until it flattens off and meets the central gully (JM Goes Tramping) then tend slightly right to gain the rib on the upper part of the face, which leads straight up to the summit.

routes.name: JM Goes Tramping
routes.description:
The central ice gully which tops out high on the West Ridge.
Named after the climber absconded from an Otago University Tramping Club trip over Ball Pass to link up solo ascents of Turner and Pibrac.

routes.name: South Ridge
routes.description: Access Proud Pass either from the Mona Glacier (by skirting beneath the West Ridge), or over Turner Peak. From Proud Pass, an exposed scramble leads to the summit. The small peak between Proud Pass and the summit can be avoided if necessary, by sidling on the west side and then climbing a 40 degree gully.

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki/mt-c.name: Mt Wakefield
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/aoraki/mt-c.description:
Mt Wakefield has been described as the focal point of Aoraki / Mount Cook National Park, and it certainly feels that way when you take in the view from the summit on a fine day.
A fast descent alternative to the south ridge in dry conditions is a scree slope from 1550m that drops directly to the valley floor. There are a number of glued moraine esque gullies that drop onto it, but the one at 1550m is the most mellow. There is also a large boulder at the top of the ~20m gully that a rope could be looped over to allow a rap onto the scree directly, but this should be executed with care to avoid rockfall, and certainly not during or after rain. See topo for entry point.

routes.name: Routeless Guide
routes.description:
The most direct line to Mt Wakefield’s summit. From the viewpoint at the end of the Hooker valley track, access the nearest scree fan descending from Mt Wakefield (the second large scree fan on the east side of the Hooker valley). Start on a compact sandstone staircase on the true right of the scree (grade 10–12), then follow a broken ridge to the cliff bands, which are the crux of the climb. Trend right from the flat col at the top of the ridge on superb weathered greywacke to behind the obvious pink notch on the right edge of the cliff bands. This bypasses the cliffs via another sandstone staircase (crux) to finish on easier ground and gullies to the summit.
Numerous direct lines through the cliff bands exist with rock quality varying between take-home-with-you and excellent, with adequate protection available with cams 0.5-2. See topo for bypass route and variations.

routes.name: Guideless Buttress
routes.description:
Also known as the Ranger Route, this 800m route was first climbed by local DOC staff in the summer of 2013 and offers some of the finest alpine scrambling near the village: enjoyable rock with some fantastic views and exposure. A fun and challenging day trip.
From the viewpoint at the end of the Hooker valley track, access the nearest scree fan descending from Mt Wakefield (the second large scree fan on the east side of the Hooker valley). Climb the buttress on the true left of the scree. Either start directly up the base of the buttress, which is steep and scrubby, or head further right and follow up a stream that gains the crest of the buttress at about 1250m. Negotiate multiple towers and gendarmes to where the buttress eases off to lower angle rubble and the broad upper basins of Mt Wakefield, exiting just under the radio towers at 2000m. A more challenging direct start (grade 18–19) has been climbed higher up the scree (Lewis Ainsworth, 2018).
routes.ascent: Sam Bamford, Rod Barker, Erin Hawke, Marcus Reid, February 2013

routes.name: Wakefield Gullies
routes.description:
A number of gullies on both sides of the South West Ridge have been climbed when filled with snow and ice. Details about these routes are scarce – please add more information if you have it:

The first major scree fan in the East Hooker is one of these, known as the Winter Western Gully.
The gullies just past the second swing bridge have been climbed, including one by Joe Friend and Colin Monteath in 1972 known as the Gully of a Thin Man.
The gully that begins at the large scree downstream of the second swingbridge, on the south side of the South West Ridge, is called Bad Obsession.
The right-hand variant (looking up) to the Bad Obsession gully is called Psych Ward.
These latter gullies are also used as (bold!) ski lines. They encounter steep terrain at about 1700m, which could be unclimbed as it’s possible to abort by traversing either right or left.

routes.name: South West Ridge (Guides Route)
routes.description:
This ridge was used as a training climb for guides in the early 1900s.There are several variations on the lower part of this ridge.
From the true left end of the second swingbridge of the Hooker valley track, turn off onto a faint ground trail on the true left of the valley  and begin climbing  anywhere from near the second swingbridge as far as the first really large scree slope on the east side of the Hooker valley, near the third swingbridge. (The second scree up valley from the second swingbridge seems to lead to the most pleasing line.) Some great pockets of solid red rock can be found, but the main challenge is avoiding the scrub. Higher up, the overall angle eases, but the rock quality deteriorates. The variations converge just below a small cheval around 1680m. The upper ridge merges into a series of basins and spurs south of the summit. Descend via the South Ridge.
routes.ascent: Probably Otto Frind, Conrad Kain, January 1914

routes.name: The Old Man and the Scree
routes.description: This route is accessed from the first swingbridge on the Hooker valley track, along an old track that follows down the true left bank of the Hooker River. Visible from the village is a prominent scree slope and a series of buttresses leading to the ridge between Pt 1827m and Pt 1566m. Ascend the scree then aim for the left side of the buttress that separates a large hidden gully from the main scree. Climb slabs immediately right of a big corner and finish up the chimney. Two 60m pitches (grade 15), sparse protection, and loose rock. Walk off the back. According to Trev, it’s a ‘pretty worthless route for the effort to get there.’

routes.name: South Ridge
routes.description: This is an excellent day or overnight trip, with panoramic views. From the Tasman valley road bridge over the Hooker River, climb up the vegetated spur that eventually leads over scree and boulder fields to the summit. The true summit is a long way beyond the highest point that you can see from the village. Navigation on the upper ridge can be difficult in cloudy conditions. Descend the same way.

routes.name: From Mueller Hut
routes.description: Up easy rock from the slopes behind Mueller Hut. There are numerous variations. Take care if cloud comes in while you’re out – the hut is harder to find when descending than you think.

routes.name: From Wicks Col
routes.description: A straightforward ridge traverse. Good skiing on the Horace Walker névé.
routes.ascent: Christopher Johnson, Scott Russell, Archie Scott, January 1935

routes.name: From Lucy Walker Pass
routes.description: Moderately steep snow leads between rock bluffs in early summer. Without much snow the bluffs would probably involve some straightforward rock climbing. There is huge exposure from this ridge over the south-east face. The Johnson et al party probably descended this ridge before the first ascent.
routes.ascent: Frank Alack, Tom Christie, H G Courtenay, 1935

routes.name: From Pilkington Glacier or Horace Walker névé
routes.description: A straightforward snow climb, with some rock scrambling in late summer. An amazing ski descent off the Pilkington Glacier can be ridden all the way to the snowline to connect with the Conical Hill ridge and a potential exit to the Karangarua.

routes.name: From Douglas névé
routes.description: Mostly a straightforward snow climb, with some rock scrambling, which is more sustained in late summer. Good short steep skiing lines.

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/arthurs-pas.name: Mt Franklin
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/arthurs-pas.description: A very imposing pinnacle of rock. On many occasions it still manages to pierce the notorious West Coast cloud (something of a redeeming quality). It is by far the best climb east of Arthur’s Pass.

routes.name: North Ridge
routes.description: From the Good Luck Creek basin, ascend to and cross over Pt 1652m on the West Ridge, descending to the 1560m contour at the head of the unnamed stream below the northwestern slopes of Mt Franklin. From here sidle scree slopes in a northeasterly direction, aiming for the low point on the ridge between Mt Franklin and Pt 1806m. The ridge is mostly good rock scrambling (up to Grade 10) with moderate exposure to about three-quarters height. Here the ridge steepens with two 40–50m pitches of Grade 12, with one short section up to Grade 14 (although it may be possible to avoid this). The summit is a further 100m of about Grade 10 scrambling.

routes.name: West Ridge
routes.description: Approach from Good Luck Creek basin via the Deception River route or alternatively via the densely wooded spur that leaves the Deception River at K33 974151, on the true left of the stream that drains the Franklin-Russell escarpment. This ridge is notoriously long and loose, and has multiple gendarmes. Once committed to this route there are no escape routes, however travel tends to be fast over large sections. Considered a mid spring climb when ice clings to it. The ridge can be dangerously corniced under winter conditions, making it extremely hard to negotiate. Descend by the south ridge.

routes.name: South Ridge
routes.description: Reach the Good Luck Creek basin, and Lake Anna, by ascending the scree slide upstream of Upper Deception Hut to the scrub line and then sidling at the 1400–1500m contour into the head of the creek. Above Lake Anna, gain the col at 1890m and traverse slabby rock and shattered pinnacles. If good snow ramps exist this section can be bypassed by climbing a snow lead and short couloir further left under the South Ridge. The South Ridge rises steeply to merge with the West Ridge. An excellent route. The upper ridge can be dangerously corniced under winter conditions, making it extremely hard to negotiate.
routes.ascent: A C Snowden, A S Ahnfeldt, November 1930

routes.name: South West Ridge
routes.description:
A long climb. From opposite Goat Pass Hut utilise the obvious deep gully and notch to gain the ridge. The initial ridge to Pt 1975m point is generally straightforward. Not far past this point a significant notch in the ridge requires a short, steep and exposed down-climb on the Deception side, and several gendarmes must be negotiated on the ridge to reach the Lake Anna col and the South Ridge.
Descend the South Ridge and Good Luck Creek route via Lake Anna.

routes.name: South West Ridge Couloirs
routes.description: This route can be climbed in winter to late spring by reaching the head of the Deception River from Goat Pass Hut. Scree or snow slopes head through the lower bluff to reach the steep snowfield (avalanche danger!) below Pt 1975m on the South West Ridge. In a normal season three 150m couloirs gain the South West Ridge. Continue along the South West Ridge and South Ridge to the summit. Return via Lake Anna and the Good Luck Creek basin route.

routes.name: Mt Oates-Mt Franklin Ridge
routes.description: This ridge is a very long journey from Goat Pass and would be better tackled from a camp near Lake Mavis. Gain the ridge along the Main Range above the lake, following its initially broad back to the second knoll (1864m). From here the ridge narrows, taking a steep approach to the summit of the next buttress (1876m). The ridge turns west over the exposed slabs above Lake Sally and the deep gut of the upper Deception, climbing steeply over broken ground to join the South West Ridge. From here descend to the col above Lake Anna then climb the steep South Ridge to the summit. Be well prepared for a forced bivvy as it is a very long day’s outing!

places.name: From Lake Sally
places.access: Lake Sally is at best difficult to approach. Access is from the Otehake River West Branch, either by the ridge and loose, bush-covered slopes south of the stream which drains the lake, or alternatively by ascending slopes on the north side of the same stream and sidling around the base of the East Ridge to reach the lake.
places.description: There are several routes on the eastern aspects of Mt Franklin. A high camp at Lake Sally is strongly recommended, under the knoll near its outflow. Under winter conditions the routes can all be fraught by overhanging cornices. Eastern descents from Mt Franklin tend to be very steep but natural anchors are available to abseil directly onto the snowfield.

routes.name: Way Down Sally
routes.description:
Take the narrow couloir that starts on the right-hand side of the main
buttress in the centre of the South East Face. Ascend 3 pitches to the
snowfield at mid-height. Trend left up the snow field for 1 pitch to the rock
rib. Follow the gully to the right of this onto the upper snowfields. Eight
pitches in total. Join the South Ridge (8.7) approximately 75m to the SW of
the summit. Descend via the South Ridge.

routes.name: Sally Can’t Dance
routes.description:
2 pitches of WI 3 ice lead to a snow couloir, which widens and joins the main ridge 30m south of the summit. Descent made via east ridge and upper east ridge snow fields requiring one abseil.
To the R of the French/Wright line Way down Sally.

routes.name: East Ridge
routes.description:
The steep, jagged East Ridge merges into the East Face of the mountain.
Traverse northwards to gain the steep gullies ascending to the summit.

routes.name: Upper East Snowfield Couloirs
routes.description:
From the permanent snowfield north of the East Ridge, three very steep
couloirs gain the summit directly. These all tend to provide better climbs
during the frozen winter months.

routes.name: North East Ridge
routes.description:
From the Lake Sally outlet, head north and sidle under the North East
Ridge’s southern flank, climbing the first possible gully to its crest. The
ridge is followed cautiously to the summit.

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/arthurs-pas.name: Mt Russel
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/arthurs-pas.description: tba

pitches.description: Approached via the heavily wooded spur that ascends from the Deception River. This spur is on the true-right of the stream that drains the amphitheatre under its summit. Very ugly best describes this route

routes.name: East Face (The Last Bush Ranger)
routes.description:
Aim for the northern corner at the base of the east face and scramble low angle slabs to the bottom of a gut between Mt Russel and its north east outlier. Climb left out of the gut to gain broader slabs and trend straight up, passing a small overlap on the left via a slab with thin moves (first crux). Ascend more easy slabs to where the rock steepens before trending right via a vague ledge system and the second crux before the angle eases off again. Ascend the remaining slabs directly to the summit. Crux sections around Ewbank grade 12-13 with the remainder of the route mostly grade 10. Generally sufficient protection but you have to work to find it.
Descend Mt Russel via the west ridge to approximately halfway between Mt Russel and pt1689 to low point on the ridge. Descend south via scree and ledges back to scree field south west of Mt Russel.
Access: Best approached via the Good Luck Creek route out of the Deception River. Cross Mt Franklin west ridge at accessible low points, then under or on the Aicken Range towards Mt Russel.

pitches.description: Approached from the lower Deception Valley by ascending Midday Creek and its slide. Bear south towards the saddle above Spray Creek and then onto Mt Russell via one very exposed section of rotten ridgeline.

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/arthurs-pas.name: Mt Tarapuhi
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/arthurs-pas.description: tba

pitches.description: Approached from the lower Deception Valley by ascending Midday Creek and its slide. Once clear of the scrub, continue climbing towards Tarapuhi,a very difficult/horrendous route. From the saddle above Spray Creek a short, very steep, pitch can be climbed on the Otehake side towards Mt Tarapuhi.
Gain Waharoa saddle via Paruta stream before traversing the tops.  The final 1km ridge has several sharp, exposed sections making for an exciting winter climb or a straight forward summer scramble.

routes.name: Warnocks Bluff

pitches.description: Climbed from the Otira Valley. Where the foot-bridge crosses the Otira River (about halfway up the valley) follow a vague track that crosses the vegetated moraine wall high on the true left. It then zigzags up the scree slide that leads to the base of the bluffs separating Warnocks Knob from Philistine’s East Ridge. Connecting ramps and gullies, find a path through the bluffs, giving access to the easier slopes above. In winter these bluffs are extremely dangerous when covered in loose snow or ice. An alternative route through the bluffs follows a stepped creek found further to the north, though this has similar winter problems. Above the bluffs continue following the ridge, staying true left of the east ridge buttress, then climbing snow slopes to join the saddle adjacent the Rolleston Glacier. The loose main ridge is easily climbed from here.

routes.ascent: A P Harper and M Dixon, 9 November 1891

pitches.description: Climbable via the giant gully that rises steeply for 1100 metres from the Rolleston River track (1.5km upstream of the railway bridge). This gut can be threatened by rock or ice fall in almost any season, and is invariably a very steep ice/loose scree climb for the final 200 metres to the col between Mt Philstine and its northwest summit (1780m). Warnocks Knob should be used as the preferred descent route.

From the head of the Rolleston River, climb via a steep, narrow couloir. This leaves the river via initial scree (K33 885121) and proceeds into a narrow rock gut for 200m before opening out to onto another scree slope. Keep the adjacent rock on the true left. Towards the top ascend diagonal rock gullies to join the west ridge on to the summit. Post winter route when avalanche risk is low.

places.name: Philistine Bluffs
places.description:
Difficult direct face routes or ice gully climbs are present from the Upper Otira Valley by way of the Philistine Bluffs. The most popular of these is the Philistine Ramp, which follows an avalanche chute to the southwest corner of the Rolleston Glacier. Most other routes top out under the East Ridge buttress or the Rolleston Glacier icefall. From the névé of the Rolleston Glacier, routes can also be chosen that follow steep snow slopes or loose rock ribs to join the Philistine-Rolleston ridge.
Use Warnock’s Bluff Route or the Philistine Ramp Route (to the left) for descent.

pitches.description: Only in conditon late spring early summer due to build up of avalanche debris. Follwow obvious avalanche chute towards SW corner of Rolleston Gl. Some seasons the headwall can be vertical ice. An alternative rock route climbs through the gullies and slabs on the true right of the ravine.

Ice only.
3rd avalanche gut upstream from the bridge.
Rock or Ice. 2nd avalanche gully above the bridge

Rock or Ice.
Starts on slope betwwen the first two avalanche gullies above bridge.

Rock only. Start directly under a 60deg crack system that runs into the wall on to East Ridge of Philistine. Climb vertically to the left of the crack for 25m on poor pro to intersect parallel 60deg crack, avoiding moss & water. Continue climbing crack untila small terrace is reached. Break left onto a broad, less steep facemoving upwards to a gut theat tops out onto screes under the East Ridge.

(Rock or ice).   Follow faint buttress line diagonally right through mixed ground for 5 pitches, traverse left at a short wall and up a short couloir to climb steep ice covered slabs and then head diagonally right over exposed mixed ground to a short 4m wall ( extremely loose rock), climb delicately over this to reach steep snow at first and then onto the main snowfield below Mt Philistine. Return via route H

Ice Only.
Climb Scree from bridge towards the massive boulder at its head. The route climbs the 45deg RH ramp for 50m, then up steep buttress rock to meet a sweeping RH couloir. After 40m this leads into a less steep  gully for a further 150m climbing parallel to a wall on the true R. The head breaks out onto the avalanche slopes underneath the East Ridge of Philistine.

Ice Only.
From bridge follow normal Warnock’s Bluff route, however stay in large scree gully.
The obvious gully that runs across to the left as you look up is met at the head of the  scree. 2 ½ easy pitches gain a small saddle followed by a traverse into a steeper snow field. The gully line is picked up, more steeply to join the broad ridge above.

routes.name: Double Blind Route
routes.description:
Access as for Waterfall Route but veer left towards two obvious ice flows.
Climb the right one and continue straight up on steep ice towards the
slightly overhanging rock face. Follow good ice on the right hand side of the
rock face to easing snow slopes. 3 pitches. Good climbing with easy access.
Potential for other variations here exists.
routes.ascent: Ben Ellis and Sarwan Chand, August 2016

pitches.description: Easy climb by the scree slide which runs from the valley floor to the main ridge 600m upstream of the hut.

routes.name: Via Avalanche Peak Track or Scotts Track

pitches.description: From Arthur's Pass village, Avalanche Peak can be reached from two directions, either by the Avalanche Peak Track (begins opposite the Public Shelter), or Scotts Track (begins opposite Devils Punchbowl Creek). Both are easy ascents. WARNING: Do not attempt to cross the basins above Avalanche Creek or Rough Creek if there is deep snow. The avalanche danger in both these basins is extreme.

A very long day outing from Carroll Hut. You must firstly climb Kellys Hill, descending steeply to the saddle on the Bald Range, and then follow a series of terraces to avoid the numerous buttresses on the ridgeback. There are steep ascents on slabby rock as the final approach to the summit is made. The track leading to the Taipo River is overgrown.

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/arthurs-pas.name: Anderson Pk
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/arthurs-pas.description: Waimakariri

pitches.description: A long climb that can be done by fit parties in a day from Otira. Follow the Rolleston River Route to where it leaves the scrub and crosses the river. Climb west, to the spur separating the Rolleston River from the stream draining Lake Florence, and sidle towards the saddle above Lake Florence.
From Mt Barron via the Barron Range takes a good day along a ridgeback that is a minefield of loose rock.
From Mt Armstrong, descend to the col above Lake Florence and continue on to the peak.

routes.name: From Waimakariri Col

pitches.description: A short snow climb from Waimakariri Col. A traverse to, and descent off, Carrington Peak can also be achieved. The icecap of Mt Armstrong can be quite unstable at times, as can the glacier descending on to Waimakariri Col.

routes.ascent: H R Reid, A Anderson, January 1928

pitches.description: A long climb that can be done by fit parties in a day from Otira. Follow the Rolleston River Route to where it leaves the scrub and crosses the river. Climb west to the spur separating the Rolleston River from the stream draining Lake Florence, and continue up to the summit. The icecap of Mt Armstrong can be quite unstable at times.

routes.name: South East Spur
routes.description: At the head of the Rolleston River make your way up through the rock buttress on the true-left of the river to gain access to the Southeast Spur, from here follow a line of good rock that takes you up to the 2010m point of the east ridge. The East Ridge can be followed all the way to the summit of Mt Armstrong. Starting as a broad ridge at 2010m, the east ridge progressively narrows until it involves climbing around some loose pinnacles of rock with a decent amount of exposure on both sides, before broadening out again just before the summit.

routes.name: East Face
routes.description: From the head of the Rolleston River sidle north across the scree slopes on the true-left of the river to access the east face of Mt Armstrong. Towards the northeast corner of the face a large rock toe protrudes onto the scree and can be used as a starting point to climb up the face towards point 2010m directly above. The climb takes place on a mixture of good, solid rock and loose scree/rotten rock. Halfway up the face is a short but steep rock step that must be climbed. Once point 2010m is reached, follow the East Ridge all the way to the summit.

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/arthurs-pas.name: Mt Avoca
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/arthurs-pas.description: tba

pitches.description: Mt Avoca can be reached via Mt Greenlaw using the very jagged joining ridge.

Pick a route on scree through steep rock and bluffs, initially making a rising traverse to the
north-west, to reach the glacier north-east of the summit of Mt Avoca. From here gain the
North East Ridge and climb loose rock to the top.

About 4 km from Weka-Burnett Bivouac take a prominent scree gully south of Pt 1598 metres.
From the head of the scree traverse north to avoid bluffs and aim for the base of a broad ramp
leading to the summit. Scramble over the last steep loose rock to the top. This route is tricky
when there is no consolidated snow.

https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/arthurs-pas.name: Mt Greenlaw
https://climbnz.org.nz/nz/si/arthurs-pas.description: Lying just outside the national park boundaries, Mt Greenlaw is a sought-after peak, being the second highest in the area (after Mt Murchison) and has a reputation as a challenging climb. The North East Face is the standard route to the summit, whether approaching from the Waimakariri or Avoca Rivers.

routes.name: From Anti Crow River

pitches.description: Mt Greenlaw is the best climb from the head of the Anti Crow River. The usual route crosses Gizeh Col and descends to the upper Avoca Valley, then ascends the bluffs to the Avoca Glacier and the North East Face route. A longer, more varied route crosses Fools Col to Avoca Col, then follows a broken ridge to Greenlaw Col. From the col, either continue along the North Ridge, or traverse the snowfield and climb the North East Face.

routes.ascent: G Doig, K Coad, R G Logan, December 1934

pitches.description: Gain the Avoca Glacier as for the North East Face route. The north ridge can be reached from the glacier at various points and followed to the summit, but this is a loose, jagged and time-consuming option.
